# Preface

In our era of big data and the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, innovation and progress are often driven by harnessing the power of vast amounts of data. Yet, privacy concerns and data protection regulations have placed limitations on traditional centralized approaches to machine learning: While data are abundant, they often exist in small and isolated silos. The need for collaborative and privacy-preserving approaches to machine learning has therefore become more crucial than ever.

In this context, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as the de facto framework for distributed machine learning (ML) that preserves the privacy of data, especially in the proliferation of mobile and edge devices with their increasing capacity for storage and computation. To fully utilize the vast amount of geographically distributed, diverse, and privately owned data that is stored across these devices, FL provides a platform on which local devices can build their own local models whose training processes can be synchronized via sharing differential parameter updates. This was done without exposing their private training data, which helps mitigate the risk of privacy violation, in light of recent policies such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Such potential use of FL has since then led to explosive attention from the ML community, resulting in a vast, growing amount of both theoretical and empirical literature that pushes FL closer to being the new standard of ML as a democratized data analytic service.

Interestingly, as FL comes closer to being deployable in real-world scenarios, it also surfaces a growing set of challenges on trustworthiness, fairness, scalability, robustness, security, privacy preservation, decentralizability, and personalizability which are all becoming increasingly important in many interrelated aspects of our digitized society. Such challenges are particularly important in economic landscapes that do not have the presence of big tech corporations with big data and are instead driven by government agencies and institutions with valuable data locked up or small-to-medium enterprises, and start-ups with limited data and funding.

To develop a practical federated learning system that embraces the aforementioned challenges, multiple diverse disciplines are needed, ranging from traditional studies on distributed, decentralized optimization, cryptography, and security to more contemporary topics such as privacy-preserving, fairness, robustness, and personalizability in machine learning, many of which are relatively new and widely scattered across a sheer, growing volume of research papers. This might pose a challenge for a graduate student or a new researcher in the field who needs to get familiar with all these relevant literature and have a big picture of how the field is being developed. To ease this hassle, we have been seeking help from our colleagues who are experts in this field to compose a comprehensive introduction material, providing the fundamentals with fine details while introducing a representative collection of forefront, cutting-edge research, as well as a wide range of practical applications.

The idea of this book came from our recent workshop in New Frontiers of Federated Learning, in the NeurIPS-21 conference, which helped connect us to other colleagues in this field. Many of them provided valuable contributions and feedback to the development of this book. It comprises a series of technical discourses targeting graduate students at all levels as well as researchers who are interested in the field of Federated Learning. The main content is structured in three parts. Part 1 features a detailed exposition of optimization fundamentals (see Chapter [1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml) in particular) and core challenges in secure federated learning, spanning numerous security issues and their algorithmic solutions. In Part 2, the book discusses emerging challenges stemming from many socially driven concerns of Federated Learning as a future public machine learning service. Finally, to bridge the gap between academic and industrial research on the topic, Part 3 explores a wide array of industrial applications of FL as well as ethical considerations, showing its immense potential in driving innovation while safeguarding sensitive data.

We hope this book will serve as a valuable resource to those who seek a streamlined pathway to acquire the fundamentals of Federated Learning. It aims to provide an insightful exposition of a representative set of rigorous results on the foremost frontier of this field, while not delving into hyper-rigorous and exhaustive indexing of the entire domain. Our intention is for this book to serve as a good primer for a beginner in his or her quest to explore this field.

Part 1: Optimization fundamentals for secure federated learning

# Chapter 1: Gradient descent-type methods

Background and simple unified convergence analysis

Quoc Tran-Dinh^([a](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#aff0010)); Marten van Dijk^([b](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#aff0015),[c](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#aff0020))    ^aDepartment of Statistics and Operations Research, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, NC, United States  
^bCWI, Amsterdam, Netherlands  
^cVU University Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands

## Abstract

In this book chapter, we briefly describe the main components that constitute the gradient descent method and its accelerated and stochastic variants. We aim at explaining these components from a mathematical point of view, including theoretical and practical aspects, but at an elementary level. We will focus on basic variants of the gradient descent method and then extend our view to recent variants, especially variance-reduced stochastic gradient schemes (SGD). Our approach relies on revealing the structures presented inside the problem and the assumptions imposed on the objective function. Our convergence analysis unifies several known results and relies on a general, but elementary recursive expression. We have illustrated this analysis on several common schemes.

### Keywords

Gradient descent method; Stochastic gradient method; Convex and nonconvex optimization; Convergence guarantees; Complexity estimates

## 1.1 Introduction

The core problem in many optimization applications such as signal and image processing, engineering, operations research, statistics, and machine learning is the following optimization problem, see, e.g., [\[1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0005),[2](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0010),[7](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0035),[27](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0135),[28](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0140),[49](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0245),[60\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0300):

$\\min\\limits\_{w \\in \\mathbb{R}^{p}}F(w),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si1.png)(1.1) 

where *F* : ℝ^(*p*) → ℝ ∪ { + ∞}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si2.png) is a given objective or loss function, and *w* is a vector of decision variables (also called model parameters). Depending on the form or structures of *F*, we obtain different classes of optimization problems. For instance, the following structures are common in practice:

*   •  **Nonsmooth convex optimization.** If *F* is *M*\-Lipschitz continuous (i.e., there exists *M* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si3.png) such that |*F*(*w*) − *F*(*w*^′)| ≤ *M*∥*w* − *w*^′∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si4.png) for all *w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si5.png)) and convex, but often nonsmooth, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called a nonsmooth convex minimization. Note that the *M*\-Lipschitz continuity is often imposed for nonsmooth functions such as *F*(*w*) :  = ∥*w*∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si6.png) for any norm, or for special smooth functions, e.g., the objective function $F(w): = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}\\log(1 + \\exp(y\_{i}X\_{i}^{\\top}w))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si7.png) of a logistic regression, where (*X*[*i*], *y*[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si8.png) is given for *i* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si9.png). Obviously, the Lipschitz continuity also holds if we consider *F* to be continuous on a given compact set 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png).
*   •  **Smooth and convex optimization.** If *F* is *L*\-smooth (i.e., there exists *L* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si11.png) such that ∥∇*F*(*w*) − ∇*F*(*w*^′)∥ ≤ *L*∥*w* − *w*^′∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si12.png) for all *w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si5.png)) and convex, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called a smooth and convex minimization. Examples of *L*\-smooth and convex functions are vast. For example, a least-squares function $F(w): = \\frac{1}{2}{\\| X^{\\top}w - y\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si13.png) for a given data matrix *X* and an output vector *y* is *L*\-smooth with *L* :  = ∥*X**X*^⊤∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si14.png). The logistic regression function above is also convex and *L*\-smooth with $L: = \\frac{1}{4}\\| XX^{\\top}\\|$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si15.png). However, exponential functions such as $F(w): = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}\\exp(X\_{i}^{\\top}w)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si16.png) or logarithmic functions such as $F(w): = - \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}\\log(X\_{i}^{\\top}w)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si17.png) are convex, but not *L*\-smooth on their domain, unless we limit their domain on a given compact set, see, e.g., [\[64\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0320).
*   •  **Smooth and nonconvex optimization.** If *F* is *L*\-smooth and nonconvex, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called a smooth and nonconvex minimization. The *L*\-smoothness is a key condition required in most gradient-based methods for nonconvex optimization. Again, this assumption obviously holds if we assume that *F* is continuously differentiable and then limit the domain of *F* to a compact set. But there exist *L*\-smooth functions on the entire space ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si18.png). For instance, $F(w): = \\frac{1}{2}w^{\\top}Qw + q^{\\top}w$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si19.png) for given symmetric matrix *Q* and *q* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si20.png) is *L*\-smooth with *L* :  = ∥*Q*∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si21.png), but not necessarily convex.
*   •  **Composite optimization.** If *F*(*w*) :  = *f*(*w*) + *g*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si22.png), where *f* is usually *L*\-smooth and convex/nonconvex, and *g* is convex and possibly nonsmooth, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called an \[additive\] composite minimization. This model is ubiquitous in machine learning and statistical learning, where *f* presents a loss function or a data fidelity term, while *g* is a regularizer or a penalty term to promote solution structures or to handle constraints. Examples can be found, e.g., in [\[10](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0050),[52\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0260). If *g*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si23.png) is the indicator of a convex set 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png) as *g*(*w*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si24.png) if *w* ∈ 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si25.png), and *g*(*w*) =  + ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si26.png), otherwise, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) covers the constrained problem min[*w* ∈ 𝒲]*f*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si27.png).
*   •  **Finite-sum optimization.** If $F(w): = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}F\_{i}(w)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si28.png) for some *n* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si29.png), then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called a finite-sum minimization, an empirical risk minimization, or a distributed optimization depending on the context. This structure is presented in most supervised learning tasks, network and distributed optimization, and federated learning. The most interesting case is when *n* ≫ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si30.png).
*   •  **Stochastic optimization.** If *F*(*w*) :  = 𝔼\[**F**(*w*, *ξ*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si31.png), the expectation of a stochastic function **F** : ℝ^(*p*) × *Ω* → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si32.png), where (*Ω*, *Σ*, ℙ)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si33.png) is a given probability space, then [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is called a stochastic program [\[34](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0170),[43](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0215),[59\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0295). This setting also covers the finite-sum as a special case by setting *Ω* :  = {1, …, *n*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si34.png) and $\\mathbb{P}(\\xi = i) = \\frac{1}{n}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si35.png).

Apart from these individual settings, many other combinations between them are also possible; we do not list all of these here. For example, the combination of a composite structure and finite-sum is very common.

*Existence of solutions*  We first assume that *F*^⋆ :  = inf[*w*]*F*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si36.png) is bounded from below, i.e., *F*^⋆ >  − ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si37.png) to guarantee the well-definedness of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1). Many machine learning applications automatically satisfy this condition since the underlying loss function is usually nonnegative. One obvious example is the least-squares problem.

Our next question is: *Does* [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) *have an optimal solution?* To discuss this aspect, we use a coercivity concept from nonlinear analysis [\[18\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0090). We say that *F* is coercive if lim[∥*w*∥ → ∞]*F*(*w*) =  + ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si38.png). A common coercive function is $F(w): = \\mathcal{L}(w) + \\frac{\\lambda}{2}{\\| w\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si39.png), where ℒ![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si40.png) is *M*\-Lipschitz continuous (but not necessarily convex) and *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si41.png). If *F* is continuous and coercive, then by the well-known Weierstrass theorem, [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) has global optimal solutions *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png). In this case, we denote *F*^⋆ :  = *F*(*w*^⋆)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si43.png), its optimal value. If *F* is nonconvex and differentiable, then we use *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) to denote its stationary points, i.e., ∇*F*(*w*^⋆) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si44.png). If *F* is not differentiable, a generalization of stationary points is required [\[40\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0200). To keep it simple, we assume throughout this chapter that *F* is continuously differentiable.

If *F* is strongly convex, then it is continuous and coercive and [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) has a unique global optimal solution. For convex problems, our goal is to find an approximate global solution *ŵ*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si45.png) of *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) in some sense (see Section [1.2.7](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#s0065)). For nonconvex problems, we only expect to compute an approximate stationary point *ŵ*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si45.png), which can be a candidate for a local minimizer. However, we do not attempt to check if it is an approximate local minimizer or not in this chapter.

*Contribution*  Our contribution can be summarized as follows. We provide a comprehensive discussion for the main components of the gradient descent method and its variants, including stochastic schemes. We also propose a unified and simple approach to analyze convergence rates of these algorithms, and demonstrate it through concrete schemes. This approach can perhaps be extended to analyzing other algorithms, which are not covered in this chapter. We also discuss some enhanced implementation aspects of the basic algorithms.

*Outline*  The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. Section [1.2](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#s0030) reviews basic components of gradient methods. Section [1.3](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#s0085) focuses on stochastic gradient methods, while Section [1.4](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#s0105) makes some concluding remarks and raises a few possible research directions.

## 1.2 Basic components of GD-type methods

The gradient descent (GD) method is an iterative method aimed at finding an approximate solution of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1). This dates back to the works of Cauchy in the 19th century, and has been intensively studied in numerical analysis, including optimization for many decades. During the last two decades, there has been a great surge in first-order methods, especially gradient-type algorithms, due to applications in signal and image processing, modern statistics, and machine learning. In this chapter, we do not attempt to review the literature of GD-type methods, but only focus on summarizing their basic components.

Formally, the gradient descent algorithm starts from a given initial point *w*⁰ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si47.png) and, at each iteration *t* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si48.png), it updates

*w*^(*t* + 1) :  = 𝒫(*w*^(*t*) + *η*[*t*]*d*^(*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si49.png)(1.2) 

where *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) is the current iterate, *η*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si51.png) is called a step-size or learning rate, *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) is called a search direction, and 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si53.png) is an operator to handle constraints or regularizers; if this is not needed, one can set 𝒫 = 𝕀![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si54.png), the identity operator. This method generates a sequence of iterate vectors {*w*^(*t*)}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si55.png) using only first-order information of *F* (e.g., function values, proximal operators, or \[sub\]gradients). Here, we add an operator 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si53.png), which can also be used to handle constraints, regularizers, penalty, or Bregman distance (e.g., mapping between the primal and dual spaces). Let us discuss each component of the scheme [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2).

### 1.2.1 Search direction

The most important component in [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) is the search direction *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png), which determines the type of algorithm such as first-order, second-order, quasi-Newton-type, or stochastic methods. Let us consider the following possibilities:

*   •  **Descent direction.** Assuming *F* is continuously differentiable, a search direction *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) is called a descent direction at the iterate *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) if ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ < 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si56.png). We can even impose a stronger condition, called a direction of strict descent, which is ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ ≤  − *c*∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si57.png) for some *c* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si58.png). The name “descent” comes from the fact that if we move from *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) along the direction *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) with an appropriate stepsize *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png), then we have a descent, i.e., *F*(*w*^(*t* + 1)) < *F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si60.png). If 𝒫 = 𝕀![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si54.png), the identity operator, then [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) reduces to *w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) + *η*[*t*]*d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si61.png). By Taylor's expansion of *F*, we have

*F*(*w*^(*t* + 1)) = *F*(*w*^(*t*)) + *η*[*t*]⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ + *o*(*η*[*t*]²∥*d*^(*t*)∥²) < *F*(*w*^(*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si62.png)

*   for sufficiently small *η*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si51.png) due to ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ < 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si56.png).
*   •  **Steepest descent direction.** If we take *d*^(*t*) :  =  − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si63.png), then [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) becomes

*w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) − *η*[*t*]∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si64.png)(1.3) 

*   and we have ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ =  − ∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥² < 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si65.png) provided that *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) is not a stationary point of *F*. With this choice of *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png), we obtain a gradient descent or the so-called steepest descent method. It actually realizes the largest decrease of *F* at *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) as ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ ≥  − ∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si66.png) for any *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) such that ∥*d*^(*t*)∥ = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si67.png).
*   •  **Stochastic gradient direction.** If we choose *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) to be a stochastic estimator of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png), then we obtain a stochastic approximation (also called stochastic gradient descent) method. A stochastic gradient direction is generally not a descent one, i.e., ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *d*^(*t*)⟩ ≮ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si69.png). Examples of stochastic estimators include standard unbiased estimator *v*^(*t*) :  = ∇**F**(*w*^(*t*), *ξ*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si70.png) and its mini-batch version $v^{t}: = \\frac{1}{|\\mathcal{S}\_{t}|}\\sum\_{\\xi \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{t}}\\nabla\\mathbf{F}(w^{t},\\xi)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si71.png) for a minibatch 𝒮[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si72.png), and various variance-reduced estimators, see, e.g., [\[13](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0065),[29](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0145),[48](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0240),[58](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0290),[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330).
*   •  **Newton and quasi-Newton direction.** We can go beyond gradient-based methods by incorporating second-order information, or curvature of *F*, as *d*^(*t*) :  =  − *B*[*t*]^( − 1)∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si73.png), where *B*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si74.png) is a given symmetric and invertible matrix. For instance, if *B*[*t*] :  = ∇²*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si75.png), then we obtain a Newton method, while if *B*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si74.png) is an approximation to ∇²*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si76.png), then we obtain a quasi-Newton method.
*   •  **Inexact descent direction.** If we do not evaluate the gradient ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png) exactly, but allow some error as *d*^(*t*) =  − (∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) + *δ*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si77.png) for some Gaussian noise *δ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si78.png), then we obtain an inexact or noisy gradient method [\[24\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0120). Another example is called a sign gradient method, which uses *d*^(*t*) =  − *s**i**g**n*(∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si79.png), the sign of gradient, see, e.g., [\[41\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0205). Inexact Newton-type methods compute *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) by approximately solving *B*[*t*]*d*^(*t*) =  − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si80.png) such that ∥*B*[*t*]*d*^(*t*) + ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥ ≤ *c*∥*d*^(*t*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si81.png) for *c* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si58.png).

Apart from the above examples, other methods such as \[block\]-coordinate, incremental gradient, Frank–Wolfe or conditional gradient, proximal-point, prox-linear, Gauss–Newton, extragradient, optimistic gradient, and operator splitting techniques can also be written in the form [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) by formulating appropriate search directions *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png). For instance, the proximal point method can be viewed as the gradient method applied to its Moreau's envelope, see, e.g., [\[56\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0280).

### 1.2.2 Step-size

The second important component of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) is the step-size *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png). In machine learning community, this quantity is called a *learning rate*. Choosing an appropriate *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png) is a crucial step that affects the performance of the algorithm. Classical optimization techniques have proposed several strategies, which are known as globalization strategies, including (i) line-search and its variants, (ii) trust-region, and (iii) filter [\[11](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0055),[23](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0115),[49\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0245). Line-search and trust-region strategies have been widely used in numerical optimization, see [\[11](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0055),[49\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0245). In recent optimization algorithms and machine learning training tasks, we often observe the following techniques:

*   •  **Constant learning rate.** Constant learning rates are usually used to derive convergence rates or complexity bounds due to their simplicity. The algorithm often performs well with a constant learning rate if the problem is “easy”, e.g., strongly convex and *L*\-smooth, but it becomes poor if the landscape of *F* is complex such as in deep neural networks. Usually, theoretical analysis gives us a range (i.e., an interval like $\\left( 0,\\frac{2}{L} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si82.png) in standard gradient methods) to choose a constant learning rate. However, this range could easily be underestimated by using global parameters, and does not capture the desired region of optimal solutions. In practice, nevertheless, we need to tune this learning rate using different strategies such as grid search or bisection, etc.
*   •  **Diminishing learning rate.** Diminishing learning rates are usually used in subgradient or stochastic gradient methods. One common diminishing learning rate is $\\eta\_{t}: = \\frac{C}{{(t + \\beta)}^{\\nu}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si83.png) for some positive constant *C*, a shifting factor *β*, and an order *ν* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si84.png). Depending on the structure assumptions of *F*, we can choose appropriate order *ν*, e.g., $\\nu: = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si85.png) or $\\nu: = \\frac{1}{3}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si86.png). Another possibility is to choose $\\eta\_{t}: = \\frac{C}{{(\\lceil t/s\\rceil + \\beta)}^{\\nu}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si87.png) for an additional integer *s* to maintain fixed learning rate in each *s* iterations. In stochastic gradient methods, diminishing learning rates are often required if the variance of *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) is nondecreasing (i.e., *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) is not computed from a variance-reduced estimator of ∇*F*). A diminishing learning rate also determines the convergence rate of the underlying algorithm.
*   •  **Scheduled learning rate.** In practice, we often use a schedule to tune an appropriate learning rate so that we can achieve the best performance. Different ideas have been proposed such as using exponential decay rate, cosine annealing, or even with a varying mini-batch size, see, e.g., [\[37](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0185),[62\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0310).
*   •  **Adaptive learning rate.** The above strategies of learning rate selection do not take into account the local geometry of the objective function. They may perform poorly on “hard” problems. This motivates the use of adaptive learning rates which exploit local landscape or curvature of the objective function. The first common strategy is line-search, which \[approximately\] solves min[*η* > 0]*F*(*w*^(*t*) + *η**d*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si88.png) to find *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png). If *F* is quadratic, then we can compute *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png) exactly by solving this one-variable minimization problem. However, most algorithms use inexact line-search such as bisection or golden ratio search. Another strategy is using a Barzilai–Borwein step-size, e.g., *η*[*t*] :  = ∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1)∥/∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t* − 1))∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si89.png), which gives an estimate of $\\frac{1}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si90.png). (Here, *L* is the Lipschitz constant of ∇*F*.)
*   Recently, several adaptive methods have been proposed, see, e.g., [\[12](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0060),[17](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0085),[32\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0160). The underlying learning rate is usually given by $\\eta\_{t}: = C/\\sqrt{\\sum\_{j = 0}^{t}{\\| g\_{j}\\|}^{2} + \\epsilon}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si91.png), where *g*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si92.png) is some gradient estimator at iteration *j*, *C* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si93.png) is given, and *ϵ* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si94.png) is a small constant to avoid division by zero and provides numerical stability.

Among the above strategies and tricks for selecting learning rates, one can also compute them in different ways when solving a specific problem, even using a “trial-and-error” method or a combination of the above techniques. The main goal is to tune a good learning rate for such a problem, but still guarantee the convergence of the underlying algorithm.

### 1.2.3 Proximal operator

Many problems covered by [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) have constraints or nonsmooth objective terms. For example, we may have *F*(*w*) = *f*(*w*) + *g*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si95.png), where *g* is nonsmooth. In this case, we cannot use the full gradient of *F*. One way to handle the nonsmooth term *g* is to use proximal operators, and in particular, use the projections if we have simple constraints. Mathematically, the proximal operator of a proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex (or more generallly, a prox-regular) function *g* is defined as

${prox}\_{\\gamma g}(w): = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{z \\in \\mathbb{R}^{p}}\\left\\{ \\gamma g(z) + \\frac{1}{2}{\\| z - w\\|}^{2} \\right\\},\\quad\\gamma > 0.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si96.png)(1.4) 

Note that under appropriate choices of *γ*, the minimization problem in [(1.4)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq5) is strongly convex, and hence has a unique solution, leading to the well-definedness of *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si97.png). If *g* = *δ*[𝒲]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si98.png) is the indicator function of a closed and convex set 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png), i.e., *δ*[𝒲](*w*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si99.png) if *w* ∈ 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si25.png), and *δ*[𝒲](*w*) =  + ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si100.png), otherwise, then *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si97.png) reduces to the projection onto 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png), i.e., ${proj}\_{\\mathcal{W}}(w): = \\arg\\min\_{z \\in \\mathcal{W}}\\frac{1}{2}{\\| z - w\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si101.png). In terms of computation, evaluating *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si97.png) is generally as hard as solving a \[strongly\] convex problem. There are at least three ways of evaluating *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si102.png):

*   •  **Separable functions.** The most obvious case is when *g* is component-wise separable as $g(w): = \\sum\_{j = 1}^{p}g\_{j}(w\_{j})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si103.png) (e.g., *g*(*w*) :  = ∥*w*∥[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si104.png)), then evaluating *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si97.png) requires solving *p* one-variable strongly convex minimization problems, which can be done in a closed form. This idea can be extended to block separable functions, e.g., $g(w): = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\| w\_{\\lbrack i\\rbrack}\\|}\_{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si105.png), where {*w*[\[*i*\]]}[*i* = 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si106.png) are subvectors.
*   •  **Dual approach.** Moreau's identity *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*](*w*) = *w* − *γ* ⋅ *p**r**o**x*[*g*^(\*)/*γ*](*w*/*γ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si107.png) suggests that we can compute *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si97.png) from its Fenchel conjugate *g*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si108.png). Since many convex functions have simple conjugates such as norms (e.g., *g*(*w*) = ∥*w*∥[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si109.png)) or Lipschitz continuous functions, this approach is more tractable.
*   •  **Optimality approach.** If *g* is differentiable, then we can directly use its optimality condition ∇*g*(*z*) + *γ*^( − 1)(*z* − *w*) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si110.png), and solve it as a nonlinear equation in *z*. Examples include  − log det (*X*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si111.png) and $\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}\\log(1 + \\exp(y\_{i}X\_{i}^{\\top}w))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si112.png).

Note that the second and third techniques are only used for convex functions, while the first one can be used for nonconvex functions. The number of convex functions *g* where *p**r**o**x*[*γ**g*]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si102.png) can be computed efficiently is vast, see, e.g., [\[1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0005),[51\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0255) for more examples and computational techniques.

### 1.2.4 Momentum

One way to explain the role of momentum is to use a dynamical system of the form $\\overset{¨}{w}(\\tau) + \\psi(\\tau)\\overset{˙}{w}(\\tau) + \\nabla F(w(\\tau)) = 0$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si113.png) rooted from Newton's second law, where $\\psi(\\tau)\\overset{˙}{w}(\\tau)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si114.png) presents a friction or a damping factor. If we discretize this differential equation using $\\overset{¨}{w}(\\tau) \\approx (w^{t + 1} - 2w^{t} + w^{t - 1})/h\_{t}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si115.png) and $\\overset{˙}{w}(\\tau) \\approx (w^{t} - w^{t - 1})/h\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si116.png), then we obtain (*w*[*t* + 1] − 2*w*[*t*] + *w*[*t* − 1])/*h*[*t*]² + *ψ*[*t*](*w*[*t*] − *w*[*t* − 1])/*h*[*t*] + ∇*F*(*w*[*t*]) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si117.png), leading to *w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) − *h*[*t*]²∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) + (1 − *h*[*t*]*ψ*[*t*])(*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si118.png), see, e.g., [\[61\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0305). Therefore, we can specify momentum variants of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) when 𝒫 = 𝕀![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si54.png) (the identity operator) as follows:

*w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) + *η*[*t*]*d*^(*t*) + *β*[*t*](*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si119.png)(1.5) 

where *β*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si120.png) is a momentum step-size. The search direction *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) can be evaluated at *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png), leading to a so-called heavy ball method [\[54\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0270). Alternatively, if *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) is evaluated at an intermediate point, e.g., *z*^(*t*) :  = *w*^(*t*) + *β*[*t*](*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si121.png), then we obtain Nesterov's accelerated scheme in the convex case [\[44\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0220). This scheme can be written into two steps as

*z*^(*t*) :  = *w*^(*t*) + *β*[*t*](*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1)) and *w*^(*k* + 1) :  = *z*^(*t*) + *η*[*t*]*d*(*z*^(*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si122.png)(1.6) 

where *d*(*z*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si123.png) presents the direction *d*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si52.png) evaluated at *z*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si124.png) instead of *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png). Note that momentum terms do not significantly add computational costs on top of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2). Yet, they can accelerate the algorithm in convex cases [\[44](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0220),[46\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0230) (see also Section [1.2.8](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#s0070)), and possibly in some nonconvex settings, see, e.g., [\[35](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0175),[63\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0315).

### 1.2.5 Dual averaging variant

The scheme [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) can be viewed as a forward update, but in convex optimization, dual averaging schemes are also closely related to [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2). Unlike [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2), a dual averaging scheme works as follows. Starting from *w*⁰ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si47.png), for *t* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si48.png), we update

$w^{t + 1}: = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{w}\\left\\{ \\sum\\limits\_{j = 0}^{t}\\gamma\_{j}\\langle g^{j},w\\rangle + \\frac{1}{2\\eta\_{t}}{\\| w - w^{0}\\|}^{2} \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si125.png)(1.7) 

where *g*^(*j*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si126.png) are given dual directions (e.g., *g*^(*j*) :  = ∇*F*(*w*^(*j*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si127.png)), *γ*[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si128.png) are the weights of *g*^(*j*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si126.png), and *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png) is a given dual step-size. In general settings, we can replace $\\frac{1}{2}{\\| w - w^{0}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si129.png) by a general Bregman distance 𝒟(*w*, *w*⁰)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si130.png). If the norm is the Euclidean norm, then we have $w^{t + 1}: = w^{0} - \\eta\_{t}\\sum\_{j = 0}^{t}\\gamma\_{j}g^{j}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si131.png). If *η*[*t*] = *η* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si132.png) is fixed and we choose *g*^(*j*) :  = ∇*F*(*w*^(*j*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si127.png), then we have $w^{t + 1} = w^{0} - \\eta\\sum\_{j = 0}^{t}\\gamma\_{j}g^{j} = w^{0} - \\eta\\sum\_{j = 0}^{t - 1}\\gamma\_{j}g^{j} - \\eta\\gamma\_{t}g^{t} = w^{t} - \\eta\\gamma\_{t}g^{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si133.png), which is exactly covered by [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2). Therefore, for the Euclidean norm $\\frac{1}{2}{\\| w - w^{0}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si129.png), the dual averaging scheme [(1.7)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq8) is identical to the gradient descent scheme *w*^(*t* + 1) = *w*^(*t*) − *η**γ*[*t*]*g*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si134.png). However, under a non-Euclidean norm or a Bregman distance, these methods are different from each other.

### 1.2.6 Structure assumptions

One main theoretical task when designing a gradient-based algorithm is to establish its convergence. From a computational perspective, estimating the convergence rate, as well as complexity, is also critically important. However, to establish these, we require *F* to satisfy a set of assumptions. The following structures are commonly used in optimization modeling and algorithms:

*   •  **Lipschitz continuity.** Function *F* in [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is said to be *M*\-Lipschitz continuous if

|*F*(*w*) − *F*(*w*^′)| ≤ *M*∥*w* − *w*^′∥, ∀*w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si135.png)(1.8) 

*   Examples of Lipschitz continuous functions include norms, smoothed approximation of norms (e.g., $F(w): = \\sum\_{i = 1}^{p}{(w\_{j}^{2} + \\epsilon^{2})}^{1/2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si136.png) for a small *ϵ*), or continuous functions with a bounded domain. Note that when *F* is convex, *M*\-Lipschitz continuity is equivalent to *M*\-bounded \[sub\]gradient, i.e., ∥∇*F*(*w*)∥ ≤ *M*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si137.png) for all *w* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si138.png). This assumption is usually used in subgradient-type or stochastic gradient-type methods.
*   •  *L***\-smoothness.** Function *F* is called *L*\-smooth if the gradient ∇*F* of *F* satisfies

∥∇*F*(*w*) − ∇*F*(*w*^′)∥ ≤ *L*∥*w* − *w*^′∥, ∀*w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si139.png)(1.9) 

*   If *w*, *w*^′ ∈ 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si140.png) for a compact domain 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png) and *F* is continuously differentiable, then *F* is *L*\-smooth on 𝒲![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si10.png). This concept can be extended to an *L*\-average smoothness in the finite-sum or stochastic settings. For instance, if $F(w): = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}F\_{i}(w)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si28.png), then we can modify [(1.9)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq10) as $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}{\\|\\nabla F\_{i}(w) - \\nabla F\_{i}(w^{\\prime})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant L^{2}{\\| w - w^{\\prime}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si141.png) for all *w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si5.png). Alternatively, if *F*(*w*) :  = 𝔼\[**F**(*w*, *ξ*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si31.png), then we can use 𝔼\[∥∇**F**(*w*) − ∇**F**(*w*^′)∥²|*w*, *w*^′\] ≤ *L*²∥*w* − *w*^′∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si142.png) for all *w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si5.png). These assumptions are usually used in variance-reduction SGD methods, see, e.g., [\[52](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0260),[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330). Note that other extensions are possible, see, e.g., [\[34\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0170). Verifying the *L*\-smoothness is generally not straightforward. However, if $F(w): = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}\\ell\_{i}(X\_{i}^{\\top}w - y\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si143.png) as, e.g., in a generalized linear model, then we can verify the *L*\-smoothness of *F* by verifying the *L*\-smoothness of each one-variable function ℓ[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si144.png). This model is ubiquitous in machine learning.
*   One key property of [(1.9)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq10) is the following bound:

$|F(w^{\\prime}) - F(w) - \\langle\\nabla F(w),w^{\\prime} - w\\rangle| \\leqslant \\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{\\prime} - w\\|}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si145.png)(1.10) 

*   which shows that *F* can be globally upper bounded by a convex quadratic function and globally lower bounded by a concave quadratic function. If, additionally, *F* is convex, then stronger bounds as well as the co-coerciveness of ∇*F* can be obtained, see, e.g., [\[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225). One can also extend the *L*\-smoothness of *F* to a Hölder smoothness as ∥∇*F*(*w*) − ∇*F*(*w*^′)∥ ≤ *L*∥*w* − *w*^′∥^(*ν*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si146.png) for some 0 ≤ *ν* ≤ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si147.png). This concept unifies both the *L*\-smoothness (*ν* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si148.png)) and the bounded gradient (*ν* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si149.png)) conditions. It has been used in universal first-order methods for both deterministic and stochastic methods, e.g., [\[47\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0235).
*   •  **Convexity.** Function *F* is said to be *μ*\-\[strongly\] convex if

$F(\\widehat{w}) \\geqslant F(w) + \\langle\\nabla F(w),\\widehat{w} - w\\rangle + \\frac{\\mu}{2}{\\|\\widehat{w} - w\\|}^{2},\\quad\\forall w,\\widehat{w} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{p}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si150.png)(1.11) 

*   Here, ∇*F*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si151.png) can be a gradient or a subgradient of *F* at *w*. This inequality shows that *F* can be lower bounded by either a linear (*μ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si152.png)) or a quadratic approximation (*μ* ≠ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si153.png)). If *μ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si152.png), then *F* is just convex or merely convex. If *μ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si154.png), then *F* is strongly convex, and *μ* is called the strong convexity parameter. If *μ* < 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si155.png), then *F* is called weakly convex. Convexity and strong convexity are key concepts in convex analysis, optimization, and related fields, see, e.g., [\[7](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0035),[57\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0285), and we do not further discuss them here.

These are three key and also basic assumptions to analyze the convergence of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) and its variants. Nevertheless, other assumptions can also be exploited. For example, the following conditions are commonly used in different methods:

*   •  **Gradient dominance and PL condition.** Function *F* is called *σ*\-gradient dominant if *F*(*w*) − *F*(*w*^⋆) ≤ *σ*∥∇*F*(*w*)∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si156.png) for all *w* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si138.png) and *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) is a minimizer of *F*. Clearly, if *F* is strongly convex, then it is gradient dominant. However, there exist nonconvex functions that are gradient dominant. Note that one can consider local gradient dominance by limiting *w* in a neighborhood of *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png). We can also extend this concept to different variants. The gradient dominance condition allows us to obtain a convergence guarantee on the objective residual *F*(*ŵ*) − *F*(*w*^⋆)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si157.png) even in the nonconvex setting. Note that this condition is also called Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. These conditions can be used to establish linear convergence or linear-like convergence rates (i.e., linear converge to a small neighborhood of an optimal solution) [\[30](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0150),[52\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0260). 
*   •  **Uniform convexity and star-convexity.** Function *F* is said to be *μ*\-Hölder uniformly convex of order *ν* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si158.png) if $F(w^{\\prime}) \\geqslant F(w) + \\langle\\nabla F(w),w^{\\prime} - w\\rangle + \\frac{\\mu}{\\nu}{\\| w^{\\prime} - w\\|}^{\\nu}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si159.png) for all *w*, *w*^′ ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si5.png), see, e.g., [\[68\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0340). Clearly, if *ν* = 2![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si160.png), then we obtain the strong convexity. If *ν* = 2![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si160.png) and *w* = *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si161.png), a minimizer of *F*, then *F* is said to be *μ*\-star strongly convex. These conditions are often used in gradient-type methods to establish linear convergence rates [\[42\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0210).
*   •  **Sharpness, quadratic growth, and error bound conditions.** Assume that there exist *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si162.png) and *ν* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si158.png) such that $F(w) - F(w^{\\star}) \\geqslant \\frac{\\gamma}{\\nu}{\\| w - w^{\\star}\\|}^{\\nu}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si163.png) for all *w* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si138.png) and a minimizer *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) of *F*. If *ν* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si148.png), then we say that *F* is sharped at *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png). If *ν* = 2![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si160.png), then we say that *F* has a quadratic growth property. Clearly, if *F* is strongly convex, then it has a quadratic growth property. However, nonconvex functions may still have a quadratic growth property. This property can be extended to an *ω*\-convexity as in [\[14\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0070). Another related concept is error bound [\[39\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0195), which is defined as *γ*∥∇*F*(*w*)∥ ≥ ∥*w* − *w*^⋆∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si165.png) for some *γ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si162.png) and all *w* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si138.png). Both quadratic growth and error bound conditions can be used to establish \[local\] linear convergence of gradient-type methods, see, e.g., [\[16\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0080).

Other properties can be used to analyze convergence of gradient methods such as essential strong convexity, weak strong convexity, restricted secant inequality [\[30](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0150),[42\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0210), Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz (KL) condition [\[4\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0020), and Aubin's property [\[56\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0280).

### 1.2.7 Optimality certification

Finding an exact solution of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) is impractical. Our goal is to approximate a solution of this problem in some sense. Let us discuss what we can approximate for [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) in both convex and nonconvex problems.

Assume that *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) is a global optimal solution of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) with the optimal value *F*^⋆ = *F*(*w*^⋆)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si166.png) and *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) is an approximate solution produced by an algorithm. One obvious condition to certify the optimality is to compute the objective residual *F*(*ŵ*) − *F*(*w*^⋆)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si157.png). We often expect to find *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) such that *F*(*ŵ*) − *F*(*w*^⋆) ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si168.png) for a given tolerance *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si169.png). This condition is usually used for convex optimization or special classes of nonconvex problems, e.g., under a gradient dominance condition. The construction of *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) usually relies on two possible ways. The first is to simply take the last iterate *w*[*T*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si170.png) as *ŵ* :  = *w*^(*T*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si171.png), where *w*^(*T*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si172.png) is the final iterate of the algorithm. The second option is to form an averaging or a weighted averaging vector as

$\\widehat{w}: = \\frac{1}{T + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}w^{t},\\quad\\text{or}\\quad\\widehat{w}: = \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}w^{t},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si173.png)(1.12) 

where *γ*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si174.png) are given weights (usually related to the step-size *η*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si59.png), but could be different), and $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si175.png). In general, averaging vectors have better theoretical convergence rate guarantees, but they may break desired properties of solutions such as sparsity or low-rankness, etc., compared to the last-iterate *w*^(*T*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si172.png). In convex optimization, we often use Jensen's inequality to obtain $F(\\widehat{w}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si176.png) for our convergence rate bounds since we obtain a convergence rate bound for the right-hand side.

The second criterion is to use the norm of gradient of *F*, e.g., ∥∇*F*(*ŵ*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si177.png) or its squared norm. Note that ∇*F*(*w*^⋆) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si44.png) only provides us stationary points, which are candidates for local minimizers in nonconvex settings. Hence, any vector *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) such that ∥∇*F*(*ŵ*)∥ ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si178.png) for a given tolerance *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si169.png) only provides us an approximate stationary point *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1). To guarantee an approximate local solution, we may add a second-order condition such as *λ*[min](∇²*F*(*ŵ*)) ≥  − *ϵ̂*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si179.png) for some *ϵ̂* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si180.png), where *λ*[min](∇²*F*(*ŵ*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si181.png) is the smallest eigenvalue of ∇²*F*(*ŵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si182.png). The construction of *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si167.png) in the nonconvex case often relies on the best iterate from {*w*⁰, …, *w*^(*T*)}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si183.png), in the sense that ∥∇*F*(*ŵ*)∥ = min[0 ≤ *t* ≤ *T*]∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si184.png). For nonsmooth optimization, where *F* :  = *f* + *g*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si185.png), we can use the norm ∥*G*[*β*](*ŵ*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si186.png) of the gradient mapping *G*[*β*](*ŵ*) :  = *β*^( − 1)(*ŵ*−*p**r**o**x*[*β**g*](*ŵ*−*β*∇*f*(*ŵ*)))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si187.png) for some *β* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si188.png). For stochastic optimization, one needs to characterize the optimality condition using expectation 𝔼\[∥∇*F*(*ŵ*)∥²\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si189.png), 𝔼\[*F*(*ŵ*) − *F*^⋆\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si190.png), or high probability ℙ\[∥∇*F*(*ŵ*)∥ ≤ *ϵ*\] ≥ 1 − *δ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si191.png) or ℙ\[*F*(*ŵ*) − *F*^⋆ ≤ *ϵ*\] ≥ 1 − *δ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si192.png) for a small *δ* ∈ (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si193.png).

### 1.2.8 Unified convergence analysis

**(a) General approach.** Most convergence analysis of first-order methods of the form [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) relies on the following recursive inequality often generated by two or three consecutive iterates:

*D*[*t* + 1] + *Δ*[*t*] ≤ *ω*[*t*] ⋅ *D*[*t*] + *E*[*t*],

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si194.png)(1.13) 

where *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png), *Δ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si196.png), and *E*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si197.png) are nonnegative quantities, and *ω*[*t*] ∈ (0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si198.png) is a contraction factor. Very often these quantities depend on two consecutive iterates *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) and *w*^(*t* + 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si199.png), but sometimes they also depend on *w*^(*t* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si200.png). The error term *E*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si197.png) usually satisfies $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{\\infty}E\_{t} < + \\infty$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si201.png). Moreover, we often have *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png) or *ω*[*t*] → 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si203.png) for sublinear rates, and a fixed *ω*[*t*] = *ω* ∈ (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si204.png) for linear rates. The quantity *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png) can be referred to as a potential or Lyapunov function. There is no general and universal method to construct *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png), but for gradient-type methods, it is usually either ∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si205.png), ∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1)∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si206.png), *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si207.png), ∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si208.png) (in Euclidean or weighted norms), or a combination of these terms. Clearly, if *E*[*t*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si209.png), then {*D*[*t*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si210.png) is nonincreasing, showing a descent property of *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png). However, if *E*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si211.png), then we no longer have a descent property of *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png), which is usually the case in SGD or subgradient methods. There are two cases:

*   **Case 1.** If *D*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si195.png) contains an optimality measure, e.g., *S*[*t*]\[*F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si212.png), then we can show that $F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star} \\leqslant \\frac{C}{S\_{t}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si213.png) for the last iterate *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png), where *C* is a constant depending on *w*⁰![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si214.png) and possibly on *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) or *F*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si215.png).
*   **Case 2.** If *Δ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si196.png) contains an optimality measure, e.g., *γ*[*t*]∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si216.png), then we can show that $\\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant \\frac{C}{S\_{T}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si217.png) for some constant *C* and $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si175.png).

The recursive estimate [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) can be used to prove the convergence of different gradient-type methods, including standard and accelerated algorithms. Let us illustrate how to obtain [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) for some common schemes.

**(b) Subgradient method.** Let us consider the classical \[sub\]gradient method to minimize *F*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si218.png) as *w*^(*t* + 1) = *w*^(*t*) − *η*[*t*]∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si219.png), which is a special case of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2), where ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png) is a \[sub\]gradient of *F* at *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png). Then, for any *w* ∈ ℝ^(*p*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si138.png), we have

$\\eta\_{t}\\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),w^{t} - w\\rangle = \\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w\\|}^{2} - \\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w\\|}^{2} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si220.png)(1.14) 

If *F* is convex, then ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *w*^(*t*) − *w*⟩ ≥ *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si221.png). Combining this inequality and [(1.14)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq15), we obtain

$\\underset{D\_{t + 1}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w\\|}^{2}}} + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\eta\_{t}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w)\\rbrack}} \\leqslant \\underset{D\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w\\|}^{2}}} + \\underset{E\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si222.png)(1.15) 

This inequality is exactly in the form [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) with *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png). To guarantee convergence, we need to take *w* = *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si161.png) as a solution of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) and assume that ∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥ ≤ *M*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si223.png). Then, [(1.15)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq16) implies that *Δ*[*t*] ≤ *D*[*t*] − *D*[*t* + 1] + *E*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si224.png). By induction, we have $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\Delta\_{t} \\leqslant D\_{0} - D\_{T + 1} + \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}E\_{t} \\leqslant D\_{0} + \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}E\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si225.png). Therefore, we obtain

$F(\\widehat{w}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{1}{2S\_{T}}{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{M^{2}}{2S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si226.png)

where $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si227.png) and $\\widehat{w}: = \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}w^{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si228.png) as computed by [(1.12)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq13). To obtain a convergence rate bound, we require $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{\\infty}\\eta\_{t}^{2} < + \\infty$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si229.png) and $S\_{T}\\rightarrow S\_{\\infty} = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{\\infty}\\eta\_{t} = \\infty$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si230.png). These are exactly the conditions to guarantee the convergence of \[sub\]gradient methods, see, e.g., [\[8\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0040).

**(c) Gradient descent method for nonconvex problems.** If we assume that *F* is only *L*\-smooth and not necessarily convex, then using [(1.10)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq11) with *w* :  = *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si231.png) and *w*^′ :  = *w*^(*t* + 1) = *w*^(*t*) − *η*[*t*]∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si232.png), we have

$F(w^{t + 1}) \\leqslant F(w^{t}) + \\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),w^{t + 1} - w^{t}\\rangle + \\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{t}\\|}^{2} = F(w^{t}) - \\eta\_{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2} \\right){\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si233.png)(1.16) 

By adding  − *F*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si234.png), where *F*^⋆ :  = inf[*w*]*F*(*w*) >  − ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si235.png) (our assumption), to both sides and rearranging the result, inequality [(1.16)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq18) leads to

$\\begin{array}{lcl} {\\underset{D\_{t + 1}}{\\underset{︸}{F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star}}} + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\eta\_{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2} \\right){\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}}}\\ } & {\\leqslant \\ } & {\\underset{D\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star}}}.} \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si236.png)

This is exactly in the form [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) with *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png) and *E*[*t*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si209.png). Without any further assumption, we have *Δ*[*t*] ≤ *D*[*t*] − *D*[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si237.png) and, by induction, get $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\Delta\_{t} \\leqslant D\_{0} - D\_{T + 1} \\leqslant D\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si238.png), leading to

$\\min\\limits\_{0 \\leqslant t \\leqslant T}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant \\frac{F(w^{0}) - F^{\\star}}{S\_{T}},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si239.png)

where $\\gamma\_{t} = \\eta\_{t}(1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si240.png) and $S\_{T} = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si241.png), provided that $0 < \\eta\_{t} < \\frac{2}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si242.png). This result allows us to certify the best-iterate convergence rate of the algorithm to a stationary point of [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1).

**(d) Gradient descent method for smooth and convex problems.** Assume that *F* is convex and *L*\-smooth. Let us choose $\\eta\_{t}: = \\frac{1}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si243.png) in [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) to get $w^{t + 1}: = w^{t} - \\frac{1}{L}\\nabla F(w^{t})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si244.png). Then, from [(1.14)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq15) and [(1.16)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq18), and the convexity of *F*, we have

$\\left\\{ \\begin{array}{l} {\\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle = \\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{1}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2},} \\\\ {(t + 1)\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\frac{(t + 1)}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant (t + 1)\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack,} \\\\ {F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si245.png)

By summing up these three inequalities and canceling terms, we obtain

$\\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + (t + 1)\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\frac{t}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}\\quad \\leqslant \\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\ t\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si246.png)

This is exactly [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) with $D\_{t}: = \\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + t\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si247.png), $\\Delta\_{t}: = \\frac{t}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si248.png), *E*[*t*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si209.png), and *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png). This recursive estimate implies *D*[*t* + 1] ≤ *D*[0]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si249.png), and therefore, using the definition of *D*[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si250.png) and dropping $\\frac{L}{2}{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si251.png), we get

$F(w^{t + 1}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\frac{D\_{0}}{t + 1} = \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2(t + 1)},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si252.png)

which shows an 𝒪(1/*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si253.png)\-last-iterate convergence rate on *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png). It also implies that $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}t{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant L^{2}{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si254.png) (by using $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\Delta\_{t} \\leqslant D\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si255.png)) and ∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆∥ ≤ ∥*w*⁰ − *w*^⋆∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si256.png) (by using *D*[*t*] ≤ *D*[0]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si257.png)) for all *t* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si48.png).

**(e) Accelerated gradient method for smooth and convex problems.** Our last illustration follows Nesterov's accelerated gradient scheme:

$z^{t}: = w^{t} + \\beta\_{t}(w^{t} - w^{t - 1})\\quad\\text{and}\\quad w^{t + 1}: = z^{t} - \\frac{1}{L}\\nabla F(z^{t}),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si258.png)(1.17) 

where $\\beta\_{t} = \\frac{\\theta\_{t - 1} - 1}{\\theta\_{t}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si259.png) for *θ*[*t*] ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si260.png) such that *θ*[*t*](*θ*[*t*] − 1) ≤ *θ*[*t* − 1]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si261.png) with *θ*[0] :  = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si262.png). This is an accelerated variant of [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) with the momentum *β*[*t*](*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si263.png). It is well-known [\[44\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0220) that, after a few elementary transformations, [(1.17)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq24) can be written as

$z^{t}: = (1 - \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}})w^{t} + \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}}u^{t},\\ w^{t + 1}: = z^{t} - \\frac{1}{L}\\nabla F(z^{t}),\\ \\ \\text{and}\\ \\ u^{t + 1} = u^{t} - \\frac{\\theta\_{t}}{L}\\nabla F(z^{t}).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si264.png)

Let $v^{t}: = (1 - \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}})w^{t} + \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}}w^{\\star}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si265.png). Then, $z^{t} - v^{t} = \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}}(u^{t} - w^{\\star})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si266.png). Moreover, by convexity of *F*, we have $F(z^{t}) \\leqslant F(v^{t}) + \\langle\\nabla F(z^{t}),z^{t} - v^{t}\\rangle \\leqslant (1 - \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}})F(w^{t}) + \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}}F(w^{\\star}) + \\frac{1}{\\theta\_{t}}\\langle\\nabla F(z^{t}),u^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si267.png). Hence, multiplying both sides by *θ*[*t*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si268.png), we obtain

$\\begin{array}{lcl} {\\theta\_{t}^{2}\\lbrack F(z^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack\\ } & {\\leqslant \\ } & {\\theta\_{t}(\\theta\_{t} - 1)\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\theta\_{t}\\langle\\nabla F(z^{t}),u^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle.} \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si269.png)

Similar to the proof of [(1.14)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq15) and [(1.16)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq18), respectively, we have

$\\left\\{ \\begin{array}{l} {\\frac{L}{2}{\\| u^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\theta\_{t}\\langle\\nabla F(z^{t}),u^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle = \\frac{L}{2}{\\| u^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{\\theta\_{t}^{2}}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(z^{t})\\|}^{2},} \\\\ {\\theta\_{t}^{2}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\frac{\\theta\_{t}^{2}}{2L}{\\|\\nabla F(z^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant \\theta\_{t}^{2}\\lbrack F(z^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si270.png)

Summing up the last three inequalities, we obtain

$\\underset{D\_{t + 1}}{\\underset{︸}{\\theta\_{t}^{2}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\frac{L}{2}{\\| u^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}} + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{(\\theta\_{t - 1}^{2} - \\theta\_{t}(\\theta\_{t} - 1))\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack}}\\quad \\leqslant \\underset{D\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\theta\_{t - 1}^{2}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack + \\frac{L}{2}{\\| u^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si271.png)(1.18) 

which is exactly [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) with *E*[*t*] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si209.png) and *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png), provided that *θ*[*t* − 1]² − *θ*[*t*](*θ*[*t*] − 1) ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si272.png) (note that *θ*[0] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si273.png) and $\\theta\_{- 1} = \\frac{1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si274.png) satisfy this condition). The recursive estimate [(1.18)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq28) implies that *D*[*t*] ≤ *D*[0]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si257.png), leading to

$F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\frac{D\_{0}}{\\theta\_{t - 1}^{2}} = \\frac{L}{2\\theta\_{t - 1}^{2}}{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si275.png)

In particular, if we choose $\\theta\_{t - 1}: = \\frac{t + 1}{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si276.png), then $\\theta\_{t - 1}^{2} = \\frac{{(t + 1)}^{2}}{4} \\geqslant \\theta\_{t}(\\theta\_{t} - 1) = \\frac{t(t + 1)}{4}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si277.png), then we get the last-iterate convergence guarantee $F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star}) \\leqslant \\frac{2L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{{(t + 1)}^{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si278.png).

We have illustrated how to employ the unified recursive expression [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14) to analyze four different deterministic gradient-type algorithms. It provides a simple approach with a few lines to derive convergence rate analysis compared to classical techniques in the literature. We believe that this approach can be extended to analyze other methods that have not been listed here.

### 1.2.9 Convergence rates and complexity analysis

Classical optimization literature often characterizes asymptotic convergence or linear convergence rates of the underlying algorithm, while sublinear rates or oracle complexity are largely elusive, see, e.g., [\[3](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0015),[21](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0105),[22](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0110),[31](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0155),[38](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0190),[53\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0265). Sublinear convergence rates have been widely studied in convex optimization methods, see, e.g., [\[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225), while oracle complexity analysis was formally studied in [\[43\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0215). Recently, these topics have gained in popularity due to applications to large-scale problems in modern signal and image processing, machine learning, and statistical learning [\[9](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0045),[28](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0140),[67\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0335). Let us discuss these concepts in detail here.

**(a) Convergence rates.** A convergence rate characterizes the progress of the optimality measure (e.g., the objective residual *F*(*ŵ*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si279.png), the squared distance to solution ∥*ŵ*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si280.png), or the squared norm of gradient ∥∇*F*(*ŵ*^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si281.png)) with respect to the iteration *t*, where *ŵ*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si282.png) is an approximate solution. For example, in the gradient method for smooth and convex problems, we have $F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star} \\leqslant \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2(t + 1)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si283.png), showing that the objective residual *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si207.png) decreases with a speed of at least $\\frac{1}{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si284.png), which is written as *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆ = 𝒪(1/*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si285.png). We can also write $F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star} = \\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{R\_{0}^{2}L}{t + 1} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si286.png) for *R*[0] :  = ∥*w*⁰ − *w*^⋆∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si287.png) to show the dependence of the rate on *L* and *R*[0]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si288.png).

Note that we generally attempt to establish an upper bound rate, but can also show that this upper bound matches the lower bound rate (up to a constant factor) for certain classes of algorithms under a given set of assumptions on [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1), see, e.g., [\[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225). For gradient-type methods, the optimal convergence rates under only convexity and *L*\-smoothness is 𝒪(1/*t*²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si289.png), which is guaranteed by Nesterov's optimal methods. For nonconvex problems, gradient-type methods only achieve an 𝒪(1/*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si253.png) rate on ∥∇*F*(*ŵ*^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si281.png) under the *L*\-smoothness. Linear convergence rates can be achieved with additional assumptions such as strong convexity, error bound, quadratic growth, or PL condition. However, we do not further discuss these variants in this chapter.

**(b) Complexity.** The concept of complexity comes from theoretical computer science, but is widely used in computational mathematics, particularly in optimization. Formal definitions of complexity can be found, e.g., in [\[43](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0215),[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225). We distinguish two types of complexity for our gradient-type methods: iteration-complexity (or analytical complexity), and computational complexity (or sometimes called arithmetic complexity, or work complexity) [\[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225). In gradient-type methods, the overall computational complexity is generally dominated by the oracle complexity, which characterizes the total number of function and/or gradient evaluations required for finding an approximate solution. We notice that we overload the concept *oracle*, which is formally defined, e.g., in [\[45\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0225). Mathematically, the oracle complexity of *T* iterations of an algorithm (in our context) is defined as follows:

$\\text{Oracle\\ complexity}: = \\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\text{Per-iteration\\ complexity\\ at\\ iteration}\\ t.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si290.png)(1.19)
