The **per-iteration complexity** characterizes the workload (e.g., the number of gradient evaluations) at each iteration. At each iteration, we often count the most dominated computational steps such as gradient evaluations, function evaluations, proximal operations, projections, matrix–vector multiplications, or Hessian–vector multiplications. If this per-iteration complexity is fixed, then

Oracle complexity = Number of iterations × Per-iteration complexity.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si291.png)

For example, for the standard gradient descent method for smooth and convex problems, the per-iteration complexity is 𝒪(1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si292.png), i.e., requires one gradient evaluation, leading to oracle complexity $\\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{1}{\\epsilon} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si293.png) in order to obtain *w*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si50.png) such that *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆ ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si294.png). Indeed, from the convergence bound $F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star} \\leqslant \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si295.png), we infer that *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*^⋆ ≤ *ϵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si294.png) is implied by $\\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2t} \\leqslant \\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si296.png), leading to $t \\geqslant \\left\\lceil \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2\\epsilon} \\right\\rceil$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si297.png). Hence, we need at most $t\_{\\max}: = \\left\\lceil \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2\\epsilon} \\right\\rceil = \\mathcal{O}\\left( 1/\\epsilon \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si298.png) iterations, and therefore 𝒪(1/*ϵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si299.png) gradient evaluations.

### 1.2.10 Initial point, warm-start, and restart

For convex algorithms, which can converge to a global minimizer *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) starting from any initial point *w*⁰![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si214.png), the choice of *w*⁰![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si214.png) will affect the number of iterations as the term ∥*w*⁰ − *w*^⋆∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si300.png) for any solution *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png) appears in the bound of the convergence guarantee, e.g., $F(w^{T}) - F^{\\star} \\leqslant \\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{L{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{T^{\\nu}} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si301.png) for *ν* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si148.png) or *ν* = 2![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si160.png). Clearly, if *w*⁰![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si214.png) is close to *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png), then the number of iterations *T* is small.

For nonconvex algorithms, initialization plays a crucial role since different initial points *w*⁰![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si214.png) may make the algorithm converge to different approximate stationary points *w*^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si164.png), and their quality is different. Stationary points are candidates for local minimizers, but some may give us maximizers or saddle points. If we do get a local minimizer, then it may still be a bad one, which is far from any global minimizer or which gives us a bad prediction error in machine learning.

A warm-start strategy uses the output of the previous run or the previous iteration to initialize the algorithm at the current stage or iteration. It is based on the idea that the previous run already gives us a good approximation of the desired solution. Initializing from this point may give hope for a quick convergence to the target optimal solution. Warm-start is widely used in sequential iterative (e.g., sequential quadratic programming) or online learning methods.

A restarting strategy is often used in the case where the algorithm makes undesired progress and needs to be restarted. This idea has been used in accelerated gradient methods, where the objective function increases after significant decrease, causing oscillated behaviors [\[26](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0130),[50\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0250). Restarting is often combined with a warm-start and an appropriate condition to obtain good performance. Some theoretical analysis of restarting strategies can be found, e.g., in [\[20](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0100),[26](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0130),[50](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0250),[61\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0305).

## 1.3 Stochastic gradient descent methods

Let us further extend our discussion from deterministic to stochastic methods for solving [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1) when *F* is a finite-sum or an expectation function. The stochastic approximation (SA) method was initially proposed by Robbins and Monro in the 1950s [\[55\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0275). It has become extremely popular in the last decades as it has been widely used in machine learning and data science, see, e.g., [\[5](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0025),[6](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0030),[60\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0300).

### 1.3.1 The algorithmic template

In this section, we only focus on the standard stochastic optimization and discuss two types of methods: classical SGD and variance-reduced SGD. More specifically, we focus on *F*(*w*) :  = 𝔼\[**F**(*w*, *ξ*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si31.png) in [(1.1)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq1), which can be written as

$\\min\\limits\_{w \\in \\mathbb{R}^{p}}\\left\\{ F(w): = \\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\mathbf{F}(w,\\xi)\\rbrack \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si302.png)(1.20) 

where *ξ* is a random vector defined on a given probability space (*Ω*, *Σ*, ℙ)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si33.png).

Many stochastic gradient-based methods for solving [(1.20)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq32) can be described as in [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010). Here, [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) only presents a pure stochastic gradient scheme with a possible variance-reduction step, but without momentum or accelerated steps. The operator 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si53.png) presents a projection to handle constraints if required, or to add a compression. However, if it is not specified, then we assume that 𝒫(*z*) = *z*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si303.png), the identity operator. Note that [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) is a double-loop algorithm, where the inner loop carries out SGD updates, while the outer loop performs stage-wise updates, which can be expressed in an epoch-wise fashion or as a restarting mechanism.

![Algorithm 1 Unified stochastic gradient (SGD) method.](images/B9780443190377000089/gr001.jpg)

Algorithm 1 Unified stochastic gradient (SGD) method.

If *S* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si304.png), then [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) reduces to a single-loop method. If *S* > 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si305.png), then we can also transform [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) into a single loop with an “IF” statement and using the iteration counter $k: = \\sum\_{i = 0}^{s - 1}T\_{i} + t$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si306.png). If *T*[*s*] :  = *T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si307.png) is fixed, then *k* :  = (*s* − 1)*T* + *t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si308.png). This transformation allows us to inject Bernoulli's rule for the “IF” statement instead of deterministic rules. Such a modification has been implemented in Loopless-SVRG and Loopless-SARAH schemes, see, e.g., [\[33](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0165),[36\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0180).

### 1.3.2 SGD estimators

The main component of [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) is the estimator *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png). Let us review some important estimators widely used in optimization and related fields.

**(a) Classical SGD and mini-batch estimators.** Clearly, if *S* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si304.png), then we can simply drop the superscript *s* in [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010), and write the main update as

*w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) − *η*[*t*]*v*^(*t*),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si310.png)(1.21) 

which is in the form [(1.2)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq2) with *d*^(*t*) =  − *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si311.png) being a stochastic estimator of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png).

In the classical SGD, we often generate *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) as an unbiased estimator of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png) with a bounded variance, i.e.,

𝔼\[*v*^(*t*)|ℱ[*t*]\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) and 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*)∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ *M*²,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si312.png)(1.22) 

for given *M* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si313.png), where ℱ[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si314.png) is the smallest *σ*\-algebra generated by {𝒮[0], …, 𝒮[*t*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si315.png) and 𝔼\[ ⋅ |ℱ[*t*]\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si316.png) is the conditional expectation.

**(b) Variance-reduced SGD estimators.** There exists a number of variance-reduced methods, which are based on different estimators of ∇*F*(*w*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si151.png). We only focus on some of them. For simplicity, we drop the stage superscript “s”.

The first is SVRG [\[29\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0145), which generates *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) as

*v*^(*t*) :  = *v̂*^(*s*) + \[∇**F**(*w*^(*t*), 𝒮[*t*]) − ∇**F**(*ŵ*^(*s*), 𝒮[*t*])\],

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si317.png)(1.23) 

where *v̂*^(*s*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si318.png) is the full gradient or a mega-batch unbiased estimator of ∇*F* at *ŵ*^(*s*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si319.png), $\\nabla\\mathbf{F}(w^{t},\\mathcal{S}\_{t}): = \\frac{1}{b\_{t}}\\sum\_{\\xi\_{t} \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{t}}\\nabla\\mathbf{F}(w^{t},\\xi\_{t})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si320.png) and *b*[*t*] :  = |𝒮[*t*]|![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si321.png). Then, one can show that

𝔼[𝒮[*t*]]\[*v*^(*t*)\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) and 𝔼[𝒮[*t*]]\[∥*v*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²\] ≤ *σ*[*t*]²,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si322.png)

where *σ*[*t*]² :  = *L*²∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si323.png) if *F* is *L*\-average smooth, and *σ*[*t*]² :  = 4*L*\[*F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*(*w*^⋆) + *F*(*ŵ*^(*s*)) − *F*(*w*^⋆)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si324.png) if *F* is convex and *L*\-average smooth.

The second estimator is SARAH [\[48\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0240), which is expressed as follows:

*v*^(*t*) :  = *v*^(*t* − 1) + \[∇**F**(*w*^(*t*), 𝒮[*t*]) − ∇**F**(*w*^(*t* − 1), 𝒮[*t*])\].

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si325.png)(1.24) 

It is called a stochastic recursive gradient estimator. Unfortunately, this estimate is biased, i.e., 𝔼[𝒮[*t*]]\[*v*^(*t*)\] ≠ ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si326.png). However, one can prove that

𝔼[𝒮[*t*]]\[*v*^(*t*)\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)) + *e*[*t*] and 𝔼[𝒮[*t*]]\[∥*v*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²\] ≤ *σ*[*t*]²,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si327.png)

where *e*[*t*] :  = *v*^(*t* − 1) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t* − 1))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si328.png) is an error, and $\\sigma\_{t}^{2} \\leqslant \\sigma\_{t - 1}^{2} + \\frac{L^{2}}{b\_{t}}{\\| w^{t} - w^{t - 1}\\|}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si329.png) if **F** is *L*\-average smooth, see [\[52\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0260).

Another interesting estimator is the hybrid variance-reduced estimator proposed in [\[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330), which can be written as

*v*^(*t*) :  = (1 − *β*[*t*])\[*v*^(*t* − 1) + \[∇**F**(*w*^(*t*), 𝒮[*t*]) − ∇**F**(*w*^(*t* − 1), 𝒮[*t*])\]\] + *β*[*t*]*u*^(*t*),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si330.png)(1.25) 

where *β*[*t*] ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si331.png) and *u*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si332.png) is an unbiased estimator of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png) with variance *σ̂*[*t*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si333.png), i.e., 𝔼\[∥*u*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ *σ̂*[*t*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si334.png). Again, as proven in [\[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330), this is a biased estimator of ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si68.png) and, if **F** is *L*\-average smooth, then *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) satisfies 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥² ≤ *σ*[*t*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si335.png), where

$\\sigma\_{t}^{2} \\leqslant {(1 - \\beta\_{t})}^{2}\\sigma\_{t - 1}^{2} + \\ \\frac{2{(1 - \\beta\_{t})}^{2}L^{2}}{b\_{t}}{\\| w^{t} - w^{t - 1}\\|}^{2} + 2\\beta\_{t}^{2}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}\_{t}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si336.png)

One simple choice of *u*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si332.png) is *u*^(*t*) :  = ∇**F**(*w*^(*t*), 𝒮[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si337.png). In this case, we have ${\\widehat{\\sigma}}\_{t}^{2} = \\frac{\\sigma^{2}}{b\_{t}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si338.png).

### 1.3.3 Unified convergence analysis

**(a) General approach.** Let us identify what the crucial steps in convergence analysis of [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) are. One of the most important steps is to establish a recursive estimate with respect to inner iterations *t* of the form [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14), but under a conditional expectation, i.e.,

𝔼\[*D*[*t* + 1]|ℱ[*t*]\] + *Δ*[*t*] ≤ *ω*[*t*] ⋅ *D*[*t*] + *E*[*t*],

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si339.png)(1.26) 

where the related quantities are defined similarly to [(1.13)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq14). If we take the total expectation on both sides of [(1.26)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq41), and assume that $\\omega\_{t} = \\frac{\\xi\_{t}}{\\xi\_{t + 1}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si340.png) for *ξ*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si341.png) and 𝔼\[*E*[*t*]\] ≤ *θ*[*t*]²*M*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si342.png) for some *M* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si313.png) and *θ*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si343.png), then we have

*ξ*[*t* + 1]𝔼\[*D*[*t* + 1]\] + *ξ*[*t* + 1]𝔼\[*Δ*[*t*]\] ≤ *ξ*[*t*] ⋅ 𝔼\[*D*[*t*]\] + *ξ*[*t* + 1]*θ*[*t*]²*M*².

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si344.png)

By induction, we have

$\\xi\_{T + 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{T + 1}\\rbrack + \\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\xi\_{t + 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\Delta\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant \\xi\_{0}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{0}\\rbrack + M^{2}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\xi\_{t + 1}\\theta\_{t}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si345.png)(1.27) 

Let $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si175.png) with given weights *γ*[*t*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si174.png) (usually depending on *ξ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si346.png) and/or *θ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si347.png)). Dividing both sides of [(1.27)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq43) by *S*[*T*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si348.png), we obtain

$\\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\xi\_{t + 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\Delta\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{\\xi\_{0}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{0}\\rbrack}{S\_{T}} + \\frac{M^{2}}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\xi\_{t + 1}\\theta\_{t}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si349.png)(1.28) 

Both estimates [(1.27)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq43) and [(1.28)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq44) will allow us to estimate convergence rates of the underlying algorithm. Let us apply this approach to prove convergence of some variants of [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010).

**(b) SGD for nonsmooth convex problems.** Let us analyze the convergence of the SGD scheme [(1.21)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq33). Using the update [(1.21)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq33), we have ∥*w*^(*t* + 1) − *w*^⋆∥² = ∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆∥² − 2*η*[*t*]⟨*v*^(*t*), *w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆⟩ + *η*[*t*]²∥*v*^(*t*)∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si350.png). Taking conditional expectation 𝔼\[ ⋅ |ℱ[*t*]\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si316.png) of this estimate and noting that 𝔼\[*v*^(*t*)|ℱ[*t*]\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si351.png), we have

$\\eta\_{t}\\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\rangle = \\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} - \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack\\quad + \\ \\frac{\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si352.png)

If *F* is convex, then we have *F*(*w*^(*t*)) − *F*(*w*^⋆) ≤ ⟨∇*F*(*w*^(*t*)), *w*^(*t*) − *w*^⋆⟩![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si353.png). Moreover, we also have 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*)∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ *M*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si354.png). Combining these two expressions and the last inequality, we get

$\\underset{\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{t + 1}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{1}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| w^{t + 1} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack}} + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\eta\_{t}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack}} \\leqslant \\underset{D\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{1}{2}{\\| w^{t} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}} + \\underset{E\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}M^{2}}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si355.png)

This is exactly the recursive estimate [(1.26)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq41). Using [(1.28)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq44), we can show that

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(\\widehat{w}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(w^{t}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{1}{2S\_{T}}{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{M^{2}}{2S\_{T}}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si356.png)(1.29) 

where $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si227.png) and $\\widehat{w}: = \\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}w^{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si228.png). If we choose $\\eta\_{t}: = \\frac{C}{\\sqrt{T + 1}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si357.png) for some *C* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si93.png), then $S\_{T} = C\\sqrt{T + 1}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si358.png) and $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}^{2} = C^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si359.png). In this case, [(1.29)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq47) becomes

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(\\widehat{w}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{2C\\sqrt{T + 1}} + \\frac{M^{2}C}{2\\sqrt{T + 1}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si360.png)

If we choose $\\eta\_{t}: = \\frac{C}{\\sqrt{t + 1}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si361.png) for some *C* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si93.png), then

$S\_{T}: = C\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{t + 1}} \\geqslant 2C\\int\_{1}^{T + 1}\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{t}}dt = 2C(\\sqrt{T + 1} - 1)$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si362.png)

and $\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\eta\_{t}^{2} = C^{2}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\frac{1}{t + 1} \\leqslant C^{2}(1 + \\ln(T + 1))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si363.png). In this case, [(1.29)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq47) becomes

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(\\widehat{w}) - F(w^{\\star})\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{{\\| w^{0} - w^{\\star}\\|}^{2}}{4C(\\sqrt{T + 1} - 1)} + \\frac{M^{2}C(1 + \\ln(T + 1))}{4(\\sqrt{T + 1} - 1)}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si364.png)

**(c) SGD for smooth and nonconvex problems.** We consider the case *F* is *L*\-smooth. In addition, we assume that our stochastic estimator *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) is unbiased, i.e., 𝔼\[*v*^(*t*)|ℱ[*t*]\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si351.png) and has bounded variance as 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si365.png). In this case, we have 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*)∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ ∥∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥² + *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si366.png). Using this inequality, 𝔼\[*v*^(*t*)|ℱ[*t*]\] = ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si351.png), and the *L*\-smoothness of *F*, we can derive

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1})|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant F(w^{t}) - \\eta\_{t}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),v^{t}\\rangle|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant F(w^{t}) - \\eta\_{t}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} + \\ \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} + \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}\\sigma^{2}}{2} = F(w^{t}) - \\eta\_{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2} \\right){\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} + \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}\\sigma^{2}}{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si367.png)

This inequality leads to

$\\begin{array}{l} {\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\underset{D\_{t + 1}}{\\underset{︸}{F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star}}}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\eta\_{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2} \\right){\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}}} \\leqslant \\underset{D\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star}}} + \\underset{E\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}\\sigma^{2}}{2}}},\\ } \\\\ \\end{array}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si368.png)

which is exactly [(1.26)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq41) with *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png), provided that $0 < \\eta\_{t} < \\frac{2}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si242.png). By using this estimate, we can derive a convergence rate for $\\frac{1}{S\_{T}}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si369.png) with $\\gamma\_{t}: = \\eta\_{t}\\left( 1 - \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}}{2} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si370.png) and $S\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 0}^{T}\\gamma\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si175.png) as done in [\[25\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0125). We omit the details here.

**(d) Hybrid variance-reduced SGD for smooth and nonconvex problems.** We analyze one variance-reduced variant of [Algorithm 1](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#f0010) where the inner loop updates are *w*^(*t* + 1) :  = *w*^(*t*) − *η*[*t*]*v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si371.png), with *v*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si309.png) being given by [(1.25)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq39) for *b*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si372.png), see [\[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330). In addition, we do not need the outer loop, leading to a **single-loop** algorithm.

Let us analyze its convergence rate. First, by the *L*\-smoothness of *F* and the relation  − 2⟨*a*, *b*⟩ = ∥*a* − *b*∥² − ∥*a*∥² − ∥*b*∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si373.png), we can derive

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1})|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant F(w^{t}) - \\eta\_{t}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\langle\\nabla F(w^{t}),v^{t}\\rangle|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\frac{L\\eta\_{t}^{2}}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack = F(w^{t}) - \\frac{\\eta\_{t}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}}{2}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| v^{t} - \\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack\\quad - \\frac{\\eta\_{t}}{2}(1 - L\\eta\_{t})\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si374.png)

Since 𝔼\[∥*v*^(*t*) − ∇*F*(*w*^(*t*))∥²|ℱ[*t*]\] ≤ *σ*[*t*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si375.png) and $0 < \\eta\_{t} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si376.png), this inequality reduces to

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}(1 - L\\eta\_{t})}{2}{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star} - \\frac{\\eta\_{t}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}\\sigma\_{t}^{2}}{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si377.png)

Since *σ*[*t*]² ≤ (1 − *β*[*t*])²*σ*[*t* − 1]² + 2(1 − *β*[*t*])²*L*²∥*w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1)∥² + 2*β*[*t*]²*σ̂*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si378.png) and *w*^(*t*) − *w*^(*t* − 1) =  − *η*[*t* − 1]*v*^(*t* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si379.png), we have

*σ*[*t*]² ≤ (1 − *β*[*t*])²*σ*[*t* − 1]² + 2*L*²(1 − *β*[*t*])²*η*[*t* − 1]²∥*v*^(*t* − 1)∥² + 2*β*[*t*]²*σ̂*².

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si380.png)

Multiplying this inequality by $\\frac{c\_{t}}{2} > 0$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si381.png) and adding to the last estimate, we obtain

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack F(w^{t + 1}) - F^{\\star} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}(1 - L\\eta\_{t})}{2}{\\| v^{t}\\|}^{2}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\frac{(c\_{t} - \\eta\_{t})}{2}\\sigma\_{t}^{2} + \\frac{\\eta\_{t}}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}\\quad \\leqslant F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star} + \\ L^{2}c\_{t}{(1 - \\beta\_{t})}^{2}\\eta\_{t - 1}^{2}{\\| v^{t - 1}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{c\_{t}{(1 - \\beta\_{t})}^{2}}{2}\\sigma\_{t - 1}^{2} + c\_{t}\\beta\_{t}^{2}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si382.png)

For simplicity, we choose all parameters to be constant. Let us define $D\_{t}: = F(w^{t}) - F^{\\star} + \\frac{\\eta(1 - L\\eta)}{2}{\\| v^{t - 1}\\|}^{2} + \\frac{(c - \\eta)}{2}\\sigma\_{t - 1}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si383.png), and impose the following conditions:

2*L*²*η*²*c*(1 − *β*)² ≤ *η*(1 − *L**η*) and *c*(1 − *β*)² ≤ *c* − *η*.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si384.png)(1.30) 

Then, the last estimate leads to

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{t + 1}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\underset{\\Delta\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{\\eta}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}}} \\leqslant D\_{t} + \\underset{E\_{t}}{\\underset{︸}{c\\beta^{2}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}^{2}}},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si385.png)

which is exactly [(1.26)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq41) with *ω*[*t*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si202.png).

Assume that we choose $\\eta \\in (0,\\frac{1}{L})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si386.png) and *c* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si58.png) such that 2*L*²*η*²(*c* − *η*) = *η*(1 − *L**η*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si387.png), leading to $c: = \\frac{1 - L\\eta}{2L^{2}\\eta} + \\eta = \\frac{1 - L\\eta + 2L^{2}\\eta^{2}}{2L^{2}\\eta}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si388.png). Moreover, ${(1 - \\beta)}^{2} \\leqslant 1 - \\frac{2L^{2}\\eta^{2}}{1 - L\\eta + 2L^{2}\\eta^{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si389.png). Then, both conditions of [(1.30)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq57) hold with equality. In this case, we obtain $\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack D\_{t + 1}|\\mathcal{F}\_{t}\\rbrack + \\frac{\\eta}{2}{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant D\_{t} + \\frac{(1 - L\\eta + 2L^{2}\\eta^{2})\\beta^{2}}{2L^{2}\\eta}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si390.png). This inequality implies

$\\frac{1}{T + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack \\leqslant \\frac{2}{\\eta(T + 1)}D\_{0} + \\frac{(1 - L\\eta + 2L^{2}\\eta^{2})\\beta^{2}}{L^{2}\\eta^{2}}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}^{2} \\leqslant \\frac{2\\lbrack F(w^{0}) - F^{\\star}\\rbrack}{\\eta(T + 1)} + \\frac{{\\| v^{0}\\|}^{2}}{(T + 1)} + \\frac{\\sigma\_{- 1}^{2}}{2L^{2}\\eta^{2}(T + 1)} + \\frac{\\beta^{2}{\\widehat{\\sigma}}^{2}}{L^{2}\\eta^{2}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si391.png)

Finally, we choose $\\eta: = \\frac{1}{L{(T + 1)}^{1/3}} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si392.png), $\\sigma\_{- 1}: = \\frac{1}{{(T + 1)}^{1/3}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si393.png), and $\\beta: = \\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{1}{{(T + 1)}^{2/3}} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si394.png) such that ${(1 - \\beta)}^{2} \\leqslant 1 - \\frac{2L^{2}\\eta^{2}}{1 - L\\eta + 2L^{2}\\eta^{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si389.png) (such a *β* always exists). Moreover, the last estimate shows that

$\\frac{1}{T + 1}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{T}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\|\\nabla F(w^{t})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack = \\mathcal{O}\\left( \\frac{1}{{(T + 1)}^{2/3}} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000089/si395.png)

as proven in [\[66\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0330).

We have illustrated our approach by using the recursive estimate [(1.26)](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#deq41) to analyze the convergence of three SGD schemes, including variance-reduced methods. We believe that this approach can be used to analyze other variants including SVRG and SARAH.

## 1.4 Concluding remarks

We have reviewed several main components that constitute the gradient descent method and its variants, including deterministic and stochastic ones, ranging from convex to nonconvex problems. We have provided a simple and unified convergence analysis framework relying on an elementary recursive estimate under the most basic structure assumptions commonly used in the literature. While this approach can be applied to analyze several methods, we have only illustrated it on a few well-known schemes. Note that we have not proposed any new algorithms, but rather unified the convergence analysis using a simple recursive estimate. However, we believe that such an approach can be extended beyond what we have done in this chapter. The following research topics are interesting to us. First, can one still apply our analysis to accelerated variance-reduced stochastic gradient-type methods? Perhaps, this can possibly be done by using the idea from a recent work [\[15\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0075). Second, how can we extend our framework to study other optimization methods in distributed systems and federated learning? We emphasize that many algorithms in these fields can be viewed as a randomized \[block-\]coordinate methods. Therefore, extensions to coordinate and shuffling methods are promising and remain open. Third, is it possible to extend and adapt our analysis to asynchronous gradient-based algorithms? We believe that such an extension is possible as long as the delay is bounded. However, one needs to modify the recursive expression to capture with the delayed updates, leading to an extra error term in the recursive inequality. Finally, our approach can be used to analyze convergence of algorithms for minimax and variational inequality problems, which have recently gained tremendous popularity [\[19](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0095),[65\]](#Chp001_3-28_B9780443190377000089.xhtml#br0325).

# Chapter 2: Considerations on the theory of training models with differential privacy

Marten van Dijk^([a](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#aff0010),[b](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#aff0015)); Phuong Ha Nguyen^([c](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#aff0020))    ^aCWI, Amsterdam, Netherlands  
^bVU University Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands  
^ceBay Inc., San Jose, CA, United States

## Abstract

In federated learning, collaborative learning takes place by a set of clients who each want to remain in control of how their local training data is used, in particular, how each client's local training data can remain private. Differential privacy is one method to limit privacy leakage. We provide a general overview of its framework and provable properties, adopt the more recent hypothesis based definition called Gaussian DP or *f*\-DP, and discuss Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD). We stay at a meta level and attempt intuitive explanations and insights.

### Keywords

Stochastic gradient descent (SGD); DP-SGD; Differential privacy (DP); Gaussian DP

## 2.1 Introduction

Privacy leakage is a big problem in the big-data era. Solving a learning task based on big data intrinsically means that only through a collaborative effort sufficient data is available for training a global model with sufficient clean accuracy (utility). Federated learning is a framework where a learning task is solved by a loose federation of participating devices/clients which are coordinated by a central server \[[3](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0015),[7](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0035),[8](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0040),[10](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0050),[27](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0135),[28](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0140),[31](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0155),[33](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0165)–[35](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0175),[37](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0185),[38](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0190),[40](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0200),[55](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0275),[57](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0285)\]. Clients, who use own local data to participate in a learning task by training a global model, want to have privacy guarantees for their local proprietary data. For this reason, DP-SGD [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005) was introduced as it adapts distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) [\[54\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0270) with Differential Privacy (DP) \[[13](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0065)–[15](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0075),[17](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0085)\].

The optimization problem for training many Machine Learning (ML) models using a training set {*ξ*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si1.png) of *m* samples can be formulated as a finite-sum minimization problem as follows:

$\\min\\limits\_{w \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d}}\\left\\{ F(w) = \\frac{1}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{m}f(w;\\xi\_{i}) \\right\\}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si2.png)(2.1) 

The objective is to minimize a loss function with respect to model parameters *w*. This problem is known as empirical risk minimization and it covers a wide range of convex and non-convex problems from the ML domain, including, but not limited to, logistic regression, multi-kernel learning, conditional random fields and neural networks.

We want to solve [(2.1)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq1) in a distributed setting where many clients have their own local data sets and the finite-sum minimization problem is over the collection of all local data sets. A widely accepted approach is to repeatedly use the SGD [\[44](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0220),[45](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0225),[48\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0240) recursion

*w*[*t* + 1] = *w*[*t*] − *η*[*t*]∇*f*(*w*[*t*]; *ξ*),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si3.png)(2.2) 

where *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si4.png) represents the model after the *t*th iteration; *w*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si4.png) is used in computing the gradient of *f*(*w*[*t*]; *ξ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si5.png), where *ξ* is a data sample randomly selected from the data set {*ξ*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*m*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si1.png) which comprises the union of all local data sets.

This approach allows each client to perform local SGD recursions for the data samples *ξ* that belong to the client's local training data set. The updates as a result of the SGD recursion [(2.2)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq2) are sent to a centralized server who aggregates all received updates and maintains a global model. The server regularly broadcasts its most recent global model so that clients can use it in their local SGD computations. This allows each client to use what has been learned from the local data sets at the other clients. This leads to good accuracy of the final global model.

Each client performs SGD recursions for a batch of local data. These recursions together represent a local round and at the end of the local round a local model update (in the form of an aggregate of computed gradients during the round) is transmitted to the server. The server in turn adds the received local update to its global model – and once the server receives new updates from (a significant portion of) all clients, the global model is broadcast to each of the clients. When considering privacy, we are concerned about how much information these local updates reveal about the used local data sets. Each client wants to keep its local data set as private as possible with respect to the outside world which observes round communication (the outside world includes all other clients as well).

Rather than reducing the amount of round communication such that less sensitive information is leaked, differential privacy \[[13](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0065)–[15](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0075),[17](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0085)\] offers a solution in which each client-to-server communication is obfuscated by noise. If the magnitude of the added noise is not too much, then a good accuracy of the global model can still be achieved albeit at the price of more overall SGD iterations needed for convergence. On the other hand, only if the magnitude of the added noise is large enough, then good differential privacy guarantees can be given. This leads to a friction between desired differential privacy and desired utility/accuracy.

Section [2.2](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0015) starts discussing DP-SGD [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005), which implements differentially private mini-batch SGD. Section [2.3](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0055) explains differential privacy with various (divergence based) measures and properties. Section [2.4](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0075) continues detailing the state-of-the-art hypothesis testing based differential privacy, called *f*\-DP [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055), applied to DP-SGD. We conclude with open questions in Section [2.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0115).

## 2.2 Differential private SGD (DP-SGD)

We analyze the Gaussian-based differential privacy method, called DP-SGD, of [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005) in a distributed setting with many clients and a central aggregating server. A slightly generalized description of DP-SGD is depicted in [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010). The main goal of DP-SGD is to hide whether the collection of transmitted round updates $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) corresponds to a data set *d* versus a neighboring data set *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png); sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) are called neighbors if they differ in exactly one element. In order to accomplish this, DP-SGD introduces noise, which, as we will see, comes in two flavors, *clipping noise* and *Gaussian noise*.

![Algorithm 1 Differential private SGD.](images/B9780443190377000090/gr001.jpg)

Algorithm 1 Differential private SGD.

### 2.2.1 Clipping

Rather than using the gradient *a*[*h*] = ∇*f*(*w*, *ξ*[*h*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si8.png) itself, DP-SGD uses its clipped version \[∇*f*(*w*, *ξ*[*h*])\][*C*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si9.png) where

\[*x*\][*C*] = *x*/max {1, ∥*x*∥/*C*}.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si10.png)

We call this the *individual clipping* approach since each computed gradient is individually clipped. Clipping is needed because in general we cannot assume a bound *C* on the gradients (for example, the bounded gradient assumption is in conflict with strong convexity [\[44\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0220)), yet the added gradients in update *U* need to be bounded by some constant *C* in order for the DP analysis of [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005) to go through. The reason is that clipping introduces a bound on how much $U = \\sum\_{h = 1}^{m}{\\lbrack a\_{h}\\rbrack}\_{C}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si11.png) gets affected if the differentiating sample between *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) is used in its computation. Clipping forces a small distance between an update *U* that does not use the differentiating sample and an update *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png) that computes the same gradients as *U* except for one of its gradient computations which uses the differentiating sample. This means that if Gaussian noise is added to *U* and *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png), respectively, then the smaller the distance between *U* and *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png), the harder it is to figure out whether the actually observed noised update originates from *d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). This leads to a differential privacy guarantee.

Suppose that *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) influences another gradient computation, e.g., *a*[*h* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si14.png). Then, if the differentiating sample is used in the computation of *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png), this affects not only *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) but also *a*[*h* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si14.png). Even though both *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) and *a*[*h* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si14.png) will be clipped, this increases the distance between *U* and *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png), hence, this weakens the differential privacy. For this reason, the different gradient computations *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) in *U* should be independent of one another. In particular, we do not want to implement classical SGD where the computation of *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) updates the local model *w* which is used in the next gradient computation *a*[*h* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si14.png). This is the reason for implementing mini-batch SGD where each gradient *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) is computed for the same *w*.

Clipping introduces clipping noise defined as the difference between the clipped gradient \[*a*[*h*]\][*C*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si15.png) and the original gradient *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png). This affects the rate of convergence and leads to clipping bias. If convergence is towards a (local) minimum *w*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si16.png) of [(2.1)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq1), then DP-SGD will not get closer and closer to *w*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si16.png), but will converge to some model within a radius around *w*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si16.png), where the radius is composed of a clipping bias and a bias as a result of the desired DP guarantee by adding Gaussian noise, and the radius is also at least proportional to the last used step size. We notice that clipping noise may not reduce from round to round: Even though *E*[*ξ*]\[∇[*w*]*f*(*w*^(\*); *ξ*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si17.png) tends to zero (since we converge to a local minimum), the expected norm of the gradients *c*(*w*^(\*)) = *E*[*ξ*]\[∥∇[*w*]*f*(*w*^(\*); *ξ*)∥\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si18.png) generally does not converge to zero. For this reason, the clipping constant *C* must be appropriately set (and cannot be too small). For example, by using the *C* of another previous related learning task, or using a public data set for estimating *c*(*w*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si19.png) while executing DP-SGD.

### 2.2.2 Mini-batch SGD

DP-SGD is constrained to a mini-batch SGD approach where, before the start of the *b*th local round in epoch *e*, a random min-batch *S*[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si20.png) of sample size |*S*[*b*]| = *m*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si21.png) is selected out of a local data set *d* of size |*d*| = *N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si22.png). In the description of [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010), the sampling is done by a sampling procedure `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si23.png) before the start of epoch *e* for all rounds together. DP-SGD implements *subsampling* which chooses a uniformly random subset *S*[*b*] ⊆ *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si24.png) of size *m*.

The inner loop computes *m* gradients *a*[*h*] = ∇[*w*]*f*(*w*; *ξ*[*h*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si25.png). Since there are *N*/*m*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si26.png) rounds within an epoch, each epoch has (indeed) a total gradient complexity of *N* = |*d*|![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si27.png). We notice that each gradient is computed based on *w* which is the last received global model from the server through the interrupt service routine. In the original DP-SGD, a client waits at the start of a round till it receives the global model which includes the aggregated updates of all previous rounds from all clients. The formulation in [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010) allows for asynchronous behavior, including dropped (or reordering of) messages from the server which can lead to a client missing out on receiving global model versions. More importantly, the server may decide to broadcast global models at a lower rate than the rate(s) at which clients compute and communicate their noised round updates. This allows clients with different compute speeds/resources. Also, the rate at which round updates are computed is not restricted by the throughput of broadcast messages from the server to clients (of course, it remains restricted by the network throughput from the clients through aggregation nodes to the server). This implies that parameter *m* can potentially be chosen from the whole range {1, …, *N*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si28.png) including very small *m*, leading to many round updates per epoch, or large *m*, leading to only a couple round updates per epoch. We will later discuss the effect of *m* on convergence and accuracy and DP guarantee.

We notice that too much asynchronous behavior will hurt convergence of the mini-batch SGD approach and may lead to worse accuracy of the final global model. For this reason, before starting a round, a client can check to what extent the recently received global model deviates from the locally kept model. If this gets too far apart or if the last received global model happened too many rounds ago, then the client will want to wait till a new global model is received and the interrupt service routine is triggered. This implements the necessary synchronous behavior with respect to convergence and accuracy.

### 2.2.3 Gaussian noise

The clipped gradients \[*a*[*h*]\][*C*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si15.png) are summed together in round update *U*. At the end of each local round, the round update *U* is obfuscated by adding Gaussian noise

𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²)

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si29.png)

to each of *U*'s vector entries. The resulting noised round update $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) divided by the mini-batch size *m* is transmitted to the server.

For neighboring data sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png), we have that the *sensitivity* measured as the Euclidean distance between *U* based on *d* and *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png) based on *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) (see also Section [2.2.1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0020)) is at most 2*C*. An adversary trying to distinguish whether the observed update is from *d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) needs to figure out whether the observation is from

*U* + 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²**I**)   or   *U*^′ + 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²**I**).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si30.png)

Since ∥*U* − *U*^′∥ ≤ 2*C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si31.png), this is at best (for the adversary) equivalent to hypothesis testing of 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si32.png) vs. 𝒩(2*C*, (2*C**σ*)²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si33.png). After dividing by 2*C*, this is equivalent to hypothesis testing of

𝒩(0, *σ*²)   vs.   𝒩(1, *σ*²).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si34.png)(2.3) 

We see that any differential privacy guarantee for the round update is characterized by *σ*.

The argument above does not depend on the properties of function *f*. In fact, we are free in how we compute the *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) in line 14 of [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010). These may themselves depend on more than one sample as long as we start with *w* for each computation of *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png). For example, the *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) may compute updates coming from a local SGD approach (as used in federated learning), they may be computed according to a mini-batch SGD style approach, or some other momentum based approach.

The attentive reader may notice that the original DP-SGD adds 𝒩(0, (*C**σ*)²**I**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si35.png), a factor of 2 less. This is because its DP analysis and proof assume a slightly different subsampling method. In the original DP-SGD, we have that each round selects a random mini-batch of *exactly m* samples; this leads to the factor 2 since *U* and *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png) will differ in one gradient, hence, *U* − *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si36.png) cancels all gradients except for one in *U* and one in *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png), both contributing at most *C* to the norm ∥*U* − *U*^′∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si37.png), hence, the factor 2.

However, the software package Opacus [\[46\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0230) implements the sampling of DP-SGD differently: Mini-batches do not have a fixed size, they have a probabilistic size. For each sample *ξ* ∈ *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si38.png), we flip a coin and with probability *m*/*N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si39.png) we add *ξ* to the mini-batch. This means that the *expected* mini-batch size is equal to *m*. As a result, the DP analysis of [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005) holds true and the factor 2 can be eliminated. The reason is that now (in the DP analysis) *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si12.png) has all the gradients of *U* together with one extra gradient based on the single differentiating sample between *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). This implies that all gradients in *U* − *U*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si36.png) cancel except for that based on the differentiating sample, hence, ∥*U* − *U*^′∥ ≤ *C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si40.png).

In the above argument, we *assume* that the adversary does not learn the actually used mini-batch size otherwise we will again need the factor 2 (see also Section [2.4.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0100)). The observed scaled noised update $\\overline{U}/m$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si41.png) scales in expectation with the expected norm of a single computed gradient times the used mini-batch size divided by the expected mini-batch size *m*. This shows how $\\overline{U}/m$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si41.png) depends on the used mini-batch size where, for large *m* and *N*, it seems reasonable to assume that the adversary cannot gain significant knowledge about the used mini-batch size from $\\overline{U}/m$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si41.png). We conclude that a probabilistic mini-batch size is a DP technique that offers a factor 2 gain. This chapter summarizes the *f*\-DP framework explained for sampling with fixed mini-batch size leading to the extra factor 2 (the probabilistic approach can be added as a complimentary technique).

### 2.2.4 Aggregation at the server

The server maintains a global model, which we denote by *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png). The server adds to *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png) the received scaled noised round update $\\overline{U}/m$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si41.png) after multiplying with the round step size^([¹](#fn1))

$\\eta\_{(e - 1)\\frac{N}{m} + b}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si44.png)

(the same as the local model update of *w* by the client). This allows a diminishing^([²](#fn2))

Each client will select its own DP posture with own selected parameters *m*, *C*, *σ*, and own data set *d* with its own size *N*. It makes sense for the server to collect the noised round updates from various clients during consecutive time windows and broadcast updated global models at the end of each window. Rather than adding all the received $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) within a time window to the global model *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png) (after multiplying with the appropriate client-specific step sizes and dividing by the appropriate client-specific mini-batch sizes), the server will add a mix of the various local updates. The mix is according to some weighing vector giving more weight to those clients whom the server judges having ‘better’ training data sets for the learning task at hand. In federated learning, the server will ask for each time window a random subset of clients to participate in the training. In the above context, it makes sense to have the step sizes be diminishing^([³](#fn3))

### 2.2.5 Interrupt service routine

The interrupt service routine will replace the locally kept model *w* by a received global model *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png). This may happen in the middle of a round. We notice that *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png) depends on previously transmitted noised round updates by the client and other clients. We will discuss how each of these previous noised round updates have a DP guarantee. By the so-called post-processing lemma, these previously transmitted noised round updates can participate in the current computation of a round update *U* through its dependency on the global model *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png) (through the gradients in *U*) without weakening the DP guarantee for $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) (which includes Gaussian noise on top of *U*).

Similarly, the client locally updates model *w* with $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) at the end of a round. In next rounds this implies that *w* still only depends on previously transmitted noised round updates by the client and other clients, and, again by the post-processing lemma, the DP guarantees of future noised round updates do not degrade. As soon as a new global model *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png) is received by the interrupt service routine, it will overwrite *w*, that is, the current local model is discarded. This is justified because the newly received global model includes the client's own previously communicated noised updates $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) (if the corresponding messages were not dropped and did not suffer too much latency), hence, the information of its own local updates is incorporated in the newly received *ŵ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si42.png).

### 2.2.6 DP principles and utility

The strength of the resulting DP guarantee depends on how much utility we are okay with sacrificing. The differential privacy guarantee is discussed in Section [2.4](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0075). The principle of using Gaussian noise *bootstraps* DP for each round, see [(2.3)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq6); the principle of subsampling in the form of random mini-batches of size *m amplifies* DP (because only with probability *m*/*N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si39.png) a round uses the differentiating sample and can leak privacy in the first place); and the principle of *composition* of DP guarantees for each round over multiple epochs yields the overall DP guarantee.

Utility is measured in terms of the (test) accuracy of the final global model and secondary metrics are convergence rate, round complexity (*N*/*m*) ⋅ *E*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si45.png) calculated as the total number of rounds per client (communication is costly), total gradient complexity *E* ⋅ *N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si46.png) calculated as the total number of computed gradients per client, information dispersal characterized by the delay or latency of what is learned from local data sets which is calculated as the number *m* of gradient computations between consecutive round communications to the server, and client's memory usage.

The final accuracy depends on the amount of clipping noise and Gaussian noise: Once convergence sets in, the clipping noise will be small and close to zero if the clipping constant is appropriately chosen (at least a factor larger than *c*(*w*^(\*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si19.png), see Section [2.2.1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0020)). However, each round update *U* has noise sampled from 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²**I**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si47.png) added to itself. If this noise is small relative to the norm of *U*, then we expect accuracy not to suffer too much if the neural network model is sufficiently robust against noise (it turns out that deeper neural networks are quite sensitive). When convergence progresses and the clipping constant is large enough, then *U*/*m*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si48.png) behaves like an average of unclipped gradients which is an estimate of *E*[*ξ*]\[∇[*w*]*f*(*w*^(\*); *ξ*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si17.png) which tends to zero. This means that the Gaussian noise relative to the norm of *U* becomes larger, which puts a limit on how much accuracy/utility can be achieved.

Since the DP guarantee depends on *σ* but not on *C* while the added Gaussian noise scales with *C* ⋅ *σ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si49.png), we will want to implement a form of (differential private) adaptive clipping (we notice that the DP analysis of DP-SGD holds for clipping constants *C* that vary from round to round). Experimentation is needed to fine-tune the parameters *m*, (adaptive) *C*, and *σ*. Despite fine-tuning, we remark that the added clipping and Gaussian noise for differential privacy results in convergence to a final global model with smaller (test) accuracy (than what otherwise, without DP, can be achieved).

The following thought experiment shows how the batch size *m* influences utility and differential privacy. Suppose we increase *m* to *am*, a factor *a* larger. Then the norm of updates *U* will become a factor *a* larger. As a result, with respect to convergence to the final global model, we should be able to cope with a factor *a* larger Gaussian noise. That is, by keeping the relative amount of noise with respect to the norm of *U* constant, the new updates corresponding to batch size *am* can be noised with

*a* ⋅ 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²**I**) = 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ* ⋅ *a*)²**I**).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si50.png)

In fact the communicated averaged noised round update $\\overline{U}/(am)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si51.png) has noise

*a* ⋅ 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*)²**I**)/(*a**m*) = 𝒩(0, (2*C**σ*/*m*)²**I**),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si52.png)

the same as the original communicated averaged noised round update (before the thought experiment). This shows that we can use the factor *a* for increasing (1) the clipping constant *C* (which reduces the clipping noise, which is most prevalent at the start of DP-SGD, so that convergence can more easily bootstrap) and/or increasing (2) the standard deviation *σ* (which improves the DP guarantee); the resulting new clipping constant *C*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si53.png) and standard deviation *σ*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si54.png) satisfy 2*C*^′*σ*^′ = 2*C**σ* ⋅ *a*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si55.png).

However, the disadvantage of increasing the batch size with a factor *a* is a multiplicative factor *a* increased amount of gradient computations since overall we will still need the same number of rounds for convergence, or, equivalently, the same number of SGD update steps toward a local minimum *w*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si16.png). This means a factor *a* larger number of epochs (one epoch measures *N* gradient computations, hence, if *m* is increased to *ma*, we have a factor *a* smaller number of rounds per epoch). But this has a direct impact on the DP guarantee. As we will see in Section [2.4.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0100) (when discussing Gaussian DP), before the thought experiment we have a *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png)\-DP guarantee, where *μ* is proportional to $\\sqrt{Em/(N\\sigma^{2})}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si57.png) for ‘large *N* and *E*.’ The thought experiment increases *m* by *a* and increases *E* by *a*. Hence, for the same *σ* we will now have the significantly worse  ≈ *G*[*μ* ⋅ *a*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si58.png)\-DP guarantee. If the factor *a* is fully used for increasing *σ* by a factor *a*, then for ‘large *N* and *E*’ the Gaussian DP parameter *μ* ⋅ *a*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si59.png) decreases back to *μ* and the overall DP guarantee remains the same. Notice that the total number of gradient computations increases from *E* to *aE*, while the balance between utility and differential privacy seems to remain^([⁴](#fn4))

Hyperparameter search depends on the used data set. Either we adopt a hyperparameter setting from another similar learning task, or we search for hyperparameters based on the client data sets. In practice, in order to find good parameters *m*, *C*, and *σ*, we basically do a grid search by (1) fixing some standard settings (from similar learning tasks) for sample size *m*, e.g., 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256, etc., (2) fixing some standard settings (from similar learning tasks) for clipping constant *C*, e.g., 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, etc., and then (3) trying some reasonable settings for *σ* (based on the client data sets). If the grid search indeed uses client data sets, then we need to make sure that the additional privacy leakage due to the search is small. This is discussed in Appendix D of [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005), see also [\[25\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0125).

### 2.2.7 Normalization

In practice we will also want to use data normalization [\[51\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0255) as a pre-processing step. This requires computing the mean and variance over all data samples from *d*. This makes normalized data samples depend on all samples in *d*. For this reason, we need differential private data normalization. That is, a differential private noisy mean and noisy variance is revealed a priori. This leads to some privacy leakage. The advantage is that we can now rewrite 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si64.png) as an algorithm that takes as input *w*, the original data samples {*ξ*[*h*]}[*h* ∈ *S*[*b*]]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si65.png) together with the revealed noisy mean and noisy variance. This 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si64.png) first normalizes each data sample after which it starts to compute gradients, etc. In the *f*\-DP framework, privacy leakage is now characterized as a trade-off function of the differential private data normalization pre-processing composed with the trade-off function corresponding to the DP analysis of DP-SGD (which does not consider data normalization).

We notice that batch normalization is not compatible with the DP analysis of DP-SGD with its individual clipping of each gradient (since this introduces dependencies among the clipped gradients in *U* and the upper bound of 2*C* on the sensitivity does not hold). On the other hand, layer normalization as well as group and instance normalization are compatible (because these only concern single gradient computations). We notice that if *a*[*h*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si13.png) is computed itself by using a local mini-batch SGD approach, then batch normalization of the used mini-batch can be integrated within its computation.

As a final remark, our discussion assumes that we already know how to represent data samples by extracting features. We can use Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, that is, learning a set of features which we want to use to represent data samples. PCA can be made differentially private [\[6\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0030) in that the resulting feature extraction method (feature transform) has a DP guarantee with respect to the data samples that were used for computing the transform. DP-SGD can be seen as a post-processing after PCA, which is used to represent the local training data samples for which DP-SGD achieves a DP guarantee. In practice, we often already know how to represent the data for our learning task and we already know which function *f*(*w*; *ξ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si66.png) to use, i.e., which neural network topology and loss function to use (due to the success of transfer learning we can adopt data representations and *f* from other learning tasks).

## 2.3 Differential privacy

In order to prevent data leakage from inference attacks in machine learning [\[36\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0180) such as the deep leakage from gradients attack [\[21](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0105),[59](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0295),[60\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0300) or the membership inference attack [\[43](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0215),[49](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0245),[50\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0250), a range of privacy-preserving methods have been proposed. Privacy-preserving solutions for federated learning are Local Differential Privacy (LDP) solutions [\[1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005),2,[12](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0060),[26](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0130),[42](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0210),5[2\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0010) and Central Differential Privacy (CDP) solutions [\[23](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0115),[39](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0195),[42](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0210),[47](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0235),[58\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0290). In LDP, the noise for achieving differential privacy is computed locally at each client and is added to the updates before sending to the server – in this chapter we only consider LDP. In CDP, a *trusted server* (also known as trusted third party) aggregates received client updates into a global model; in order to achieve differential privacy the server adds noise to the global model before communicating it to the clients.

Differential privacy \[[13](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0065)–[15](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0075),[17](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0085)\], see [\[16\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0080) for an excellent textbook, defines privacy guarantees for algorithms on databases, in our case a client's sequence of mini-batch gradient computations on his/her training data set. The guarantee quantifies into what extent the output of a client (the collection of updates communicated to the server) can be used to differentiate among two adjacent training data sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) (i.e., where one set has one extra element compared to the other set).

### 2.3.1 Characteristics of a differential privacy measure

In DP-SGD, the client wants to keep its local training data set as private as possible. Each noised round update $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) leaks privacy. Let us define round mechanism ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png) as the round computation that outputs $\\overline{U}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si6.png) for round *b*. The input of ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png) is data set *d* together with an updated local model *w*. We have the following recursion

${\\overline{U}}\_{b}\\leftarrow\\mathcal{M}\_{b}(w\_{b};d),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si68.png)

where *w*[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si69.png) is a function of received global model updates which themselves depend on other client's round updates in combination with own previously transmitted round updates ${\\overline{U}}\_{1},\\ldots,{\\overline{U}}\_{b - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si70.png). To express this dependency, we use the notation

$w\_{b}\\leftarrow\\mathsf{W}({\\overline{U}}\_{1},\\ldots,{\\overline{U}}\_{b - 1}),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si71.png)

where W receives the global models of the server (and in essence reflects the interrupt service routine). We define the overall mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) as the (adaptive) composition of all round mechanisms ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png), i.e.,

$\\{{\\overline{U}}\_{b}\\}\\leftarrow\\mathcal{M}(d)\\text{~with~}{\\overline{U}}\_{b}\\leftarrow\\mathcal{M}\_{b}(\\mathtt{W}({\\overline{U}}\_{1},\\ldots,{\\overline{U}}\_{b - 1});d).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si73.png)

When defining a DP measure, we will want to be able to *compose* the DP guarantees for the different round mechanisms ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png): If we can prove that ℳ[*b*](`a``u``x`;  ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si74.png) has a certain DP guarantee, denoted by `D``P`[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si75.png), for *all* aux (that can be output by `W`(…)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si76.png)), then the composition ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) of all round mechanisms ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png) should have a composed DP guarantee

`D``P`[1] ⊗ `D``P`[2] ⊗ … ⊗ `D``P`[(*N*/*m*) ⋅ *E*]

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si77.png)

for some composition tensor ⊗ over DP measures.

Once a DP guarantee for mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) is proven, we do not want it to weaken due to *post-processing* of the output of ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png). In particular, the central server uses the output of ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) for keeping track of and computing a final global model for the learning task at hand. This final model should still have the same (or stronger) differential privacy posture. Let us denote the post-processing by a procedure P. If ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) has DP guarantee DP, then we want `P` ∘ ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si78.png) to also have DP guarantee DP (this is called the post-processing lemma),

\[`D``P` for ℳ] ⇒ [`D``P` for `P` ∘ ℳ].

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si79.png)

We want our DP measure to be compatible with *subsampling*: We want to be able to show that if a round mechanism ℳ[*b*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si67.png) has guarantee DP without subsampling, then ℳ[*b*] ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si80.png) has an ‘easy’ to characterize amplified guarantee `D``P`^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si81.png), ‘`D``P`^′ ≥ `D``P`![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si82.png).’

Finally, we want a differential privacy measure which fits our intuition, in particular, how privacy should be characterized and in what circumstances an attacker can learn private information from observed mechanism outputs. Differential privacy measures are about the difficulty of distinguishing whether the observed output *o* is from the distribution ℳ(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si83.png) or from the distribution ℳ(*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si84.png), where *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) are neighboring data sets in that they have all but one differentiating sample in common. The DP guarantee measures in to what extent

`Pr` [*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*)\]   and   `Pr` [*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*^′)\]

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si85.png)

are alike for *all* neighboring *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). Here, we want to reflect the intuition that for more likely observations *o* the two probabilities should be close together while for unlikely observations *o* we care less whether the two probabilities are close. This reflects how we think about the adversary. Only in rare unlikely cases, a lot or all privacy may leak, while in the common case there is very little privacy leakage. In cryptology we would want to interpret ‘rare’ as a negligible probability in some security parameter and in the common case we want the two probabilities/distributions to be ‘statistically close’ with their distance negligible in some security parameter. Such strong guarantees cannot be extracted from DP analysis where we control privacy leakage in exchange for utility/accuracy; we cannot make privacy leakage negligible.

The DP measure is characterized in terms of probabilities and statistics. This is referred to as static security or information-theoretical security and allows an adversary with unbounded computational resources in order to differentiate between the hypotheses *o* ∼ ℳ(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si86.png) and *o* ∼ ℳ(*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si87.png). For completeness, in cryptology we also have the notion of computational security meaning that the difficulty of differentiating the two hypotheses can be reduced to solving a computational hard problem (and, since the brightest mathematicians and computer scientists have not been able to find an algorithm which solves this problem efficiently with practical computational resources, we believe that the attacker cannot solve this problem in feasible time). Computational security allows one to obtain security guarantees where the attackers advantage or success is negligible in some security parameter.

The above expresses individual privacy. We can generalize towards group privacy by considering data sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) that differ in at most *g* samples. In this case we say that a mechanism has a DP guarantee with respect to a group of *g* samples.

### 2.3.2 (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-differential privacy

A randomized mechanism ℳ : *D* → *R*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si89.png) is (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP (Differentially Private) [\[14\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0070) if for any adjacent *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) in *D* and for any subset *S* ⊆ *R*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si90.png) of outputs,

`Pr` [ℳ(*d*) ∈ *S*\] ≤ *e*^(*ϵ*) ⋅ `Pr` [ℳ(*d*^′) ∈ *S*\] + *δ*,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si91.png)(2.4) 

where the probabilities are taken over the coin flips of mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png).

Historically, differential privacy was introduced [\[14\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0070) and first defined as *ϵ*\-DP [\[15\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0075) which is (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP with *δ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si92.png). In order to achieve *ϵ*\-DP even an unlikely set *S* of outputs needs to satisfy [(2.4)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq16) for *δ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si92.png). This means that the tail distributions of `Pr` [ℳ(*d*) ∈ *S*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si93.png) and `Pr` [ℳ(*d*^′) ∈ *S*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si94.png) cannot differ by more than a factor of *e*^(*ϵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si95.png). This is a much too strong DP requirement, since the probability to observe an output that corresponds to unlikely tail events is already very small to begin with. Therefore, *δ* was introduced so that tail distributions with probability ⩽*δ* do not need to be close together within a factor of *e*^(*ϵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si95.png). This allows one to achieve the more relaxed (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP guarantee where an *ϵ*\-DP guarantee cannot be proven.

The privacy loss incurred by observing an output *o* is given by

$L\_{\\mathcal{M}(d)\\|\\mathcal{M}(d^{\\prime})}^{o} = \\ln\\left( \\frac{\\mathtt{\\Pr}\\lbrack\\mathcal{M}(d) = o\\rbrack}{\\mathtt{\\Pr}\\lbrack\\mathcal{M}(d^{\\prime}) = o\\rbrack} \\right).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si96.png)(2.5) 

As explained in [\[17\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0085), (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP ensures that for all adjacent *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) the absolute value of privacy loss will be bounded by *ϵ* with probability at least 1 − *δ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si97.png) (with probability at most *δ*, observation *o* is part of the tail); (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP allows a *δ* probability of ‘catastrophic privacy failure’ and from a cryptographic perspective we want this negligibly small.
