However, when using differential privacy in machine learning, we typically use *δ* = 1/*N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si98.png) (or 1/(10*N*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si99.png)) inversely proportional with the data set size *N* (this seems to correspond well with the intuition when a local update should cause an unlikely/tail observation due to the nature of the specific batch of local data samples that was used in the computation of the local update). Concerning parameter *ϵ*, the larger the *ϵ*, the more certain the adversary is about which of *d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) caused observation *o*.

Compared to (*ϵ*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si100.png)\-DP, the relaxation by *δ* allows an improved and asymptotically tight analysis of the cumulative privacy loss incurred by composition of multiple differentially private mechanisms; [\[18\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0090) states an advanced composition theorem (a factor of one-half improvement over [\[19\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0095)): For all *ϵ*, *δ*, *δ*^′ ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si101.png), the class of (*ϵ*, *δ*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si102.png)\-DP mechanisms satisfies

$(\\sqrt{2k\\ln(1/\\delta)} \\cdot \\epsilon + k\\epsilon(e^{\\epsilon} - 1)/2,k\\delta^{\\prime} + \\delta)\\text{-DP}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si103.png)

under *k*\-fold adaptive composition. This means that only for *k* ≤ (1 − *δ*)/*δ*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si104.png) the privacy failure probability remains bounded to something smaller than 1.

For group privacy, the literature shows (*g**ϵ*, *g**e*^(*g* − 1)*δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si105.png)\-DP for groups of size *g*. Here, we see an exponential dependency in *g* due to the *g**e*^(*g* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si106.png) term in the privacy failure probability. This means that only for very small *δ*, the failure probability remains bounded to something smaller than 1.

We conclude that *k*\-fold composition and group privacy for group size *g* only lead to useful bounds for relatively small *k* and *g*. If we restrict ourselves to a subclass of mechanisms, then we may be able to prove practical DP bounds for composition and group privacy for much larger and practical *k* and *g*. We will define such subclasses by imposing properties on the privacy loss.

### 2.3.3 Divergence-based DP measures

In order to get better trade-offs for composition and group privacy, we want to weigh the tail distribution of unlikely observations in such a way that more unlikely observations are allowed to leak even more privacy. So, rather than weighing all unlikely observations equally likely, which results in the privacy failure probability *δ*, we want to be more careful. This will allow improved DP bounds for composition and group privacy.

The first idea is to treat the loss function [(2.5)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq17) as a random variable *Z* and note that in a *k*\-fold composition we observe *k* drawings of random variable *Z*. Due to the law of large numbers, the average of these drawings will be concentrated around the mean of the loss function. This leads to the notion of Concentrated Differential Privacy (CDP), first introduced in [\[18\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0090) by framing the loss function as a sub-Gaussian random variable after subtracting its mean. This was re-interpreted and relaxed by using Renyi entropy in [\[5\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0025) and its authors followed up with the notion zero-CDP (zCDP) in [\[5\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0025): A mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) is *ρ*\-zCDP if, for all *α* > 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si107.png), the Renyi divergence

$\\mathtt{D}\_{\\alpha}(\\mathcal{M}(d)\\|\\mathcal{M}(d^{\\prime})) = \\frac{\\ln(\\mathbb{E}\_{o \\sim \\mathcal{M}(d)}\\lbrack e^{(1 - \\alpha)Z}\\rbrack)}{1 - \\alpha}\\text{~with~}Z = L\_{\\mathcal{M}(d)\\|\\mathcal{M}(d^{\\prime})}^{o}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si108.png)

satisfies

`D`[*α*](ℳ(*d*)∥ℳ(*d*^′)) ≤ *ρ**α*.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si109.png)(2.6) 

This DP guarantee requires the tail of *Z* to be sub-Gaussian, i.e., `Pr` [*Z* > *t* + *ρ*\] < *e*^( − *t*²/(4*ρ*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si110.png) for all *t* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si111.png) (the tail behaves like *Z* ∼ 𝒩(*ρ*, 2*ρ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si112.png)). If the loss function satisfies this property for a collection of *k* mechanisms (each of the mechanisms is *ρ*\-zCDP), then their *k*\-fold adaptive composition is *kρ*\-zCDP. If a mechanism is *ρ*\-zCDP for individual privacy, then it is *g*²*ρ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si113.png)\-zCDP for groups of size *g*. This shows that if we can prove that our DP principles lead to a sub-Gaussian tail of the loss function *Z*, then we obtain interpretable DP guarantees even for large *k* and *g*.

After the introduction of *ρ*\-zCDP, Renyi DP (RDP) was introduced by [\[41\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0205); (*ω*, *τ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si114.png)\-RDP requires

`D`[*α*](ℳ(*d*)∥ℳ(*d*^′)) ≤ *τ* for all *α* ∈ (1, *ω*).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si115.png)

Here, *α* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si116.png) bounds the geometric mean of *e*^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si117.png), *α* = 2![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si118.png) bounds the arithmetic mean of *e*^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si117.png), *α* = 3![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si119.png) bounds the quadratic mean of *e*^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si117.png), etc., and *α* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si120.png) bounds the maximum value of *e*^(*Z*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si117.png) which is equivalent to (*τ*, 0)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si121.png)\-DP. RDP also leads to simple computable composition and group privacy. The advantage of zCDP over RDP is that it covers all *α* at once: Larger *α* put more weight on the tail of *Z*, also the mean gets larger. This means that *τ* in the RDP definition should increase with *α* and this is realized by zCDP by setting *τ* = *ρ**α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si122.png) for all *α* ∈ (1, ∞)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si123.png).

The above discussion leads naturally to the definition of (*ρ*, *ω*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si124.png)\-tCDP [\[4\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0020): A mechanism is *ω*\-truncated *ρ*\-CDP if it satisfies [(2.6)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq20) only for *α* ∈ (1, *ω*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si125.png). tCDP requires *Z* to be sub-Gaussian near the origin (like zCDP), i.e., `Pr` [*Z* > *t* + *ρ*\] < *e*^( − *t*²/(4*ρ*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si110.png) for all 0 ≤ *t* ≤ 2*ρ*(*ω* − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si126.png), but only subexponential in *Z*'s tail, i.e., we get the weaker subexponential tail bound `Pr` [*Z* > *t* + *ρ*\] ≤ *e*^((*ω* − 1)²*ρ*)*e*^( − (*ω* − 1)*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si127.png). This relaxes zCDP while still obtaining interpretable DP guarantees for composition and group privacy, and also subsampling.

The main concern with each of the divergence based DP measures is a lack of transparency of how the attacker can best distinguish the hypotheses *o* ∼ ℳ(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si86.png) and *o* ∼ ℳ(*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si87.png). The next section introduces the *f*\-DP framework which provides a hypothesis testing based approach. It introduces trade-off functions that capture all the information needed for fully characterizing privacy leakage; a trade-off function can be used to derive any divergence based DP guarantee like those discussed above (but not the other way around), see Appendix B in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055). Rather than extracting a divergence based DP guarantee from a trade-off function for DP-SGD, we will keep the trade-off function itself as it has an easy transparent interpretation.

## 2.4 Gaussian differential privacy

Dong et al. [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) introduced the state-of-the-art DP formulation based on hypothesis testing. From the attacker's perspective, it is natural to formulate the problem of distinguishing two neighboring data sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) based on the output of a DP mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) as a hypothesis testing problem:

*H*[0] :  the underlying data set is *d*     vs.     *H*[1] :  the underlying data set is *d*^′.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si128.png)

Here, neighboring means that either |*d* ∖ *d*^′| = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si129.png) or |*d*^′ ∖ *d*| = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si130.png). More precisely, in the context of mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png), ℳ(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si83.png) and ℳ(*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si84.png) take as input representations *r* and *r*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si131.png) of data sets *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) which are ‘neighbors.’ The representations are mappings from a set of indices to data samples with the property that if *r*(*i*) ∈ *d* ∩ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si132.png) or *r*^′(*i*) ∈ *d* ∩ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si133.png), then *r*(*i*) = *r*^′(*i*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si134.png). This means that the mapping from indices to data samples in *d* ∩ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si135.png) is the same for the representation of *d* and the representation of *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). In other words, the mapping from indices to data samples for *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) only differ for indices corresponding to the differentiating data samples in (*d* ∖ *d*^′) ∪ (*d*^′ ∖ *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si136.png). In this sense the two mappings (data set representations) are neighbors.

We define the Type I and Type II errors by

*α*[*ϕ*] = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*)]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]  and  *β*[*ϕ*] = 1 − 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*^′)]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\],

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si137.png)

where *ϕ* in \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si138.png) denotes the rejection rule which takes the output of the DP mechanism as input. We flip a coin and reject the null hypothesis with probability *ϕ*. The optimal trade-off between Type I and Type II errors is given by the trade-off function

$T(\\mathcal{M}(d),\\mathcal{M}(d^{\\prime}))(\\alpha) = \\inf\\limits\_{\\phi}\\{\\beta\_{\\phi}\\ :\\ \\alpha\_{\\phi} \\leqslant \\alpha\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si139.png)

for *α* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si140.png), where the infimum is taken over all measurable rejection rules *ϕ*. If the two hypotheses are fully indistinguishable, then this leads to the trade-off function 1 − *α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si141.png). We say a function *f* ∈ \[0, 1\] → \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si142.png) is a trade-off function if and only if it is convex, continuous, non-increasing, and 0 ≤ *f*(*x*) ≤ 1 − *x*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si143.png) for *x* ∈ \[0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si144.png).

We define a mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) to be *f*\-DP if *f* is a trade-off function and

*T*(ℳ(*d*), ℳ(*d*^′)) ≥ *f*

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si145.png)

for all neighboring *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). Proposition 2.5 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) is an adaptation of a result in [\[56\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0280) and states that a mechanism is (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP if and only if the mechanism is *f*[*ϵ*, *δ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si146.png)\-DP, where

*f*[*ϵ*, *δ*](*α*) = max {0, 1 − *δ* − *e*^(*ϵ*)*α*, (1 − *δ* − *α*)*e*^( − *ϵ*)}.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si147.png)

We see that *f*\-DP has the (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP formulation as a special case. It turns out that the original DP-SGD algorithm can be tightly analyzed by using *f*\-DP.

### 2.4.1 Gaussian DP

In order to proceed, [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) first defines Gaussian DP as another special case of *f*\-DP as follows: We define the trade-off function

*G*[*μ*](*α*) = *T*(𝒩(0, 1), 𝒩(*μ*, 1))(*α*) = *Φ*(*Φ*^( − 1)(1 − *α*) − *μ*),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si148.png)

where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution of 𝒩(0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si149.png). We define a mechanism to be *μ*\-Gaussian DP if it is *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png)\-DP. Corollary 2.13 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) shows that a mechanism is *μ*\-Gaussian DP if and only if it is (*ϵ*, *δ*(*ϵ*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si150.png)\-DP for all *ϵ* ≥ 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si151.png), where

$\\delta(\\epsilon) = \\Phi( - \\frac{\\epsilon}{\\mu} + \\frac{\\mu}{2}) - e^{\\epsilon}\\Phi( - \\frac{\\epsilon}{\\mu} - \\frac{\\mu}{2}).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si152.png)(2.7) 

Suppose that a mechanism ℳ(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si83.png) computes some function *u*(*d*) ∈ ℝ^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si153.png) and adds Gaussian noise 𝒩(0, (*c**σ*)²**I**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si154.png), that is, the mechanism outputs *o* ∼ *u*(*d*) + 𝒩(0, (*c**σ*)²**I**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si155.png). Suppose that *c* denotes the sensitivity of function *u*( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si156.png), that is,

∥*u*(*d*) − *u*(*d*^′)∥ ≤ *c*

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si157.png)

for neighboring *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png); the mechanism corresponding to one round update in [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010) has *sensitivity* *c* = 2*C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si158.png). After projecting the observed *o* onto the line that connects *u*(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si159.png) and *u*(*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si160.png) and after normalizing by dividing by *c*, we have that differentiating whether *o* corresponds to *d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) is in the best case for the adversary (i.e., ∥*u*(*d*) − *u*(*d*^′)∥ = *c*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si161.png)) equivalent to differentiating whether a received output is from 𝒩(0, *σ*²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si162.png) or 𝒩(1, *σ*²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si163.png); equivalently, from 𝒩(0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si149.png) or 𝒩(1/*σ*, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si164.png). This is how the Gaussian trade-off function *G*[*σ*^( − 1)]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si165.png) comes into the picture.

### 2.4.2 Subsampling

Besides implementing Gaussian noise, DP-SGD also uses subsampling: For a data set *d* of *N* samples, `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si166.png) selects a subset of size *m* from *d* uniformly at random. We define convex combinations

*f*[*p*](*α*) = *p**f*(*α*) + (1 − *p*)(1 − *α*)

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si167.png)

with corresponding *p*\-sampling operator

*C*[*p*](*f*) = min {*f*[*p*], *f*[*p*]^( − 1)}^( \* \*),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si168.png)

where the conjugate *h*^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si169.png) of a function *h* is defined as

$h^{\\ast}(y) = \\sup\\limits\_{x}\\{ yx - h(x)\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si170.png)

and the inverse *h*^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si171.png) of a trade-off function *h* is defined as

*h*^( − 1)(*α*) = inf {*t* ∈ \[0, 1\] | *h*(*t*) ≤ *α*}

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si172.png)(2.8) 

and is itself a trade-off function (as an example, we notice that *G*[*μ*] = *G*[*μ*]^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si173.png) and we say *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png) is symmetric). Theorem 4.2 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) shows that if a mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) on data sets of size *N* is *f*\-DP, then the subsampled mechanism ℳ ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si174.png) is *C*[*m*/*N*](*f*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si175.png)\-DP.

The intuition behind operator *C*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si176.png) is as follows. First, `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si166.png) samples the differentiating element between *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) with probability *p*. In this case the computations ℳ ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si177.png) and ℳ ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si178.png) are different and hypothesis testing is possible with trade-off function *f*(*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si179.png). With probability 1 − *p*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si180.png), no hypothesis testing is possible and we have trade-off function 1 − *α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si141.png). This leads to the convex combination *f*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si181.png).

Second, we notice if *h* = *T*(ℳ(*d*), ℳ(*d*^′))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si182.png), then *h*^( − 1) = *T*(ℳ(*d*^′), ℳ(*d*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si183.png). Therefore, if ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) is *f*\-DP (which holds for all pairs of neighboring data sets, in particular, for the pairs (*d*, *d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si184.png) and (*d*^′, *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si185.png)), then both *h* ≥ *f*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si186.png) and *h*^( − 1) ≥ *f*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si187.png) and we have a symmetric upper bound min {*h*, *h*^( − 1)} ≥ *f*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si188.png). Since *f* is a trade-off function, *f* is convex and we can compute a tighter upper bound: *f* is at most the largest convex function  ≤ min {*h*, *h*^( − 1)}![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si189.png), which is equal to the double conjugate min {*h*, *h*^( − 1)}^( \* \*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si190.png). From this we obtain the definition of operator *C*[*p*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si176.png).

### 2.4.3 Composition

The tensor product *f* ⊗ *h*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si191.png) for trade-off functions *f* = *T*(*P*, *Q*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si192.png) and *h* = *T*(*P*^′, *Q*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si193.png) is well-defined by

*f* ⊗ *h* = *T*(*P* × *P*^′, *Q* × *Q*^′).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si194.png)

Let *y*[*i*] ← ℳ[*i*](`aux`, *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si195.png) with `aux` = (*y*[1], …, *y*[*i* − 1])![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si196.png). Theorem 3.2 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) shows that if ℳ[*i*](`aux`,  ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si197.png) is *f*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si198.png)\-DP for all aux, then the composed mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png), which applies ℳ[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si199.png) in sequential order from *i* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si200.png) to *i* = *T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si201.png), is (*f*[1] ⊗ … ⊗ *f*[*T*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si202.png)\-DP. The tensor product is commutative.

As a special case Corollary 3.3 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) states that a composition of multiple Gaussian operators *G*[*μ*[*i*]]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si203.png) results in *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png) where

$\\mu = \\sqrt{\\sum\\limits\_{i}\\mu\_{i}^{2}}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si204.png)

### 2.4.4 Tight analysis of DP-SGD

We are now able to formulate the differential privacy guarantee of original DP-SGD since it is a composition of subsampled Gaussian DP mechanisms. Theorem 5.1 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) states that DP-SGD as introduced in [\[1\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0005) is

*C*[*m*/*N*](*G*[*σ*^( − 1)])^( ⊗ *T*)\-DP,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si205.png)

where *T* = (*N*/*m*) ⋅ *E*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si206.png) is the total number of local rounds. Since each of the theorems and results from [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) enumerated above are exact, we have a tight analysis. This leads in [\[61\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0305) to a (tight) differential privacy accountant^([⁵](#fn5))

### 2.4.5 Strong adversarial model

We assume an adversary who knows the differentiating samples in *d* ∖ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si207.png) and *d*^′ ∖ *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si208.png), but who a priori (before mechanism ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) is executed) may only know (besides, say, a 99% characterization of *d* ∩ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si135.png)) an estimate of the number of samples in the intersection of *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png), i.e., the adversary knows |*d* ∩ *d*^′| + *n**o**i**s**e*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si209.png) where the noise is large enough to yield a ‘sufficiently strong’ DP guarantee with respect to the size of the used data set (*d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png)). Since ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png) does not directly reveal the size of the used data set, we assume (as in prior literature) that the effect of *N* = |*d*| ≠ *N*^′ = |*d*^′|![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si210.png) contributes at most a very small amount of privacy leakage, sufficiently small to be discarded in our DP analysis, that is, we may as well assume *N* = *N*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si211.png) in our DP analysis.

This means that the tight *f*\-DP analysis of DP-SGD holds, even if we use the definition of neighboring data sets stating that either |*d* ∖ *d*^′| = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si129.png) or |*d*^′ ∖ *d*| = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si130.png); the original *f*\-DP analysis considers the case |*d* ∖ *d*^′| = |*d*^′ ∖ *d*| = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si212.png) and this requires the factor 2*C**σ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si213.png) in [Algorithm 1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#f0010). If we assume no knowledge about the exact data set sizes (as discussed above) and if we assume probabilistic sampling (see Section [2.4.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0100)), then we may only use *Cσ* saving a factor of 2 (which helps convergence to a higher accuracy).

In the setting of *N* = *N*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si211.png), the DP analysis in prior work considers an adversary 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png) who can mimic mechanism ℳ ∘ Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si215.png) in that it can replay, to a large extent, how Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si216.png) samples the used data set (*d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png)): We say a round has *k* differentiating data samples if Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si216.png) sampled a subset of indices which contains exactly *k* indices of differentiating data samples from (*d* ∖ *d*^′) ∪ (*d*^′ ∖ *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si136.png). The adversary knows how Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si216.png) operates and can derive a joint probability distribution ℙ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si217.png) of the number of differentiating data samples for each round within the sequence of rounds that define the series of epochs during which updates are computed.

Adversary 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png) does not know the exact instance drawn from ℙ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si217.png) but is, in the DP proof, given the ability to realize for each round the trade-off function *f*[*k*](*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si218.png) that corresponds to hypothesis testing between ℳ ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si177.png) and ℳ ∘ `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*](*d*^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si178.png) if `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si23.png) has selected *k* differentiating samples in that round. In the DP analysis that characterizes *f*[*k*](*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si218.png), adversary 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png) is given knowledge about the mapping from indices to values in *d* or *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). Here (as discussed before), the mapping from indices to values in *d* ∩ *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si135.png) is the same for the mapping from indices to values in *d* and the mapping from indices to values in *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png). Furthermore, the adversary can replay how Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si216.png) samples a subset of *m* indices from^([⁶](#fn6))

In the DP analysis, adversary 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png) is given knowledge about the number *k* of differentiating samples when analyzing a single round. That is, it is given an instance of ℙ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si217.png) projected on a single round. We notice that in expectation the sensitivity (see Section [2.4.1](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0080)) of a single round as observed by adversary 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png) for neighboring data sets is equal to (1 − *p*) ⋅ 0 + *p* ⋅ 2*C* = (*m*/*N*) ⋅ 2*C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si224.png) and this gives rise to an ‘expected’ trade-off function *G*[1/(*σ**N*/*m*)]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si225.png). A composition over *c*²(*N*/*m*)²![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si226.png) rounds gives *G*[*c*/*σ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si227.png). This leads us to believe that *C*[*m*/*N*](*G*[*σ*^( − 1)])^( ⊗ *T*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si222.png) converges to *G*[*c* ⋅ *h*(*σ*)]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si228.png) for *T* = *c*²(*N*/*m*)² → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si229.png) (or, equivalently, $\\sqrt{T} \\cdot m/N = c$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si230.png) with *T* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si231.png) and *N* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si232.png)) where *h*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si62.png) is some function that only depends on *σ* (see below). This intuition is confirmed by Corollary 5.4 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055), and is also indirectly by [\[53\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0265) which shows that DP-SGD is (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP for $\\sigma = \\sqrt{2(\\epsilon + \\ln(1/\\delta))/\\epsilon}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si233.png) for a wide range of parameter settings *N*, *m*, *T* with *T* at most  ≈ *ϵ*(*N*/*m*)²/2![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si234.png), and which matches Corollary 5.4 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) in that the upper bound on *T* can at most be a constant factor ≈4 larger (without violating the corollary).

By using *T* = (*N*/*m*) ⋅ *E*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si206.png), we have convergence to *G*[*c* ⋅ *h*(*σ*)]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si228.png) for $c = \\sqrt{mE/N}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si235.png) with *E* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si236.png) and *N* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si232.png). By using a Taylor series expansion, we have

$h(\\sigma) = \\sqrt{2(e^{\\sigma^{- 2}}\\Phi(\\frac{3\\sigma^{- 1}}{2}) + 3\\Phi( - \\frac{\\sigma^{- 1}}{2}) - 2)} = \\sigma^{- 1} \\cdot \\sqrt{1 + \\frac{15}{8}\\frac{\\sigma^{- 1}}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} + O(\\sigma^{- 2})}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si237.png)

This shows that for ‘large *N* and *E*’ DP-SGD is approximately *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png)\-DP with $\\mu = \\sqrt{mE/(N\\sigma^{2})}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si238.png). Notice that *σ* cannot be too small otherwise *h*(*σ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si62.png) behaves like $\\sqrt{2} \\cdot e^{1/(2\\sigma^{2})}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si239.png) which yields a very weak DP guarantee.

Clearly, a weaker (than 𝒜*d**v*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si214.png)) adversary with less capability (less knowledge of the used randomness by Sample[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si216.png) and ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png)) achieves a trade-off function  ≥ *C*[*m*/*N*](*G*[*σ*^( − 1)])^( ⊗ *T*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si240.png) closer to the ideal 1 − *α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si141.png). It remains an open problem to characterize realistic weaker adversaries that lead to larger (lower bounds of) trade-off functions.

### 2.4.6 Group privacy

Theorem 2.14 in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) analyzes how privacy degrades if *d* and *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si7.png) do not differ in just one sample, but rather in *g* samples. If a mechanism is *f*\-DP, then it is

\[1 − (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *g*)\]-DP

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si241.png)

for groups of size *g* (where ∘*g* denotes the *g*\-fold iterative composition of function 1 − *f*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si242.png), where 1 denotes the constant integer value 1 and not the identity function, i.e., (1 − *f*)(*α*) = 1 − *f*(*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si243.png)). This is a tight statement in that *there exist f* such that the trade-off function for groups of size *g* cannot be bounded better. In particular, for *f* = *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si244.png) we have *G*[*g**μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si245.png)\-DP for groups of size *g*.

The intuition behind the \[1 − (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *g*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si246.png)\-DP result is that the adversary can create a sequence of data sets *d*[0] = *d*, *d*[1], …, *d*[*g* − 1], *d*[*g*] = *d*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si247.png) such that each two consecutive data sets *d*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si248.png) and *d*[*i* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si249.png) are neighboring. We know that *T*(ℳ(*d*[*i*]), ℳ(*d*[*i* + 1])) ≥ *f*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si250.png). For each rejection rule, we may plot a point (in *x* and *y* coordinates)

(𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i*])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\], 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i* + 1])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si251.png)

Since *f*(*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si179.png) is a lower bound on the Type I vs. Type II error curve, the resulting collection of points is upper bounded by the curve 1 − *f*(*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si252.png). We have that *α* = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i*])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si253.png) is mapped to

𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i* + 1])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\] ≤ 1 − *f*(*α*) = (1 − *f*)(*α*).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si254.png)

By transitivity, we have that *α* = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d* = *d*[0])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si255.png) is mapped to

𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*^′ = *d*[*g*])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\] ≤ (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *g*)(*α*).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si256.png)

This yields the lower bound

*T*(ℳ(*d*), ℳ(*d*^′)) ≥ 1 − (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *g*)

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si257.png)

on the Type I vs. Type II error curve.

Let *ϕ*\[*α*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si258.png) denote a rejection rule that realizes the mapping from

*α* = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i*])]\[*ϕ*\[*α*\](*o*)\]   to   (1 − *f*)(*α*) = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i* + 1])]\[*ϕ*\[*α*\](*o*)\].

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si259.png)

Then the mapping from (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *i*)(*α*) = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i*])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si260.png) to (1 − *f*)^( ∘ (*i* + 1))(*α*) = 𝔼[*o* ∼ ℳ(*d*[*i* + 1])]\[*ϕ*(*o*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si261.png) is realized by *ϕ* = *ϕ*\[(1 − *f*)^( ∘ *i*)(*α*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si262.png). This shows that the lower bound 1 − (1 − *f*)^( ∘ *g*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si263.png) is tight only if we can choose all *ϕ*\[(1 − *f*)^( ∘ *i*)(*α*)\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si264.png) equal to one another. In general, this may not be the case for DP-SGD and future work may be able to produce an improved analysis for DP-SGD.

### 2.4.7 DP-SGD's trade-off function

We remind the reader that we can directly infer (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si88.png)\-DP guarantees from [(2.7)](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#deq28); function *δ*(*ϵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si265.png) turns out to only depend on $\\mu \\approx \\sqrt{mE/(N\\sigma^{2})}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si266.png), see Section [2.4.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0100). This leads to a dependency on data set size *N*, which, see Section [2.3.2](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0065), by setting *δ*(*ϵ*) = 1/*N*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si267.png) favorably biases smaller data sets.

Appendix B in [\[11\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0055) shows how to infer divergence based DP guarantees. In particular, *G*[*μ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si56.png)\-DP implies $(\\omega,\\frac{1}{2\\mu^{2}} \\cdot \\omega)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si268.png)\-RDP (Renyi differential privacy) for any *ω* > 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si269.png), hence, we have

$\\frac{1}{2\\mu^{2}}\\text{-zCDP}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si270.png)

For group privacy with *g* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si271.png), we have *G*[*μ* ⋅ *g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si272.png)\-DP and RDP and zCDP scale with another factor *g*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si273.png).

## 2.5 Future work

We are still in the midst of bringing DP-SGD to practice where we want to achieve good convergence to and accuracy of the final global model and where we have a strong DP guarantee (the trade-off function should be close to 1 − *α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si141.png) which represents random guessing between the two hypotheses). Towards finding a good balance between utility and privacy, we discuss a couple future directions in next subsections.

### 2.5.1 Using synthetic data

One main problem is that local data is used for training models for various learning tasks. Each application of DP-SGD will leak privacy since the local data set is being reused. One way to control and be in charge of the amount of privacy leakage is to have data samples in local client data expire according to some expiration date (per sample). This is problematic because in our current data economy, data is a valuable asset which we do not want to give a limited lifetime.

In order to cope with this problem, a client may decide to not use its own local data set in each of these DP-SGD instantiations. Instead, differential private GAN [\[24\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0120) modeling can be used to learn a distribution model based on a local data set that generates synthetic data with a similar distribution. Due to the post-processing lemma, we can freely use the synthetic data in any optimization algorithm and FL approach. This circumvents multiple use of DP-SGD, but requires the design of differential private GAN which produces ‘high’ quality synthetic data. This is an open problem: GAN modeling is itself a learning task which can use the DP-SGD approach for the discriminator (which is very noise sensitive). Here, we use DP-SGD only once and as soon as a GAN model is learned, it can be published and transmitted to the central server who uses the GAN models from all clients to generate synthetic samples on which it trains a global model for a learning task of its choice. Of course, as a caveat, working with synthetic data may not lead to a global model with good test accuracy on real data. Notice that by using synthetic data we avoid the FL paradigm altogether since the large amounts of data distributed over clients are now compressed into (relatively short transmittable) representations that code GAN models.

In the same line of thinking, if differentially private GAN models do not lead to high quality synthetic data, then we will want to research other general methods for pre-processing local data that filter or hide features that are considered privacy sensitive. This brings us back to the basics of how a membership or inference attack is actually implemented in order to understand what type of information should be filtered out for making reconstruction of certain types of private data hard or unreliable.

### 2.5.2 Adaptive strategies

We need to fine-tune parameters and this can be done during DP-SGD's execution: Consecutive segments of multiple rounds may work with their own *m*, *σ*, and *C*. To what extent does an adaptive approach work, where the current convergence rate and test accuracy (preferably based on public data at the server so as not to leak additional privacy) of the current global model are used to determine (*m*, *σ*, *C*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si274.png) for the next segment?

In Section [2.2.6](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0045) we discussed the benefit of adaptive reducing the clipping constant *C* (based on prior rounds or based on using a DP approach within a round to collect information that influences the choice of the used *C* in that round). Similarly, since a smaller *σ* directly reduces the amount of noise added to the global model and therefore increases the final accuracy, it makes sense to reduce *σ* once convergence has been achieved. After reducing *σ*, new convergence to an improved global model may start. The problem is that a lower *σ* leads to more privacy leakage. For this reason, we want to lower *σ* to a smaller *σ̂*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si275.png) only for, say, the final epoch.

We may also modify the noise distribution: DP-SGD selects noise *N* from a Gaussian distribution. Before adding *N* to the round update, we may replace *N* by *a* ⋅ `a``r``s``i``n``h`(*a*^( − 1) ⋅ *N*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si276.png) where $\\mathtt{arsinh}(x) = \\ln(x + \\sqrt{x^{2} + 1})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si277.png) as suggested for tCDP [\[4\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0020). The result resembles the same Gaussian but with exponentially faster tail decay and this may help in improving the convergence to and accuracy of the final global model. Here, we notice that for the same reason of faster tail decay, DP-SGD chooses to use Gaussian over Laplace noise.

Finally, DP-SGD can be placed in a larger algorithmic framework with DP guarantees for a more general clipping strategy (including clipping a batch of gradients) which allows more general optimization algorithms (beyond mini-batch SGD), and more general sampling strategies (in particular a sampling strategy based on ‘shuffling’).

It remains an open problem to unveil adaptive strategies possibly in a more general algorithmic framework that optimally balance utility and differential privacy. Here we prefer to discover adaptive strategies that proactively provide the DP guarantee based on changed parameter settings, i.e., we do not want to change parameters based solely on utility and discover later (by using a differential privacy accountant) that this has violated or is about to violate our privacy budget.

### 2.5.3 DP proof: a weaker adversarial model

Section [2.4.5](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0100) explains the strong adversarial model used in DP analysis under which the derived DP guarantee is tight. In practice, this is too strong. In general, we may assume a weaker adversary with less capability in terms of knowledge about the used randomness by `S``a``m``p``l``e`[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si23.png) and ℳ![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si72.png). By explicitly stating the knowledge of a weaker adversary in combination with assumptions on the data set itself, we may be able to derive an *f*\-DP guarantee with *f*(*α*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si179.png) closer to 1 − *α*![Image](images/B9780443190377000090/si141.png). It remains an open problem to exploit such a line of thinking.

### 2.5.4 Computing environment with less adversarial capabilities

In order to impose restrictions on adversarial capabilities, we may be able to use confidential computing techniques such as secure processor technology [\[9\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0045), homomorphic computing with secret sharing and/or secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) [\[30\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0150), and possibly even hardware-accelerated fully homomorphic encryption [\[20](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0100),[22\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0110); for a survey, see [\[29](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0145),[32\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0160). These techniques hide round updates in encrypted form. Hence, only the final global model itself (if it is published) or querying the final global model (if it is kept private) can leak information about how local data sets shaped the final model. This means that CDP, see Section [2.3](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#s0055), is still needed. CDP has a better trade-off between privacy and utility compared to LDP as discussed in this chapter. However, confidential computing does not come for free: Either we need to assume a larger Trusted Computing Base (TCB) in the form of trusted hardware modules or processors at the clients, intermediate aggregators, and server or we need a Trusted Third Party (TTP). For example, in the secure MPC solution of [\[30\]](#Chp002_29-55_B9780443190377000090.xhtml#br0150), the generation of Beaver triples is outsourced to a TTP, otherwise impractical additional communication among clients and server is needed (for an oblivious transfer phase in MPC). We are still studying balanced and practical combinations of confidential computing techniques including the use of differential privacy.
