# Chapter 3: Privacy-preserving federated learning: algorithms and guarantees

Xinwei Zhang; Xiangyi Chen; Bingqing Song; Prashant Khanduri; Mingyi Hong    University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN, United States

## Abstract

In federated learning (FL), multiple clients coordinate to learn a global model using locally held private data. The clients' private data may contain sensitive user information that needs to be protected during the FL training. Differential privacy (DP) is a useful mechanism that provides quantifiable privacy guarantees while training a machine learning (ML) model. In this chapter, we discuss two popular and useful notions of DP that often arise in the context of FL: sample-level DP and client-level DP, where the former provides privacy protection for each data sample, while the latter protects each client's identity. We further discuss differentially private FL algorithms and the associated performance guarantees under different settings. Two common operations in developing differentially private algorithms for FL are: *1)* adding perturbation and *2)* clipping the gradients/models before transmission. A majority of research has been focused on analyzing the effect of different perturbation distributions on the performance of DP algorithms. However, the effect of clipping on the performance of FL algorithms has not been well understood. In the second part of this chapter, we (empirically and theoretically) discuss the effect of clipping on the performance of an FL algorithm. Specifically, we demonstrate the effect of clipping bias on the utility/privacy trade-off of the FL algorithms. Finally, we present some open problems and various avenues for future research.

### Keywords

Federated learning (FL); Differential privacy (DP); Sample and client level differential privacy; Utility-privacy trade-off; Model clipping

## 3.1 Introduction

Federated learning (FL) has become indispensable for building machine learning (ML) models in distributed systems with multiple data sources and/or computing nodes. FL is a distributed learning paradigm where multiple agents, each having access to a (possibly private) local dataset, collaboratively solve a joint problem under the orchestration of a server. A standard FL problem with *n* agents is given by

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{w} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d}}\\left\\{ g(\\mathbf{w}) ≔ \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{n}g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}) ≔ \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{n}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\mathcal{D}\_{m}}\\left\\lbrack \\ell\_{m}(\\mathbf{w};\\mathbf{x}\_{m},c\_{m}) \\right\\rbrack \\right\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si1.png)(3.1) 

where *g* : ℝ^(*d*) → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si2.png) is the loss function; **w** is the model to be optimized; *g*[*m*] : ℝ^(*d*) → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si3.png) is the local loss at the *m*th agent and is defined as *g*[*m*](**w**) ≔ 𝔼[𝒟[*m*]]\[ℓ[*m*](**w**;**x**[*m*],*c*[*m*])\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si4.png) where 𝒟[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si5.png) is the distribution of data feature and label pairs (**x**[*m*], *c*[*m*]) ∼ 𝒟[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si6.png) at the *m*th agent. The objective of an FL system is to find a high-quality solution for problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1), to ensure the agents' data privacy, while reducing the communication and computation overhead in the meantime.

Ever since the seminal paper [\[15\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0075) appeared in 2016, a number of algorithms have been developed to solve problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1), as well as many of its variations. Among these algorithms, the Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm [\[21\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0105) is arguably the most well known and popular. The idea of FedAvg is simple: the agents are responsible for updating the model using only local data, while the server will repeatedly collect the agents' local models, and broadcast the averaged versions of the models back to the agents. FedAvg improves the communication efficiency of FL by (i) *client sampling*, wherein only a fraction of agents participate in training within each communication round, and (ii) *intermittent model sharing*, wherein each agent is required to update their respective models multiple times before model averaging. However, it is not clear if FedAvg actually preserves the agents' data privacy. It is important to note that although the agents in FedAvg do not directly share the data among each other (i.e., they only share the models, or sometimes the gradients), some recent works have shown that FL algorithms may still suffer from privacy leakage, i.e., the adversaries can infer some sensitive information about the agents and/or training data [\[20](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0100),[24](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0120),[26](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0130),[36](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0180),[41](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0205),[42\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0210). As a consequence, it is necessary to develop FL algorithms with provable privacy guarantees while achieving desirable learning performance on problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1).

Differential privacy (DP) provides ML practitioners with a mechanism to provide quantifiable privacy guarantees for training ML models [\[6\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0030). The DP originally developed for centralized algorithms is referred to as *sample-level* DP. It ensures that by observing the algorithm's output, an adversary will not be able to infer if a particular data sample was included in training or not. However, in FL setting where *a large number of* agents participate in training (i.e., the so-called *cross-device* setting), it is important to protect each agent's identity. To address this, a new and more stringent notion of DP referred to as *client-level DP* has been developed recently [\[8](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0040),[22\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0110). In this chapter, we will discuss these notions of DP in more detail and will provide a survey of recent works addressing the two notions. The focus of this chapter will be to provide the reader with an understanding of DP in the context of FL, to discuss major challenges associated with developing DP algorithms for FL, and to pose various open problems for future research.

## 3.2 Background and preliminaries

In this section, we provide some basics about FL algorithms and discuss different notions of DP used in FL training.

### 3.2.1 The FedAvg algorithm

As discussed earlier, the goal of an FL algorithm is to solve problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1) while ensuring communication and computation efficiency, as well as data privacy. The recent couple of years have seen an exponential growth in the FL research with many algorithms achieving state-of-the-art performance for different problem classes [\[13](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0065),[14](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0070),[19](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0095),[40\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0200). However, the most popular FL algorithm remains to be the standard FedAvg, stated in [Algorithm 1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0010). More specifically, in each communication round *t*, a subset 𝒞[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si7.png) of clients is sampled. Then using the aggregated parameter from the previous round, the sampled clients update their local models by employing SGD as the local optimizer. After *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si117.png) local updates, the sampled clients share total update differences *Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si9.png) with the server. The server then aggregates the collected model differences to update the global model. Note that FedAvg presented in [Algorithm 1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0010) employs a *two-sided* learning rate where *both* local agents and the server use a well-calibrated learning rate to update the local and global models, respectively [\[37\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0185). This covers the vanilla version of FedAvg as a special case, where the server's learning rate is set as *η*[*g*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si10.png) [\[21\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0105).

![Algorithm 1 Federated averaging algorithm \[FedAvg\].](images/B9780443190377000119/gr001.jpg)

Algorithm 1 Federated averaging algorithm \[FedAvg\].

### 3.2.2 Differential privacy

DP is defined using the notion of adjacent datasets that can be characterized in an application-specific manner. The majority of ML practitioners utilize the (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png) definition of DP [\[5\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0025), a slight variant of the original definition of DP given in [\[6\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0030). The (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)\-DP is defined as follows.

Definition 3.1

A randomized algorithm 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si12.png) is (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)\-DP for some *ϵ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si13.png) and *δ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si14.png) if, for any two adjacent datasets 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si15.png) and 𝒟^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si16.png) and for any subset of outputs 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si17.png) of algorithm 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si12.png), we have

*P*(𝒜(𝒟) ∈ 𝒮) ≤ *e*^(*ϵ*) ⋅ *P*(𝒜(𝒟^′) ∈ 𝒮) + *δ*.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si18.png)(3.2) 

The above definition states that for an algorithm to achieve (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)\-DP, the output of the algorithm on two adjacent datasets should have similar distributions. This implies that any adversary having access to 𝒜(𝒟)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si19.png) and 𝒜(𝒟^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si20.png) will not be able to distinguish between the two datasets, hence ensuring privacy for the two datasets. As noted earlier, the adjacent datasets can be defined in an application-specific manner. This gives rise to sample- and client-level notions of DP in FL, which we define next.

Definition 3.2

Sample-level differential privacy (DP)

Consider a dataset $\\mathcal{D} = \\bigcup\_{m = 1}^{n}\\mathcal{D}\_{m}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si21.png), where *m* is an individual agent as defined in problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1). Then an algorithm achieves (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png) sample-level DP if [(3.2)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq2) holds where the adjacent datasets 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si15.png) and 𝒟^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si16.png) differ by at most a single sample (**x**[*m*], *c*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si22.png) at an agent *m* ∈ \[*n*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si23.png).

Sample-level DP is designed in settings where individual data samples might reveal sensitive information. For example, the training data in medical diagnosis might contain patients' private information and needs to be protected. In FL, the sample-level DP is often utilized in the *cross-silo* setting where individual agents are usually organizations (e.g., hospitals in the medical diagnosis example) and the number of agents is small.

On the other hand, there are situations where individual agents' identities also need to be protected. For example, in a typical *cross-device* FL setting where lots of mobile devices participating in a join training session, the clients might not want to reveal their identity. An example is the Google Keyboard application [\[9\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0045) where each agent is an application user and to protect user's personal information protecting the identity of the user is necessary. For such cases, a stronger notion of DP referred to as *client-level DP* is needed.

Definition 3.3

Client-level differential privacy (DP)

Consider a data set 𝒟 = {𝒟[*m*]}[*m* = 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si24.png), where *m* ∈ \[*n*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si23.png) is an individual agent as defined in problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1). Then an algorithm achieves (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png) client-level DP if [(3.2)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq2) holds where the adjacent datasets 𝒟![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si15.png) and 𝒟^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si16.png) differ by at most a complete dataset, 𝒟[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si5.png), at an agent *m* ∈ \[*n*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si23.png).

Notice that client-level DP is a relatively stronger notion of DP compared to sample-level DP since it masks the identity of a complete dataset rather than just a single sample. Some useful properties of DP that make it particularly attractive for FL applications are:

1.  **1.**  **Post-processing,** stating that if a mechanism is DP then no further information about the database can be extracted by the adversaries. Formally, it states that

Theorem 3.1

Post-processing [\[6\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0030)

*Let* 𝒜 : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si25.png) *be* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)*\-DP and* *f* : ℝ → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si27.png) *be an arbitrary function, then* *f* ∘ 𝒜 : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si28.png) *is also* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)*\-DP.*

1.  Note that [Theorem 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0025) makes no assumption about the computational power of *f*, i.e., no matter how powerful an adversary is, it cannot affect the privacy guarantees of a DP mechanism 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si12.png).
2.  **2.**  **Group privacy,** implying that the DP will degrade gracefully with the size of the group.

Theorem 3.2

Group privacy [\[6\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0030)

*Let* 𝒜 : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si25.png) *be* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)*\-DP, then* 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si12.png) *is also* (*k**ϵ*, *k**e*^((*k* − 1)*ϵ*)*δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si30.png)*\-DP for groups of size k.*

1.  
2.  **3.**  **Composition,** implying that multiple DP mechanisms can be combined to construct more advanced DP mechanisms.

Theorem 3.3

Composition [\[6\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0030)

*Let* 𝒜[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si31.png) *for* *i* ∈ \[*k*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si32.png) *be* (*ϵ*[*i*], *δ*[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si33.png)*\-DP mechanisms, then the composition* 𝒜![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si12.png) *of all* 𝒜[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si31.png)*s defined as* 𝒜(*x*) = (𝒜[1](*x*), …, 𝒜[*k*](*x*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si34.png)*, is* $(\\sum\_{i = 1}^{k}\\epsilon\_{i},\\sum\_{i = 1}^{k}\\delta\_{i})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si35.png)*\-DP.*

1.  [Theorem 3.3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0035) states that if we have *k* mechanisms, each guaranteeing (*ϵ*/*k*, *δ*/*k*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si36.png)\-DP, then the overall mechanism will guarantee (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)\-DP. We note that the result of this composition can be improved from 𝒪(*ϵ*/*k*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si37.png) to $\\mathcal{O}(\\epsilon/\\sqrt{k})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si38.png) to achieve better dependence on *k* [\[7\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0035).

These properties of DP are crucial for the development and analyses of more advanced DP mechanisms including DP-guaranteeing algorithms for FL. In the next section, we discuss algorithms for both sample and client-level DP with their associated performance guarantees.

## 3.3 DP guaranteed algorithms

In this section, we will discuss FedAvg and other FL algorithms for obtaining some form of DP. First, we discuss the standard procedure to obtain DP in a centralized setting for a vanilla SGD algorithm. Later in the chapter, similar ideas will be utilized to develop DP algorithms for FL.

The usual mechanism to endow any algorithm with DP guarantees is by first employing a clipping operation on the output of the algorithm, such as parameters and gradients, and then adding a carefully calibrated perturbation. One can customize the centralized SGD to provide DP guarantees by adding clipping and perturbation to the gradients. Moreover, the adjacent datasets in the centralized setting are defined as two datasets differing by only a single sample (see sample-level DP in [Definition 3.2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0015)), thereby ensuring privacy for each sample. The differentially private SGD with gradient clipping (referred to as DP-SGD) with tight DP guarantees is proposed in [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005); see [Algorithm 2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0015) for detailed steps. Specifically, at each iteration *t*, the algorithm samples a random sample ℬ^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si39.png) of size *B* and computes the stochastic gradients *g̃*^(*t*, *i*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si40.png) for each *i* ∈ ℬ^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si41.png). Then per-sample gradient is clipped using the gradient clipping operation [(3.3)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq3).

![Algorithm 2 Differentially private SGD \[DP-SGD\].](images/B9780443190377000119/gr002.jpg)

Algorithm 2 Differentially private SGD \[DP-SGD\].

**Gradient clipping** [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005)**,** where the (per-sample) gradient *g̃*[*m*]^(*t*, *i*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si42.png) is clipped at each step (see [Algorithm 2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0015), line 5) as

${clip}({\\widetilde{g}}^{t,i},C) = {\\widetilde{g}}^{t,i}/\\max\\left( 1,\\frac{\\left\\| {\\widetilde{g}}^{t,i} \\right\\|\_{2}}{C} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si43.png)(3.3) 

with *C* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si44.png) being a constant. This per-sample clipping ensures that when ∥*g̃*^(*t*, *i*)∥[2] ≤ *C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si45.png), we keep *g̃*^(*t*, *i*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si40.png) unchanged; otherwise we scale the gradient so that ∥*g̃*^(*t*, *i*)∥[2] = *C*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si46.png). The clipping operation is a key step that ensures bounded sensitivity in output when changing training samples and allows one to obtain provable DP guarantees, where the sensitivity refers to the maximum change in the size of the output when a single data point is changed. After the clipping operation, we add a carefully calibrated noise to the individual stochastic gradients in line 6, and average the resulting quantities to update the model in line 7. The next result states the precise DP guarantees for DP-SGD [Algorithm 2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0015). 

Theorem 3.4

DP-SGD [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005)

*There exist constants* *c*[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si47.png) *and* *c*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si48.png) *so that, given the sampling probability* *q* = *B*/|𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si49.png) *and the number of steps τ, for any* *ε* < *c*[1] ⋅ *q*² ⋅ *τ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si50.png)*,* [Algorithm 2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0015) *is* (*ε*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si51.png)*\-differentially private for any* *δ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si14.png)*, if we choose*

$\\sigma \\geqslant c\_{2}\\frac{C \\cdot q\\sqrt{\\tau \\cdot \\log(1/\\delta)}}{\\varepsilon},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si53.png)

*where* |*D*|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si54.png) *is the total number of samples.*

The proof of [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040) follows the standard approach of approximating the final output of the algorithm by a sequential composition of bounded-norm stochastic gradients and designing the noise variance to guarantee DP. In fact, [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005) provides a tighter DP guarantee compared to the simple application of the composition theorem ([Theorem 3.3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0035)) by utilizing the information of the injected noise distribution. Specifically, the proof in [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005) utilizes a moments accountant technique where the bounds on moments of the privacy loss random variable are tracked throughout the execution of the algorithm. These moment bounds are then used to find the tail bounds of the differential privacy random variable, thereby, guaranteeing DP.

Next, we discuss how to extend DP-SGD to FL models.

### 3.3.1 Sample-level DP

Sample-level DP in FL follows the same notion as centralized-DP [\[1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0005), which aims to protect each sample in the union of all datasets $\\mathcal{D} = \\bigcup\_{m = 1}^{n}\\mathcal{D}\_{m}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si21.png) (see [Definition 3.2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0015)). As discussed earlier, this notion of DP is useful for *cross-silo* FL problems. Similar to DP-SGD, a natural approach to ensure sample-level DP for FedAvg is to introduce gradient clipping and noise injection during the local updates in step 7 of [Algorithm 1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0010). Below, we discuss FedAvg with sample-level DP guarantees.

#### 3.3.1.1 Algorithms and discussion

In [Algorithm 3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0020), we state the Sample-Level DP FedAvg. Note that [Algorithm 3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0020) ensures sample-level DP guarantees by adding a clipping and a noise injection procedure for the stochastic gradients evaluated at each local update. Sample-level DP has been proposed in [\[30\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0150), in a more general form with secure multi-party encryption protocol deployed for secure aggregation of the model parameters. Though [\[30\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0150) has not provided convergence or DP guarantees for the proposed approach, it has numerically demonstrated its effectiveness. In [\[12\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0060), convergence guarantees for [Algorithm 3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0020) have been established for the case when individual clients use a single-step gradient descent for local updates, the per sample gradient norm is bounded, no gradient clipping is used, and all the clients participate in training. Specifically, [\[12\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0060) showed the following result.

Theorem 3.5

Sample-level DP-FedAvg [\[12\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0060)

*For* *ϵ*, *δ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si55.png)*, if the loss* ℓ[*m*](**x**[*m*], *c*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si56.png) *is G-Lipschitz then* [Algorithm 3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0020) *is* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)*\-DP if we choose*

$\\sigma \\geqslant c\\frac{G \\cdot \\sqrt{\\tau \\cdot \\log(1/\\delta)}}{|\\mathcal{D}| \\cdot \\epsilon},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si57.png)

*where* *c* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si58.png) *is some constant and* |𝒟|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si59.png) *is the total number of samples.*

Note that the above guarantee resembles that in [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040), but there is no privacy amplification compared to [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040) as the local nodes utilize full gradients for the local updates. The authors in [\[12\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0060) also provide optimization guarantees for the cases when the objective function *g*(**w**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si60.png) (see Problem [(3.1)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq1)) is strongly convex or satisfies the Polyak–Lojasiewicz condition. Later [\[17\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0085) extended sample-level DP-FedAvg developed in [\[12\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0060) for stochastic local updates and partial client participation. Different from [Algorithm 3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0020), the authors in [\[17\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0085) injected noise only after all the local updates are concluded, also since the per-sample gradient norms have been assumed to be bounded, the clipping operation was not used. Specifically, [\[17\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0085) shows that to achieve an (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png)\-privacy guarantee for each communication round, we require

$\\sigma \\geqslant \\sup\\limits\_{m \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack}\\left\\{ c\\frac{G \\cdot \\tau\_{m}^{2} \\cdot q\_{m} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\log(1.25q/\\delta)}}{\\epsilon} \\right\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si61.png)(3.4) 

for some constant *c* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si58.png) and where *q*[*m*] = *B*[*m*]/|𝒟[*m*]|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si63.png) with *B*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si64.png) being the batch size and |𝒟[*m*]|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si65.png) the dataset size at agent *m*. The above Eq. [(3.4)](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#deq6) implies that if we choose a larger batch size *B*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si64.png), and a large number of local updates *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si117.png), we will need a higher noise level for DP protection. In contrast, for FedAvg it is observed that a larger batch size and a larger number of local updates might help speed-up convergence [\[27\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0135). This implies that there is a trade-off between the DP guarantees and the algorithm's convergence speed. The authors in [\[17\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0085) further analyze the optimization performance of sample-level DP FedAvg to understand this trade-off.

![Algorithm 3 Sample-level differentially private FedAvg.](images/B9780443190377000119/gr003.jpg)

Algorithm 3 Sample-level differentially private FedAvg.

Next, we discuss some other works that address sample-level DP in the context of FL. In [\[11\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0055), the DP algorithm based on alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), DP-ADMM, is proposed. Similarly, [\[18\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0090) develops a stochastic primal–dual algorithm for FL with differential privacy. The authors in [\[3\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0015) propose a coordinate decent algorithm that incorporates the DP framework. In [\[4\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0020), with the goal of reducing the communication overhead while keeping the information private, the normalized and quantized gradients are transmitted. The work in [\[23\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0115) investigates the trade-off between communication costs and training variance under a resource-constrained FL system.

In the next subsection, we discuss the client-level DP for FL in detail.

### 3.3.2 Client-level DP

In this subsection, we discuss the algorithms for the client-level DP where the goal is to protect the identities of clients in contrast to individual samples (see [Definition 3.3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0020)) so that an adversary could not identify which client has participated in the training by the information transmitted. Similar to sample-level DP, clipping and noise injection are the two mechanisms that ensure client-level DP. However, in contrast to sample-level DP where we clip the stochastic gradients before *each* local update, in client-level DP, there are multiple ways to implement the clipping operation. Below we discuss the major clipping strategies that protect the client-level DP for FL algorithms.

#### 3.3.2.1 Clipping strategies for client-level DP

Three different clipping strategies are often utilized to guarantee client-level DP: the **gradient** clipping, the **local model** clipping, and the **local update difference** clipping. In the gradient clipping (see Section [3.3](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#s0030)), we clip the local stochastic gradients before each local update [\[22\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0110), while in model clipping and model difference clipping, we perform the clipping operation once every communication round. Since the total number of samples accessed by the algorithm is much larger than the total communication rounds, the gradient clipping is too expensive thus it is seldom used in FL algorithms. Below, we describe the **local model** clipping and **local update difference** clipping strategies:

**Model clipping** [\[35\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0175)**.** The clients directly clip the models sent to the server. For FedAvg algorithm, this means performing clip(**w**[*m*]^(*t*, *τ*[*m*]), *C*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si66.png). This method appears to be straightforward, but clipping the model directly results in a relatively large clipping threshold, so it requires adding larger perturbations.

**Difference clipping** [\[8\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0040)**.** The clients clip the local update difference between the initial model and the output model *Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si9.png). In this method, the clients need to record the initial model. The update difference typically has smaller magnitudes than the model itself, so the clipping threshold and the perturbation can be smaller than using model clipping. Note that when *τ*[*m*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si67.png) (i.e., only one local update step) and batchsize is one for stochastic gradient evaluation, the difference clipping is equivalent to the gradient clipping used in the DP-SGD, but in the general case where *τ*[*m*] > 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si68.png), their behaviors are very different.

To better compare the performance of model clipping and difference clipping strategies, we have the following two results [\[39, Claims 2.1, 2.2\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0195):

1.  **1.**  Given any constant clipping threshold *C*, there exists a convex quadratic problem for which FedAvg with model clipping *does not* converge to the global optimal solution with *any* fixed *τ*[*m*] ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si69.png) and *η*[ℓ] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si70.png). This can be shown by constructing a problem such that its optimal solution **w**^⋆![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si71.png) has a larger magnitude than the clipping threshold *C*.
2.  **2.**  For any linear regression problem with a fixed clipping threshold *C*, there exist *η*[ℓ]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si116.png) and local update step *τ*[*m*] ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si69.png) such that FedAvg with difference clipping converges to the global optimal solution. Furthermore, there exists a linear regression problem such that under the same *C*, *η*[ℓ]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si116.png), and *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si117.png), FedAvg with difference clipping converges to a better solution with a smaller loss than the original FedAvg.

These two results indicate that the difference clipping should outperform the model clipping in terms of convergence guarantees. Therefore, in the subsequent sections, we focus on understanding a particular FL algorithm that uses difference clipping.

#### 3.3.2.2 Algorithms and discussion

To begin with, let us introduce the Clip-enabled DP-FedAvg, which is described in [Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025). The difference between FedAvg in [Algorithm 1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0010) and DP-FedAvg in [Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025) is line 11, where the clients first apply the clipping operation to the local update difference *Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si9.png) and then add the privacy noise **z**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si74.png) which follows the Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0, *σ*²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si75.png). During the communication step, we assume that the adversary can only observe the aggregated update ∑[*m* ∈ 𝒞[*t*]]*Δ̃***w**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si76.png), and this can be guaranteed for example by using secure aggregation [\[2\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0010).

![Algorithm 4 Client-level differentially private FedAvg \[DP-FedAvg\].](images/B9780443190377000119/gr004.jpg)

Algorithm 4 Client-level differentially private FedAvg \[DP-FedAvg\].

The key intuition for DP-FedAvg to protect client-level DP is that we expect the clients' dataset sizes to be large enough so that after performing multiple local update steps, the resulting client models have relatively good performance. By doing so, the number of communication rounds, *τ*, can be largely reduced and so does the corresponding privacy noise added per communication. It is worth pointing out that DP-SGD is a special case of DP-FedAvg in the following problem setting: 1) client number *n* is the same as the size of the dataset, 2) the local dataset size becomes 1; and 3) the number of local update is set to *τ*[*m*] = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si67.png).

**Related works.** The client-level DP schemes were first proposed in [\[8\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0040) and [\[22\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0110), which consider a two-stage scheme: *1)* select a subset of clients to update local models; *2)* distort the sum of all local updates by clipping operation and then inject noise to the global model update. There are a number of follow-up works in guaranteeing client-level DP. In [\[31\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0155), the perturbation is directly performed on local models with the assumption that model parameters are upper and lower bounded; [\[34](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0170),[35\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0175) propose a method to clip the local models parameter; [\[29\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0145) adapts the Bayesian privacy accounting method to the federated setting. A few other works focus on reducing the communication cost while still maintaining required privacy level, for example, [\[33\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0165) proposes a method to leverage the discrete Gaussian mechanism in FL. The majority of these works only provide DP guarantee for the proposed algorithm \[[8](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0040),[29](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0145)–[31](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0155)\], which is more or less straightforward. However, only a small subset of these works \[[33](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0165)–[35](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0175)\] provide convergence analysis, but these analyses are limited since they often rely upon some restrictive assumptions (e.g., it is assumed that the problem is convex and satisfies the Polyak–Lojasiewicz condition in [\[34](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0170),[35\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0175)). Due to space limit, we will not discuss these works in detail. Instead, in the next section we will provide a recent result that *simultaneously* characterizes the convergence and privacy guarantees for the DP-SGD with difference clipping.

## 3.4 Performance of clip-enabled DP-FedAvg

In the previous section, we discussed various clipping strategies used for ensuring client-level DP and observed why model difference clipping should be the strategy of choice for FL applications. We introduced DP-FedAvg ([Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025)) that utilizes model difference clipping and adding perturbation after clipping to ensure DP. In this section, we perform a thorough theoretical and empirical investigation of [Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025) with the goal of understanding the privacy and convergence guarantees associated with the algorithm.

### 3.4.1 Main results

The main theoretical result for FL algorithm with DP consists two parts: one is the convergence guarantee which states how well the trained model can perform; and the second part is the privacy guarantee which describes how well the algorithm can preserve the privacy in the training procedure. In most cases, privacy protection comes with the price of sacrificing the model performance, so we need to trade-off between the model performance and the privacy guarantee.

To proceed, let us first state the assumptions:

Assumption 3.1

The objective of a problem satisfies

*g*(**w**) ≥ *g*^⋆ >  − ∞, *for some constant* *g*^⋆, ∀ **w**.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si77.png)(3.5) 

Assumption 3.2

Lipschitz gradient

The gradient of the clients' functions satisfies

∥∇*g*[*m*](**w**)−∇*g*[*m*](**w**^′)∥ ≤ *L*∥**w**−**w**^′∥, ∀ *m*, **w**, **w**^′,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si78.png)

where *L* is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient.

Assumption 3.3

Bounded variance

The stochastic gradient of the clients' functions is unbiased, i.e., 𝔼\[*g̃*[*m*]\] = ∇*g*[*m*](**w**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si79.png) and its variance satisfies

𝔼∥*g̃*[*m*]−∇*g*[*m*](**w**)∥² ≤ *σ*[ℓ]², ∀ *m*, **w**,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si80.png)

for some constant *σ*[ℓ]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si81.png).

Besides these standard assumptions, in the analysis for DP-FedAvg, the following additional assumptions are needed.

Assumption 3.4

Bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD)

The inter-gradient variance between the local and global problems is bounded by some constant *σ*[*g*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si82.png), i.e.,

∥∇*g*(**w**)−∇*g*[*m*](**w**)∥² ≤ *σ*[*g*]², ∀ *m*, **w**.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si83.png)

Assumption 3.5

Bounded gradient

The gradient of each client's functions is upper bounded by some constant *G*, i.e.,

∥∇*g*[*m*](**w**)∥² ≤ *G*, ∀ *m*, **w**.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si84.png)

The BGD assumption have been used in many FL proofs (cf. [\[13](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0065),[40\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0200)) to characterize the non-i.i.d.-ness of the client data distribution. Bounded gradient is a stricter assumption to replace the BGD assumption and has been used in the earlier works in FL algorithms (cf. [\[16\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0080)) and in the analysis for DP algorithm [\[23](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0115),[32](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0160),[33\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0165). With the above assumptions, we are ready to present the theoretical results for DP-FedAvg ([Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025)).

#### 3.4.1.1 Convergence theorem

Theorem 3.6

Convergence of DP-FedAvg, [\[39, Theorem 3.1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0195)

*Under* Assumptions [3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0050)–[3.5](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0070)*, by letting* $\\eta\_{g}\\eta\_{\\ell} \\leqslant \\min\\{\\frac{n\_{t}}{96\\tau\_{m}^{2}},\\frac{n\_{t}}{6\\tau\_{m} \\cdot L(n\_{t} - 1)}\\}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si85.png) *and* $\\eta\_{\\ell} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{60}\\tau\_{m} \\cdot L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si86.png)*, for* [Algorithm 4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0025)*, we have*

$\\frac{1}{\\tau}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t}{\\|\\nabla g(\\mathbf{w}^{t})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack\\quad \\leqslant \\textit{FedAvg\\ Term} + \\underset{\\text{caused\\ by\\ clipping}}{\\underset{︸}{G^{2}\\frac{4}{\\tau}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{n}(|\\alpha\_{m}^{t} - {\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t}| + |{\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t} - {\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t}|) \\right\\rbrack}}\\qquad + \\underset{\\text{caused\\ by\\ clipping}}{\\underset{︸}{\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot L \\cdot \\tau\_{m}G^{2}\\frac{6}{\\tau}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\frac{1}{n\_{t}}\\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{n}(|\\alpha\_{m}^{t} - {\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t}|^{2} + |{\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t} - {\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t}|^{2}) \\right\\rbrack}}\\qquad + \\underset{\\text{caused\\ by\\ privacy\\ noise}}{\\underset{︸}{\\frac{2\\eta\_{g} \\cdot L \\cdot d \\cdot \\sigma^{2}}{\\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot \\tau\_{m} \\cdot n\_{t}}}},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si87.png)

 *where* $\\alpha\_{m}^{t}: = \\frac{C}{\\max(C,\\|\\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t}\\|)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si88.png)*,* ${\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t}: = \\frac{C}{\\max(C,\\|\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t}\\rbrack\\|)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si89.png)*,* ${\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t}: = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{m = 1}^{m}{\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si90.png)*; d is the dimension of* **w***,* $\\gamma\_{1}(\\tau) = \\frac{1}{\\tau}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t}\\rbrack \\leqslant 1$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si91.png)*,* $\\gamma\_{2}(\\tau) = \\frac{1}{\\tau}\\sum\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{({\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t})}^{2}\\rbrack \\leqslant 1$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si92.png)*, and*

$\\textit{FedAvg\\ Term}: = \\frac{4(g(\\mathbf{w}^{0}) - g^{\\star})}{\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot \\tau \\cdot \\tau\_{m}} + \\frac{25}{2}\\eta\_{\\ell}^{2} \\cdot L \\cdot \\tau\_{m}(\\sigma\_{\\ell}^{2} + 6\\tau\_{m} \\cdot \\sigma\_{g}^{2})\\gamma\_{1}(\\tau)\\quad + \\frac{6\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot L \\cdot \\sigma\_{\\ell}^{2}}{n\_{t}}\\gamma\_{2}(\\tau).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si93.png)

In the bound of [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075), the *FedAvg Term* is inherited from standard FedAvg with two-sided learning rates which can yield a convergence rate of $O(\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n\_{t} \\cdot \\tau \\cdot \\tau\_{m}}} + \\frac{1}{\\tau})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si94.png) when setting $\\eta\_{g} = \\sqrt{n\_{t} \\cdot \\tau\_{m}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si95.png) and $\\eta\_{\\ell} = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\tau}\\tau\_{m} \\cdot L}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si96.png). It recovers the standard convergence bounds for FedAvg up to a constant, cf., [\[38, Theorem 1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0190) when clipping operation and DP noise do not appear. Aside from the *FedAvg Term*, there are two extra terms caused by the privacy noise **z**[*m*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si74.png) and the clipping operation, respectively. The error term caused by privacy noise is the price for privacy protection and can be found in the analysis for DP-SGD algorithms (cf. [\[11](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0055),[32](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0160),[35\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0175)).

Let us focus on the terms caused by clipping operation, which depends on |*α*[*m*]^(*t*)−*α̃*[*m*]^(*t*)|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si98.png) and |*α̃*[*m*]^(*t*)−*ᾱ*^(*t*)|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si99.png). The term

$\\left| \\alpha\_{m}^{t} - {\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t} \\right| = \\left| \\frac{C}{\\max(C,\\|\\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t}\\|)} - \\frac{C}{\\max(C,\\|\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack\\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t}\\rbrack\\|)} \\right|$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si100.png)

characterizes the difference between the stochastic local update difference ∥*Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si101.png) and its expectation ∥𝔼*Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si102.png). It becomes zero as the variance of the stochastic gradient *σ*[ℓ]² → 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si103.png). The other term |*α̃*[*m*]^(*t*)−*ᾱ*^(*t*)|![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si99.png) depends on the variance of the magnitude of the update difference across clients. Specifically, let us define the normalized variance of the magnitude of the update difference as degree of concentration (DoC), i.e., DoC:= ${Var}(\\left\\| \\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t} \\right\\|)/{\\bar{\\left\\| \\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t} \\right\\|}}^{4}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si104.png). When clipping is activated, i.e., *α*[*m*]^(*t*) = *C*/∥*Δ***w**[*m*]^(*t*)∥![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si105.png), with a first-order Taylor expansion, we can approximate this term by 

$\\left| {\\widetilde{\\alpha}}\_{m}^{t} - {\\bar{\\alpha}}^{t} \\right| \\approx C \\cdot \\sqrt{{Var}(\\left\\| \\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t} \\right\\|)/{\\bar{\\left\\| \\Delta\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{t} \\right\\|}}^{4}} = C \\cdot \\sqrt{DoC}.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si106.png)

This term is affected by the gradient dissimilarity *σ*[*g*]²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si82.png), since large gradient heterogeneity may induce quite disparate update difference distributions across clients.

#### 3.4.1.2 DP guarantee

The privacy guarantee of DP-FedAvg can be characterized by standard privacy theorems on Gaussian mechanism [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040). We can analyze the privacy–utility trade-off of DP-FedAvg by substituting *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si107.png) from [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040) into [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075). To get more insights on how parameters like *τ*, *η*[*g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si108.png), *η*[ℓ]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si116.png), and *ϵ* affect DP-FedAvg, let us simplify [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075) to [Corollary 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0080) by substituting *C* ≥ *η*[ℓ] ⋅ *τ*[*m*] ⋅ *G*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si109.png) and *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si107.png).

Corollary 3.1

Convergence with privacy guarantee, [\[39, Corollary 3.2.1\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0195)

*Under* Assumptions [3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0050)–[3.5](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0070)*, for any clipping threshold* *C* = *η*[ℓ]*τ*[*m*]*C*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si110.png) *with* *C*^′ ≥ *G*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si111.png)*, and set* *σ*²![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si107.png) *as in* [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040)*, for any* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si11.png) *satisfying the constraints in* [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040)*, we have*

$\\frac{1}{\\tau}\\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{\\tau - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\|\\nabla g(\\mathbf{w}^{t})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack \\leqslant \\underset{\\text{standard\\ terms\\ for\\ FedAvg}}{\\underset{︸}{O\\left( \\frac{1}{\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot \\tau \\cdot \\tau\_{m}} + \\eta\_{\\ell}^{2} \\cdot \\tau\_{m}^{2} + \\frac{\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell}}{n\_{t}} \\right)}}\\quad + \\underset{\\text{caused\\ by\\ privacy\\ noise}}{\\underset{︸}{O\\left( \\frac{\\eta\_{g} \\cdot \\eta\_{\\ell} \\cdot \\tau \\cdot \\tau\_{m} \\cdot d\\ln(\\frac{1}{\\delta})}{n^{2} \\cdot \\epsilon^{2}} \\right)}},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si113.png)(3.6) 

*and the best rate one can get from the above bound is* $\\widetilde{O}(\\frac{\\sqrt{d}}{n \\cdot \\epsilon})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si114.png) *by optimizing* *η*[*g*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si108.png)*,* *η*[ℓ]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si116.png)*, τ, and* *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si117.png)*.*

A direct implication of [Corollary 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0080) is that the big-*O* convergence rate of DP-FedAvg is the same as that of DP-SGD in terms of *d*, *ϵ*, and *n* (the number of samples in DP-SGD). This rate is obtained under the setting that clipping is deactivated with *C* ≥ *η*[ℓ] ⋅ *τ*[*m*] ⋅ *G*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si109.png). If *C*^′ < *G*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si118.png) in [Corollary 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0080), then there will be extra bias terms inherited from the bound in [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075).

So far, we have provided the theoretical analyses for DP-FedAvg algorithm, including the convergence analysis with the error decomposition and the privacy guarantee. Next, we will show numerical results as the verification for the error decomposition and see how different choices of the hyper-parameters can affect the algorithm performance.

### 3.4.2 Experimental evaluation

In the experiment, we compare the performance of FedAvg (no clipping, no DP noise), clip-enabled FedAvg (no DP noise), and DP-FedAvg on EMNIST and Cifar-10 datasets. We set the client number *n* = 1920![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si119.png), the number of client participates in each round *n*[*t*] = 80, ∀ *t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si120.png), the number of local iterations *τ*[*m*] = 32![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si121.png), and the mini-batch size 64. The clipping thresholds for clip-enabled FedAvg and DP-SGD are set to 50% of the average (over clients and iterations) of local update magnitudes recorded in FedAvg. For DP-FedAvg, the privacy budget is *ϵ* = 1.5![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si122.png), *δ* = 10^( − 5)![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si123.png) (if not specified) and follows [Theorem 3.4](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0040) to obtain the noise variance that needs to be added. These hyper-parameters are optimized for DP-FedAvg.

**Error Decomposition.** To understand how clipping and DP noise affect the algorithm performance, we first use the digit part of the EMNIST dataset, which has 240 K training samples and 40 K testing samples. Each client has 125 samples from 10 classes, where 109 samples belong to 2 of the classes and the other 16 samples belong to the remaining 8 classes. We conduct experiments on a 2-layer MLP with one hidden layer, AlexNet, ModelNetV2 [\[25\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0125), and ResNet-18. The results are listed in [Table 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#t0010).

[Table 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#cf0520)

| Model || *d* || Acc. (%) || Clipping (diff.) (%) || DP (diff.) (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MLP || 159 K || 94.0 || 93.1 (−1.84) || 92.8 (−0.29) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AlexNet || 3.3M || 96.4 || 94.9 (−1.47) || 94.7 (−**0.16**) |
| MobileNetV2 || 2.3M || 97.8 || 97.4 (−0.35) || 95.8 (−1.62) |
| ResNet-18 || 11.1M || 95.2 || 95.3 (+**0.15**) || 91.5 (−3.76) |

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/t0010.png)

The second dataset we use is the Cifar-10 dataset, which has 50 K training samples and 10 K testing samples. Each client has 500 samples which can overlap with those on the other clients and the samples on each client are uniformly distributed in 10 classes. We conduct experiments on a 2-layer MLP with one hidden layer, AlexNet and ResNet-18. The results are listed in [Table 3.2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#t0015).

[Table 3.2](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#cf0525)

The accuracy difference between (a) FedAvg and CE-FedAvg and (b) CE-FedAvg and DP-FedAvg on IID Cifar-10 dataset.

 
| Model || *d* || Acc. (%) || Clipping (diff.) (%) || DP (diff.) (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MLP || 616 K || 51.90 || 44.51 (−7.39) || 43.60 (−0.90) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AlexNet || 3.3M || 66.01 || 61.18 (−4.83) || 61.36 (+**0.18**) |
| ResNet-18 || 11.1M || 76.36 || 75.83 (−**0.53**) || 70.68 (−5.15) |

![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/t0015.png)

**Degree of Concentration and Clipping Error.** In [Fig. 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#f0030), we compare a 2-layer MLP, AlexNet, ResNet-18, and GoogLeNet [\[28\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0140) on IID and Non-IID Cifar-10 datasets and plot the accuracy drop caused by clipping versus DoC averaged over all iterations. In the Non-IID case, each client has 50 samples which can overlap with those of the other clients, and the samples of each client are uniformly distributed in 10 classes. The lighter side of the line denotes the result of IID data, and the darker side denotes the Non-IID data. We can see that when DoC is small (i.e., the update differences' magnitudes are more concentrated), then the accuracy drop caused by the clipping is also small, and vice versa. From the experiments, we have the following observations:

1.  **1.**  It appears that when the underlying machine learning model is *structured* (e.g., many layers, has convolution layers, skip connections, etc.), the update difference of FedAvg becomes *concentrated*, yielding a better clipping performance (as suggested by the terms related to clipping in [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075)).
2.  **2.**  When the model has too many parameters, they are sensitive to privacy noise. This is reasonable since the error term caused by the privacy noise in [Theorem 3.6](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#enun0075) linearly depends on the size of the model *d* and the square of the Lipschitz constant *L* (note, that *η*[ℓ] ∝ 1/*L*![Image](images/B9780443190377000119/si124.png)). From [\[10, Corollary 3.3\]](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#br0050), we know that *L* increases exponentially with the number of layers. Therefore, larger and deeper models are potentially more sensitive to privacy noise.
3.  **3.**  We conjecture that, to ensure good performance of DP-FedAvg, we need to pick a neural network that is structured enough, while not having too many variables and too many layers.

[Figure 3.1](#Chp003_57-74_B9780443190377000119.xhtml#cf0530) The relationship between averaged degree of concentration of the update differences and the clipping accuracy drop for IID (light end) and Non-IID (dark end) Cifar-10 dataset.

## 3.5 Conclusion and future work

In this chapter, we first discussed sample- and client-level DP, then reviewed DP-FedAvg along with analyses on the effects of clipping and noise. FL with DP is still an active area of research and there are still plenty of open problems. The characterization of the clipping effect and noise effect unlocked many future research opportunities. One future direction is to characterize more rigorously the impact of network architecture on update distribution to provide guidance on designing network architectures that are more clipping-friendly or noise-resilient. Another opportunity is to come up with new loss functions/model components/clipping methods/training algorithms to improve model performance, coping with the effect of clipping, noise, and local updates.
