![Figure 6.3 Reconstruction results under different defenses with batch size being 1, 16, and 32. When the batch size is 32, combining gradient pruning and Intra-InstaHide makes the reconstruction almost unrecognizable (the last column).](images/B9780443190377000144/gr003.jpg)

Figure 6.3 Reconstruction results under different defenses with batch size being 1, 16, and 32. When the batch size is 32, combining gradient pruning and Intra-InstaHide makes the reconstruction almost unrecognizable (the last column).

**No defense.** Without any defense, when batch size is 1, the attack can recover images well from the gradient. Increasing the batch size makes it difficult to recover well, but the recovered images are visually similar to the originals (see [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#f0020)).

**Gradient pruning (GradPrune).** [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#f0020) shows that as the pruning ratio *p* increases, there are more artifacts in the reconstructions. However, the reconstructions are still recognizable even when the pruning ratio *p* = 0.9![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si58.png), thus the previous suggestion of using *p* = 0.7![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si59.png) by [\[51\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0255) is no longer safe against the state-of-the-art attack. Our results suggest that, for CIFAR-10, defending the strongest attack with gradient pruning may require the pruning ratio *p* ≥ 0.999![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si60.png). As a trade-off, such a high pruning ratio would introduce an accuracy loss of around 10% (see [Table 6.2](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#t0015)).

**MixUp** introduces a small computational overhead to training. Indeed, MixUp with *k* = 4![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si61.png) only has a minor impact (~2%) on test accuracy, but it is not sufficient to defend against the gradient inversion attack (see [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#f0020)). Increasing *k* from 4 to 6 slightly reduces the leakage, however, the reconstruction is still highly recognizable. This suggests that MixUp alone may not be a practical defense against the state-of-the-art gradient inversion attack.

**Intra-InstaHide** with *k* = 4![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si61.png) incurs an extra ~2% accuracy loss compared with MixUp, but it achieves better defense performance: when the batch size is 32, there are obvious artifacts and color shift in the reconstruction (see [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#f0020)). However, with a batch size of 32, Intra-InstaHide alone also cannot defend against the state-of-the-art gradient inversion, as structures of private images are still vaguely identifiable in reconstructions.

### 6.5.3 Performance of combined defenses

We notice that two types of defense (i.e., perturbing gradient and encoding inputs) are complementary to each other, which motivates an evaluation of combining gradient pruning with MixUp or Intra-InstaHide.

As shown in [Fig. 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#f0020), when the batch size is 32, combining Intra-InstaHide (*k* = 4![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si61.png)) with gradient pruning (*p* = 0.9![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si58.png)) makes the reconstruction almost unrecognizable. The combined defense yields a higher LPIPS score than using gradient pruning with *p* = 0.999![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si62.png), but introduces a smaller accuracy loss (~7% compared with a no-defense pipeline).

[Table 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#t0020) shows time estimates for the end-to-end recovery of a single image in a federated learning setting with GradPrune or InstaHide defense. We do not estimate for MixUp since it has been shown to be a weak defense (see Section [6.5.2](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0090)).

![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/t0020.png)

Our time estimates consider three fairly small dataset sizes. The largest size in our estimate is a small fraction of a dataset of ImageNet scale. We consider a client who holds a dataset of *N* private images and participates in federated learning, which trains an ResNet-18 model with batch size *b* = 128![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si63.png). Assumes that the resolution of the client's data is 32 × 32 × 3![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si64.png). If the attacker uses a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti GPU as his computation resource and runs gradient inversion with 10,000 iterations of optimization, then *t*, the running time for attacking a single batch, is ~0.25 GPU hours (batch size *b* has little impact on the attack's running time, but a larger *b* makes the attack less effective).

**Non-defended and gradient pruning.** Recovering a single image in a non-defended pipeline (or a pipeline that applies gradient pruning alone as the defense) only requires the attacker to invert the gradient of a single step of training, which takes time *t*.

**InstaHide.** When InstaHide is applied, the current attack [\[8\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0040) suggests that recovering a single image would involve recovering the whole dataset first. As discussed in Section [6.4](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0060), Carlini et al.'s attack consists of two steps: 1) recovering InstaHide images from the gradient of *T* epochs – this would take (*N**T*/*b*) × *t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si65.png) GPU hours; and 2) running the decode attack [\[8\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0040) on InstaHide images to recover the private dataset, which involves:

1.  **2a**  Training a neural network to detect similarity in recovered InstaHide images. Assume that training the network requires at least *n* recovered InstaHide images, then collecting these images by running gradient inversion would take (*n*/*b*) × *t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si66.png) GPU hours. The training takes 10 GPU hours according to [\[8\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0040), so training the similarity network would take (*n*/*b*) × *t* + 10![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si67.png) GPU hours in total.
2.  **2b**  Running the combinatorial algorithm to recover the original images. Running time of this step has been shown to be at least quadratic in *m*, the number of InstaHide encodings [\[9\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0045). This step takes 1/6 GPU hours with *m* = 5 × 10³![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si68.png). Therefore, for *m* = *N**T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si69.png), the running time is at least $1/6 \\times {(\\frac{NT}{5 \\times 10^{3}})}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si70.png) GPU hours.

In total, an attack on InstaHide in this real-world setting would take $(NT/b) \\times t + (n/b) \\times t + 10 + 1/6 \\times {(\\frac{NT}{5 \\times 10^{3}})}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si71.png) GPU hours. We use *T* = 50![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si72.png) (used by [\[8\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0040)), *n* = 10, 000![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si73.png) and give estimates in [Table 6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#t0020). As shown, when InstaHide is applied on a small dataset (*N* = 5, 000![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si74.png)), the end-to-end recovery of a single image takes  > 3, 000×![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si75.png) longer than in a no-defense pipeline or GradPrune pipeline; when InstaHide is applied on a larger dataset (*N* = 500, 000![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si76.png)), the computation cost for end-to-end recovery is enormous.

## 6.6 Conclusion

This chapter first pointed out that some recent gradient inversion attacks had made strong assumptions about knowing BatchNorm statistics and private labels. Relaxing such assumptions can significantly weaken these attacks.

We then reported the performance of a set of proposed defenses against gradient inversion attacks, and estimated the computation cost of an end-to-end recovery of a single image in different dataset sizes. Our evaluation showed that InstaHide without mixing with data from a public dataset combined with gradient pruning can defend against the state-of-the-art attack, and the estimated time to recover a single image in a medium-sized client dataset (e.g., of 500,000 images) is enormous.

Based on our evaluation of the attack by [\[18\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0090) and multiple defenses for *plain-text* gradients, we have several observations.

First, *using BatchNorm layers in your deep net but not sharing BatchNorm statistics of the private batch during federated learning weakens the attack*. We have demonstrated in Section [6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0020) that exposing BatchNorm statistics to the attacker significantly improves the quality of gradient inversion. So a more secure configuration of federated learning would be to use BatchNorm layers, but not share BatchNorm statistics in training, which has been shown feasible in [\[3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0015),[33\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0165).

Second, *using a large batch size weakens the attack; a batch size smaller than 32 is not safe*. We have shown that a larger batch size hinders the attack by making it harder to guess the private labels (Section [6.3](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0020)) and to recover the private images even with correct private labels (Section [6.5](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0080)). Our experiments suggested that even with some weak defenses applied, a batch size smaller than 32 is not safe against the strongest gradient inversion attack.

Third, *combining multiple defenses may achieve a better utility–privacy trade-off*. In our experiment, for a batch size of 32, combining InstaHide (*k* = 4![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si61.png)) with gradient pruning (*p* = 0.9![Image](images/B9780443190377000144/si58.png)) achieved the best utility–privacy trade-off, by making the reconstruction almost unrecognizable at a cost of ~7% accuracy loss (using InstaHide also made the end-to-end recovery of a single image more computationally expensive). Best parameters would vary for different deep learning tasks, but we strongly encourage federated learning participants to explore the possibility of combining multiple defensive mechanisms, instead of only using one of them.

## 6.7 Future directions

We would like to discuss several emerging topics and future directions in the area of gradient inversion attacks and defenses.

### 6.7.1 Gradient inversion attacks for text data

Federated learning has been used for privacy-sensitive applications with text data such as virtual mobile keyboards and analysis of electronic health records in hospitals [\[32\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0160), which also motivates the investigation of privacy leakage in federated learning with text data.

The earliest attempt to study the leakage of text from gradients is Zhu et al. [\[51\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0255), which briefly presented leakage results in masked language modeling [\[13\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0065). Their attack aimed to match target gradients with continuous representations and mapped them back to words that were closest in the embedding matrix. Deng et al. [\[12\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0060) improved Zhu et al. [\[51\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0255) by adding a regularization term that prioritizes the gradient matching in layers that are closer to the input data. However, both works only presented results with a batch size of 1 and do not work well with larger batch sizes.

Apart from the above-mentioned optimization with continuous representations, Dimitrov et al. [\[14\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0070) proposed to reconstruct private sentences via discrete text transformation that minimizes both the gradient matching loss and the prior text probability computed by an auxiliary language model. They could recover a mini-batch of 4 sentences with binary classification tasks using the BERT [\[13\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0065) model. More recently, Gupta et al. [\[20\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0100) took a distinct approach that first identifies a set of words from gradients and then directly reconstructs sentences based on beam search and a prior-based reordering strategy; the attack is capable of recovering text from a large batch size of up to 128 sentences for a GPT-2 model [\[39\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0195).

### 6.7.2 Gradient inversion attacks in variants of federated learning

**Inversion attack in vertical federated learning.** Vertical federated learning (VFL) is designed for application scenarios where multiple data owners share the same data identity but their data differ in feature space. For instance, in the healthcare industry, data of the same patient across different institutions may need to be aggregated for diagnosis. Despite the prevalence of VFL applications [\[4](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0020),[21](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0105),[40](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0200),[44\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0220), to the best of our knowledge, Jin et al.'s paper [\[26\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0130) is the only work that extends and improves the gradient inversion attack to the VFL setting, where the attacker leverages the data index and internal representation alignments in VFL to reconstruct private images.

**A malicious and active server.** Apart from the honest-but-curious attacker demonstrated in the previous sections, recent works [\[6](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0030),[17\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0085) show that a malicious attacker locating on the central server in federated learning can significantly amplify the leakage of private data in gradient leakage by adversarially manipulating the model's weights. These attacks further suggest that federated learning systems based on the limited trust of the central server may expose clients to more severe privacy risks. However, it is still unclear whether the attacker under such a threat model is realistic, as their adversarial manipulations to gradients can be easily detected [\[17\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0085).

### 6.7.3 Defenses with provable guarantee

As previously discussed in Section [6.4](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#s0060), defenses against gradient leakage attacks in federated learning can be briefly categorized into (1) gradient encryption, (2) gradient perturbation, and (3) input encryption. Although end-to-end encryption protocols (category 1) such as secure multi-party computation provide provable guarantees, they usually require special setups and can be costly to implement in production. However, defenses in categories 2 and 3 usually do not provide a provable guarantee for the worst-case leakage from gradients: Gradient pruning [\[51\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0255) was proposed as an empirical defense and has been shown to have a weak connection with privacy preservation [\[24\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0120); DPSGD [\[1\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0005) ensures that each gradient update and the trained model are differentially private, but it is still unclear how to interpret differential privacy's guarantee against a reconstruction attacker [\[5](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0025),[19\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0095), especially in the federated learning setting; InstaHide [\[23\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0115) presents average-case guarantee for single encryption. An adaptive attack [\[8\]](#Chp006_105-122_B9780443190377000144.xhtml#br0040) to this approach was proposed for a local setting. Whether there is an effective attack for a federated learning setting, especially when combining it with other defense methods such as the gradient pruning approach as described in this chapter, is a question to be answered.

We advocate a future study of novel defense methods (or adaptations of previously proposed defenses) with a provable guarantee against reconstruction attackers to preserve privacy for the user's training data.

# Chapter 7: Personalized federated learning: theory and open problems

Canh T. Dinh^([a](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#aff0010)); Tung T. Vu^([b](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#aff0015)); Nguyen H. Tran^([a](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#aff0010))    ^aThe University of Sydney, Darlington, NSW, Australia  
^bQueen's University Belfast, Belfast, United Kingdom

## Abstract

Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed and privacy-preserving machine learning technique in which a group of clients collaborates with a server to learn a global model without sharing clients' data. One challenge with FL is statistical diversity among clients, which restricts the global model from delivering good performance on each client's task. A common approach to address this challenge is to find a “personalized model” that is stylized for each client's data. This chapter introduces and reviews several current personalized federated learning (pFL) methods to address this challenge. To give more insights, state-of-the-art pFL algorithms are then discussed and compared with detailed experiments. Finally, open problems are highlighted for potential future works.

### Keywords

Personalized federated learning

## 7.1 Introduction

The abundance of data generated in a massive number of hand-held devices these days has stimulated the development of federated learning (FL) [\[28\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0140). The setting of FL is a network of clients connected to a server, and its goal is to build a global model from clients' data in a privacy-preserving and communication-efficient manner. The current techniques that attempt to fulfill this goal mostly follow three main steps: (i) at each communication iteration, the server sends the current global model to clients; (ii) the clients update their local models using their local data; (iii) the server collects the latest local models from a subset of sampled clients in order to update a new global model, repeated until convergence [\[20](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0100),[28](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0140),[29](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0145),[31\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0155).

Despite its benefits of data privacy and communication reduction, FL faces the main challenge that affects its performance and convergence rate: statistical diversity, which means that data distributions among clients are distinct (i.e., non-i.i.d.). When learning on non-i.i.d. data, FedAvg [\[28\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0140) witnessed a dramatic decrease in terms of accuracy. This decrease in performance is caused by the phenomenon of client drift [\[20\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0100) when the average global model is far from the global optimal solution. Thus, the global model is hardly well-generalized on each client's data. When the statistical diversity increases, generalization errors of the global model on clients' local data also increase significantly [\[7](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0035),[24\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0120). On the other hand, individual learning without FL (i.e., no client collaboration) will also have large generalization errors due to insufficient data. This issue raises the question: *How can we leverage the global model in FL to find a “personalized model” that is stylized for each client's data?* Motivated by the critical roles of personalized models in several business applications of healthcare, finance, and AI services [\[24\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0120), in this chapter, we study different approaches for pFL to handle statistical heterogeneity under the FL setting.

Multiple approaches have been proposed to achieve personalization in FL including *mixing models, meta-learning, multi-task learning, weight sharing, and clients clustering*. One early approach is finding a personalized model by *mixing* the global and local models. Hanzely and Richtárik [\[16\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0080) combined the optimization of the local and global models by proposing a communication-efficient variant of SGD known as the Loopless Local Gradient Descent (L2GD) algorithm. Mansour et al. [\[27\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0135) introduced three personalization approaches including client clustering, data interpolation, and model interpolation. While data interpolation needs meta-features from all clients (which is not feasible in FL due to privacy concerns), an Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning (APFL) algorithm proposed a method to mix a client's local model with the global model. We can also link the concept of personalization to *meta-learning*. Per-FedAvg [\[13\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0065), influenced by Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) [\[14\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0070), built an initial meta-model to update the local models effectively after one more gradient descent step. During meta-optimization, however, MAML theoretically requires computing the Hessian term, which is computationally prohibitive. Therefore, several works including [\[12](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0060),[14](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0070),[30\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0150) attempted to approximate the Hessian matrix. Khodak et al. [\[21\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0105) based its framework, ARUBA, on online convex optimization and meta-learning, to integrate into FL to improve personalization. Jiang et al. [\[19\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0095) discovered that FedAvg is able to interpret as meta-learning and proposed combining FedAvg with Reptile [\[30\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0150) for pFL. Dinh et al. [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) proposed pFedMe using *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si1.png)\-norm regularization to decouple personalized model optimization from the global model learning in a bi-level problem. In the sense of *multi-task learning*, [\[35\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0175) first introduced federated multi-task learning (FMTL) and proposed a systems-aware optimization framework MOCHA for handling stragglers and fault tolerance in FL settings. Dinh et al. [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) formulated the FMTL problem using Laplacian regularization to explicitly leverage the relationships among the models of clients for multi-task learning. Li et al. [\[25\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0125) introduced an FMTL algorithm to deal with the issues of accuracy, fairness, and robustness in FL. The personalization methods exploiting *weight sharing* in deep neural networks are [\[2](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0010),6,2[6\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0030), in which a network is divided into base and personalized layers. While only the base layers are sent to the server and then aggregated, both types of layers will be trained by clients to create a personalized model. The approach *clients clustering* of [\[27\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0135) has been studied in [\[4](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0020),[10](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050),[15](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0075),[34\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0170). While [\[34\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0170) based on cosine similarity of the gradient updates from the clients to clusters clients, [\[4\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0020) used the global model as input of the agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithm at each client to generate multiple clusters. Ghosh et al. [\[15\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0075) proposed the Iterative Federated Clustering Algorithm (IFCA) to construct *K* global models and assigned each client to one of the *K* clusters to archive the lowest loss value on the client's data. FedGroup [\[10\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050) performs clustering on the local client updates using the KMeans++ algorithm [\[10\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050) based on the Euclidean distance of the Decomposed Cosine similarity (EDC).

## 7.2 Problem formulation of pFL

In the traditional FL network, there are *n* clients, located at different sites and communicating with a server to learn a single global model **w**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si2.png) which is a solution to the following problem:

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx001.jpg)(7.1) 

where the function *g*[*m*] : ℝ^(*d*) → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si3.png), *m* = 1, …, *n*![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si4.png), denotes the expected loss over the data distribution of the *m*th client. Each client *m* has a local dataset *D*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si5.png) containing a collection of |*D*[*m*]|![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si6.png) samples (**x**[*m*]^((*i*)),*c*[*m*]^((*i*)))[*i* = 1]^(*D*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si7.png), where **x**[*m*]^((*i*)) ∈ ℝ^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si8.png) is an input sample and *c*[*m*]^((*i*)) ∈ ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si9.png) can be a target response (or label). Then the local loss function of client *m* is the average of losses on its data points as follows^([^(20)](#fn20))

$g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\frac{1}{|D\_{m}|}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{|D\_{m}|}\\ell\_{m}(\\mathbf{w};(\\mathbf{x}\_{m}^{(i)},c\_{m}^{(i)})).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si10.png)

Among examples of the function ℓ[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si11.png) are linear regression with $\\ell\_{m}(\\mathbf{w};(\\mathbf{x}\_{m}^{(i)},c\_{m}^{(i)})) = \\frac{1}{2}{(\\langle\\mathbf{x}\_{m}^{(i)},\\mathbf{w}\\rangle - c\_{m}^{(i)})}^{2}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si12.png) and logistic regression with ℓ[*m*](**w**; (**x**[*m*]^((*i*)), *c*[*m*]^((*i*)))) = log (1+exp(−*c*[*m*]^((*i*))⟨**x**[*m*]^((*i*)),**w**⟩))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si13.png), *c*[*m*]^((*i*)) ∈ { − 1, 1}![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si14.png), where ⟨**x**, **w**⟩![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si15.png) denotes the inner product of vectors **x** and **w**.

While traditional object aims to find a single optimal solution for Eq. [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1), most of pFL models in the literature are trained by minimizing specifically structured optimization problems which differ from Eq. [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1) to find not only a single global model but also the personalized models for each client. Hanzely et al. [\[17\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0085) provide a general formulation for most of the current pFL approaches as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx002.jpg)(7.2) 

where **w** is shared global parameter, **θ** = (**θ**[1], …, **θ**[*n*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si16.png) are personalized models, $g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}) = \\frac{1}{|D\_{m}|}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{|D\_{m}|}\\ell\_{m}((\\mathbf{w},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m});(\\mathbf{x}\_{m}^{(i)},c\_{m}^{(i)}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si17.png) is the local loss function of the *m*th client, and 0 ≤ *d*[*w*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si18.png), *d*[*θ*] ≤ *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si19.png). The formulation [(7.2)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq3) covers most of the existing convex and nonconvex pFL approaches by carefully constructing the local loss *g*[*m*](**w**, **θ**[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si20.png) [\[17\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0085) and traditional FL objective [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1) when *d*[**θ**] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si21.png) and *d*[**w**] = *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si22.png). Consequently, training different pFL models is equivalent to solving a particular instance of problem [(7.2)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq3) and enables obtaining of a wide range of novel pFL formulations as a special case. In the cases of linear regression, logistic regression, or SVM, the general pFL's problem [(7.2)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq3) is a convex problem. More complicated cases arise in the context of deep neural networks (DNN), convolutional neural networks (CNN), or recurrent neural networks (RNN) where a nonlinear mapping is used rather than the linear mapping **x**^(*T*)**w**![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si23.png). DNN, CNN, or RNN make predictions through a set of layers with a nonconvex function of the feature vector **x** by using nonlinear activation functions such as tanh, ReLu, Softmax. Then, Eq. [(7.2)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq3) is nonconvex.

## 7.3 Review of personalized FL approaches

In this section, we provide a systematic review of existing pFL approaches.

### 7.3.1 Mixing models

The general idea for mixing model context is to learn a personalized model for each client that is the optimal mixture of optimal local and global models. Common works using mixing technique are APFL [\[7\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0035), L2GD [\[16\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0080), and model interpolation [\[27\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0135). In the APFL algorithm, a mixing parameter *α*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si24.png) for each client *m* is adaptively learned during the pFL training process to control the mixing weights between the global and local models. The formulation of APFL is given as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx003.jpg)(7.3) 

where **w**^(\*) = *a**r**g* *m**i**n*[**w** ∈ ℝ^(*d*)] *g*(**w**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si25.png) is the solution to problem [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1) and *α*[1], …, *α*[*m*] ∈ (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si26.png) are adaptive weights to control the degree of personalization for each client. At each global communication round *t*, each client maintains three different models: local version of the global **w**[*m*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si27.png), its own local model **θ**[*m*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si28.png), and the mixed personalized model ${\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}^{(t)} = \\alpha\_{m}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}^{(t)} + (1 - \\alpha\_{m})\\mathbf{w}\_{m}^{(t)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si29.png). The weighting factor *α*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si24.png) can be found by solving *α*[*m*]^(\*) = *a**r**g* *m**i**n*[*α*[*m*] ∈ \[0, 1\]] *g*[*m*](*α*[*m*]**θ** + (1 − *α*[*m*]))**w**![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si30.png). The value of *α*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si24.png) is expected to be smaller if the local and global data distributions are close, and vice versa. A similar approach with APFL involving the mixing of local and global models has also been proposed in [\[27\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0135).

In the L2GD algorithm [\[16\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0080), another formulation that learns personalized models using a mixture of global and local models to balance generalization with personalization is

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx004.jpg)(7.4) 

where $\\overline{\\mathbf{w}} = \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\_{m = 1}^{n}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si31.png). If ![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx005.jpg)is the unique solution to problem [(7.4)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq5) for a given value of *λ*, client *m* learns an individual local model **θ**[*m*](*λ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si32.png). The penalty parameter *λ* ∈ (0, ∞)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si33.png) is used to discourage the local models from being too dissimilar from the mean model. Pure local model learning occurs when *λ* is set to zero. As *λ* increases, mixed model learning occurs and the local models become increasingly similar to each other. The setting approximates global model learning in which all local models are forced to be identical when *λ* approaches infinity. In this way, the degree of personalization can be controlled. The author also provided a communication-efficient framework in which more local GD steps performed will reduce the communication rounds.

### 7.3.2 Model-based approaches: meta-learning

Meta-learning is known as a “learning to learn” method that can learn new and heterogeneous tasks quickly and effectively [\[14](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0070),[30\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0150). MAML [\[14\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0070) and Reptile [\[30\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0150) are two well-known meta-learning algorithms and are widely used by their ability to fast adapt to new heterogeneous tasks. A common meta-learning process includes meta-training and meta-testing steps. The meta-training step in MAML can be mapped to the FL global model training process, while the meta-testing step can be mapped to the FL personalization process. Inspired by the idea of applying meta-learning to find the meta global model which can quickly adapt to the client's data to improve the performance of FL over non-i.i.d. data, the authors of [\[13\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0065) and [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) came up with Per-FedAvg and pFedMe algorithms for pFL. Specifically, Per-FedAvg in [\[13\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0065) aims to find a global model **w** which client *m* can use as an *initialization* to perform one more step of gradient update with respect to its own loss function to obtain its personalized model **θ**[*m*](**w**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si34.png). The formulation of Per-FedAvg is provided as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx006.jpg)(7.5) 

where *α* is the step size, *g*[*m*](**w**−*α*∇*g*[*m*](**w**))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si35.png) is the meta-function associated with client *m*. In order to solve [(7.5)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq6), there is a need to compute second-order gradients which is costly in terms of computation. The authors provided two methods including FO-MAML [\[14\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0070) and HF-MAML [\[12\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0060) to approximate the Hessian, hence reducing the computational cost.

Having a similar idea of finding a global model as a good initialization point for personalized models, [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) proposed the new problem formulation as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx007.jpg)(7.6) 

where

$g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d}}\\left\\{ \\ell\_{m}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}) + \\frac{\\lambda}{2}{\\|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m} - \\mathbf{w}\\|}^{2} \\right\\}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si36.png)(7.7) 

is the well-known Moreau envelope, which incorporates an *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si1.png)\-norm regularization to control the balance between personalization and generalization performance. Model **θ**[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si37.png) denotes the personalized model of client *m* and *λ* is a regularization parameter that controls the strength of the global model **w** to the personalized model. While large *λ* can benefit clients with unreliable data from the abundant data aggregation, small *λ* helps clients with sufficient useful data prioritizing personalization. Note that *λ* ∈ (0, ∞)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si33.png) to avoid extreme cases of *λ* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si38.png), i.e., no FL, or *λ* = ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si39.png), i.e., no pFL. Overall, the idea is to allow clients to pursue their own models with different directions, but not to stay far away from the “reference point” **w**, to which every client contributes. While **w** is found by exploiting the data aggregation from multiple clients at the outer level, **θ**[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si37.png) is optimized with respect to client *m*'s data distribution and is maintained a bounded distance from **w** at the inner level. Compared to problem [(7.5)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq6), problem [(7.6)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq7) has a similar meaning of **w** as a “meta-model,” but instead of using **w** as the initialization, pFedMe pursues in parallel both the personalized and global models by solving a bi-level problem, which has several benefits. First, while Per-FedAvg is optimized for one-step gradient update for its personalized model, pFedMe is agnostic to the inner optimizer, which means [(7.7)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq8) can be solved using any iterative approach with multi-step updates. Second, by rewriting the personalized model update of Per-FedAvg as

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\mathbf{w} - \\alpha\\nabla g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}) = \\underset{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d}}{arg\\, min}\\left\\{ \\langle\\nabla g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}),\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m} - \\mathbf{w}\\rangle + \\frac{1}{2\\alpha}{\\|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{m} - \\mathbf{w}\\|}^{2} \\right\\},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si40.png)

we can see that apart from the similar regularization term, Per-FedAvg only optimizes the first-order approximation of *g*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si41.png), whereas pFedMe directly minimizes *g*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si41.png) in [(7.7)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq8). Third, Per-FedAvg (or generally several MAML-based methods) requires computing or estimating Hessian matrix, whereas pFedMe only needs gradient calculation using the first-order approach.

### 7.3.3 Multi-task learning

The main goal of the multi-task approach is to exploit commonalities and differences across the tasks to allow multiple related tasks to learn simultaneously. In FL setting, MOCHA [\[35\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0175) and FedU [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) consider each client as a single task, then capture the relationships among clients based on the client's data and learn multi-personalized models instead of a single global model to handle the non-i.i.d. data. The general formulation for FMTL is provided as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx008.jpg)(7.8) 

where the matrix **Θ** = \[**θ**[1], …, **θ**[*n*]\] ∈ ℝ^(*d* × *n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si42.png) contains collective personalized model vectors and *R*(**Θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si43.png) comprises the regularization functions. We notice that [(7.8)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq10) is relevant to the traditional FL problem [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1) when **θ**[1] = **θ**[2] = … = **θ**[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si44.png). MOCHA and FedU come with different definitions of *R*(**Θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si43.png) to encourage the models of the neighboring clients to be close to each other. The formulation of MOCHA is written as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx009.jpg)(7.9) 

where *Ω* ∈ ℝ^(*n* × *n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si45.png) denotes the model relationships among tasks, and obtained independently with data or estimated while simultaneously learning task models. The problem formulation of FedU is defined as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx010.jpg)(7.10) 

where 𝒩[*k*] = 𝒩 ∖ {*k*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si46.png), *a*[*m**k*] :  = \[**A**\][*m**k*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si47.png), and **A** ∈ ℝ^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si48.png) is a symmetric, weighted adjacency matrix. The relationship between clients *m* and *k* is presented by *a*[*m**k*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si49.png). Here, *a*[*k*ℓ] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si50.png) means no relationship between the models of clients *m* and *k*. The value of *a*[*m**k*] > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si51.png) shows that client *m* is a neighbor of client *k* and also determines the strength of the relationship between these two clients' models.

### 7.3.4 Weight sharing

Weight sharing (WS) aims to achieve pFL by decoupling the local private layer from the global FL model parameters. Clients train their own private layer locally and do not share with the FL server. This enables learning task-specific representations for enhanced personalization. There are generally two configurations used in WS for deep neural networks. The first is to use global representation and personalize last layers proposed by FedPer [\[2\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0010) and FedRep [\[6\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0030). In this setting, clients keep personalized layers for local training and share the global representation with the rest. The second design in [\[26\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0130) considers personalized feature representations for each client and all clients share the common last layer.

In the WS setting, parameters **w**, ***θ*** correspond to different layers of the same neural network but are used for global parameters and personalized parameters, respectively. For example, in [\[26\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0130), **θ**[1], …, **θ**[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si52.png) could be the weights of the first few layers of a neural network, while **w** are the weights of the remaining layers. Alternatively, in [\[2](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0010),[6\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0030), each of **θ**[1], …, **θ**[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si52.png) corresponds to the weight of the last few layers, while the remaining weights are included in the global parameter **w**. Overall, the problem formulation of WS can be written as

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx011.jpg)(7.11) 

where *d* = *d*[*w*] + *d*[*θ*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si53.png) is the feature dimension. Decoupling the neural network into the global and personal layers reduces the dimension of sharing global weight and brings benefits in both communication and computation.

### 7.3.5 Clients clustering

In FL, when there is a significantly large number of participating clients, the clients with similar characteristics (e.g., location, time, age, gender) are likely to have similar behaviors. Thus, training multiple FL models for each homogeneous group of closed relation clients becomes more suitable. Several works [\[4](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0020),[10](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050),[15\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0075) have focused on applying the clustering technique for pFL with the assumption that there are existing client groups in which clients have related data distribution. Each client group or cluster trains a single personalized model.

The work in [\[4\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0020) uses an unsupervised algorithm named hierarchical clustering to cluster clients into groups based on the client's model. At first, the global model is trained for *τ* communication round. Each client then fine-tunes the global model using its private data. To generate multiple client clusters, all fine-tuned models **w**[1], …, **w**[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si54.png) of *n* clients become inputs to the hierarchical clustering algorithm to separate *n* clients into **C**\-clusters. The traditional FL training process then performs on each cluster to produce a personalized model for each cluster. When there are a large number of clients, however, computing the pairwise distance of parameters between all clients is computationally intensive. Other clustering approaches [\[10](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050),[15\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0075) necessitate the selection of a fixed number of clusters at the start of FL training. Ghosh et al. [\[15\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0075) proposed a simple one-shot clustering algorithm IFCA that does not require a centralized clustering algorithm hence reducing the computational cost on the server side. The WS approach is applied to learn the shared representation layer and the separate final layer is personalized for each individual cluster. However, IFCA has a *K* times higher communication overhead than FedAvg as the server needs to broadcast *K* cluster models to all clients in each communication round. FedGroup, a FL clustering framework proposed by [\[10\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0050), implements a static client clustering strategy and a newcomer client cold start mechanism. FedGroup uses the KMeans++ algorithm [\[3\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0015) to cluster client's model updates based on the similarity of gradient update direction of each client.

## 7.4 Personalized FL algorithms

In this section, we give more insights by discussing two state-of-the-art pFL algorithms including pFedMe for the model-based approach and FedU for FMTL approach.

### 7.4.1 pFedMe

Instead of solving the traditional FL problem [(7.1)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq1), pFedMe takes a different approach by using a regularized loss function with *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si1.png)\-norm for each client and solve the problem [(7.6)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq7). pFedMe algorithm is presented in [Algorithm 1](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#f0010). At the *t*th communication round, the server broadcasts the latest global model **w**^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si55.png) to all clients. After all clients perform *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si56.png) local updates, the server will receive the latest local models from a uniformly sampled subset 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si57.png) of clients to perform the model averaging. Note that pFedMe uses an additional parameter *β* for the global model update in order to speed up convergence rates, which includes FedAvg's model averaging when *β* = 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si58.png), though a similar parameter at the server side was also used in [\[20](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0100),[33\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0165). Specifically, pFedMe aims to solve the bi-level problem and has two key differences compared with FedAvg. First, at the inner level, each client *m* solves [(7.12)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq14) to obtain its personalized model ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si59.png) where **w**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si60.png) denotes the *local model* of client *m* at the global round *t* and local round *r*:

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx012.jpg)(7.12) 

Similar to FedAvg, the purpose of local models is to contribute to building global model with reduced communication rounds between clients and server. Second, at the outer level, the local update of client *m* using gradient descent is with respect to *g*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si41.png) (instead of *l*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si61.png)) as follows:

**w**[*m*, *r* + 1]^((*t*)) = **w**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*)) − *η*∇*g*[*m*](**w**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*))),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si62.png)

where *η* is the learning rate and $\\nabla g\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)}) = \\lambda(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)} - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si63.png).

![Algorithm 1 pFedMe.](images/B9780443190377000107/gr001.jpg)

[Algorithm 1](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#cf0350) pFedMe.

For the practical algorithm, pFedMe uses a *δ*\-approximation of ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si59.png), denoted by ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si65.png) satisfying $\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\|{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)}) - {\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})\\| \\right\\rbrack \\leqslant \\delta$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si66.png), and correspondingly uses $\\lambda(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)} - {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si67.png) to approximate ∇*g*[*m*](**w**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*)))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si68.png) (cf. line 8). The reason of using the *δ*\-approximate ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si65.png) is twofold. First, obtaining ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si59.png) according to [(7.7)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq8) usually needs the gradient ∇*l*[*m*](**θ**[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si69.png), which, however, requires the distribution of a random sample *ξ*[*m*]^((*i*)) = (**x**[*m*]^((*i*)), *c*[*m*]^((*i*)))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si70.png). In practice, pFedMe uses the following unbiased estimate of ∇*l*[*m*](**θ**[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si69.png) by sampling a mini-batch of data *B*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si71.png):

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx013.jpg)

such that 𝔼\[∇*l̃*[*m*](**θ**[*m*],*B*[*m*])\] = ∇*l*[*m*](**θ**[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si72.png). Second, in general, it is not straightforward to obtain ${\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si59.png) in closed-form. Instead, pFedMe uses iterative first-order approach to obtain an approximate ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si65.png) with high accuracy. Defining

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx014.jpg)(7.13) 

we suppose choosing *λ* such that *h̃*[*m*](**θ**[*m*]; **w**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*)), *B*[*m*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si73.png) is strongly convex with a condition number *κ* (which quantifies how hard it is to optimize [(7.13)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq17)), then gradient descent (resp. Nesterov's accelerated gradient descent) can be used to obtain ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m}(\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si65.png) such that

${\\|\\nabla{\\widetilde{h}}\_{m}({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{m};\\mathbf{w}\_{m,r}^{(t)},B\_{m})\\|}^{2} \\leqslant \\nu,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si74.png)(7.14) 

with the number of ∇*h̃*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si75.png) computations ![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/fx015.jpg)[\[5\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0025), where *d* is the diameter of the search space, *ν* is an accuracy level, and 𝒪( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si76.png) hides constants. The computation complexity of each client in pFedMe is *K* times that in FedAvg. The detailed proof can be found in [\[8\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0040).

### 7.4.2 FedU

The FedU algorithm for solving the formulated FL problem [(7.10)](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#deq12) under a communication-centralized manner is presented in [Algorithm 2](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#f0015). First, at each communication round *t*, the server uniformly samples a subset of clients 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si57.png) and sends the latest update of local model **θ**[*m*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si28.png) to each client *m*, ∀*m* ∈ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si78.png). Then, after *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si56.png) local update steps are performed, the server receives the latest local update from the sampled clients to perform model regularization for each local model.

![Algorithm 2 FedU.](images/B9780443190377000107/gr002.jpg)

[Algorithm 2](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#cf0385) FedU.

FedU has a key difference compared to the conventional FL algorithms (e.g., FedAvg [\[28\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0140)) and the pFL algorithms (e.g., pFedMe [\[8\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0040), and Per-FedAvg [\[13\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0065)). Instead of updating the personalized models only at the clients using a global model from the server, FedU directly updates each local model at both client and server sides without building a global model. Specifically, in each communication round, each client *m* ∈ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si79.png) copies its current local model received from the server, **θ**[*m*, 0]^((*t*)) = **θ**[*m*]^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si80.png), and performs *τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si56.png) local updates of the form

**θ**[*m*, *r* + 1]^((*t*)) ← **θ**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*)) − *η*∇*g̃*[*m*](**θ**[*m*, *r*]^((*t*))),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si81.png)

where *μ* is the local step-size. Then the server receives {**θ**[*m*, *τ*[*m*]]^((*t*))}![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si82.png) from sampled clients *m* ∈ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si79.png), and updates

**θ**[*m*, *τ*[*m*]]^((*t*)) ← **θ**[*m*]^((*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si83.png)

for any non-sampled client *m* ∉ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si84.png). Finally, the server performs its regularization update for any sampled client *m* ∈ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si79.png) as

**θ**[*m*]^((*t* + 1)) ← **θ**[*m*, *τ*[*m*]]^((*t*)) − *μ̃**λ*∑[*k* ∈ 𝒩[*m*] ∩ 𝒮^((*t*))]*a*[*m**k*](**θ**[*m*, *τ*[*m*]]^((*t*)) − **θ**[*k*, *τ*[*m*]]^((*t*))),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si85.png)

and for any non-sampled client *m* ∉ 𝒮^((*t*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si84.png) as

**θ**[*m*]^((*t* + 1)) ← **θ**[*m*]^((*t*)),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si86.png)

where *μ̃* = *μ**τ*[*m*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si87.png) is a global step-size. This step finishes one round of communication.

## 7.5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate the performance of important pFL works including FedU, MOCHA, pFedMe, Per-FedAvg, APFL, FedRep, and the vanilla FedAvg when the data are heterogeneous and non-i.i.d. in both strongly convex and nonconvex settings.

### 7.5.1 Experimental settings

We consider classification problems using four real datasets generated in federated settings, including Human Activity Recognition (HAR), Vehicle sensor, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.

*   •  **HAR.** Data is gathered from accelerometers and gyroscopes of cell phones from 30 individuals performing six different activities including lying-down, standing, walking, sitting, walking-upstairs, and walking-downstairs [\[1\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0005). Each client classifies 6 different activities. 
*   •  **Vehicle Sensor.** Data is collected from 23 distributed wireless sensors including acoustic (microphone), seismic (geophone), and infrared (polarized IR sensor) [\[11\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0055). We consider each sensor as a client performing the binary classification predicting two vehicle types: Assault Amphibian Vehicle (AAV) and Dragon Wagon (DW).
*   •  **MNIST.** A handwritten digit dataset [\[23\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0115) includes 10 labels and 70,000 instances. The whole dataset is distributed to *n* = 100![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si88.png) clients. Each client has a different local data size and consists of 2 over 10 labels.
*   •  **CIFAR-10.** An object recognition dataset [\[22\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0110) includes 60,000 color images belonging to 10 classes. We partition the dataset to *n* = 20![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si89.png) clients and 3 labels per client.

The detailed statistics of all datasets are summarized in [Table 7.1](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#t0010). In practical FL networks, some clients have significantly limited data sizes and need collaborative learning with others. For each dataset, we consider two different scenarios including a **down-sample** with 80% of data belonging to a half of the total clients and the **full-sample** in [Table 7.1](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#t0010) to observe the behavior of all algorithms. All datasets are split randomly with 75% and 25% for training and testing, respectively.

Table 7.1

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

We use a multinomial logistic regression (MLR) with cross-entropy loss functions and *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000107/si1.png)\-regularization term as the strongly convex model for HAR, Vehicle Sensor, and MNIST. For the nonconvex setting, we use a simple DNN with one hidden layer, an ReLU activation function, and a softmax layer at the end of the network for HAR and Vehicle Sensor. The size of hidden layer is 100 for HAR and 20 for Vehicle Sensor. In the case of MNIST, we use DNN with 2 hidden layers and both layers have the same size of 100. For CIFAR-10, we follow the CNN structure of [\[28\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0140). We follow the setting and the implementation of [\[9\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0045) for the experiment.

## 7.6 Open problems

In this section, two promising future research directions for personalized federated learning, i.e., transfer learning and knowledge distillation, are briefly introduced.

### 7.6.1 Transfer learning

The aim of transfer learning (TL) is to transfer knowledge from a source domain to a desired domain [\[32\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0160). The key idea is that the model does not need to build from scratch because the knowledge of the source domain is a pre-trained model. This idea can be applied to model personalization in FL. The parameters of the pre-trained global model, i.e., the extracted knowledge, are used as an initialization for a re-learning process at each client [\[38\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0190). In this re-learning process, each client only needs to fine-tune the global model on its local data. For deep neural networks, the lower layer of the global model should be transferred and used as lower level genetic features in the local models in order to reduce the overhead. The challenge in TL-based pFL is to reduce the domain discrepancy between the pre-trained global model and the local model for improving personalization. To overcome this challenge, one solution is to add an alignment layer which is the correlation alignment (CORAL) layer [\[36\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0180) before the softmax layer to adapt the second-order statistic of both the source and desired domains.

### 7.6.2 Knowledge distillation

Knowledge distillation (KD) was introduced by [\[18\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0090) for distilling the knowledge of a large teach network into a lightweight student network by letting the student mimic the teacher. KD originally aimed to reduce the communication and computation resource requirements for a learning system. However, it can be useful for personalizing models in FL in several ways [\[37\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0185). The knowledge of the local models benefits in forming better personalized models while the knowledge of the global models benefits in improving the personalized performance of each client. The knowledge distillation can perform in a bi-directional manner at both the client and server sides. The challenge in KD-based pFL is to overcome over-fitting at each client due to the small size of the local data. Yu et al. [\[39\]](#Chp007_125-141_B9780443190377000107.xhtml#br0195) proposed a solution to overcome this challenge, in which the global model plays the role of the teacher, while the personalized model plays the role of the student.

## 7.7 Conclusion

This chapter has provided a systematic review of existing personalized federated learning approaches to deal with the statistical diversity among clients in federated learning. The chapter also discussed and compared the state-of-the-art algorithms of these approaches with real-data experiments to gain more insights. Finally, future research directions for personalized federated learning were introduced.

# Chapter 8: Fairness in federated learning

Xiaoqiang Lin^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); Xinyi Xu^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); Zhaoxuan Wu^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); Rachael Hwee Ling Sim^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); See-Kiong Ng^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); Chuan-Sheng Foo^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010)); Patrick Jaillet^([b](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0015)); Trong Nghia Hoang^([c](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0020)); Bryan Kian Hsiang Low^([a](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#aff0010))    ^aNational University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore  
^bMassachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, United States  
^cWashington State University, Pullman, WA, United States

## Abstract

Federated learning (FL) enables a form of collaboration among multiple clients in jointly learning a machine learning (ML) model without centralizing their local datasets. Like in any collaboration, it is imperative to guarantee *fairness* so that the clients are willing to participate. For instance, it is unfair if one client benefits significantly more than others, or if some client benefits disproportionately to its contribution in the collaboration. Additionally, it is also unfair if the ML model makes biased predictions against certain groups of clients. This chapter discusses three specific notions of fairness by highlighting their motivations from real-world use-cases, examining several specific definitions for each notion and lastly describing the corresponding algorithms proposed to achieve each notion of fairness. At the end, this chapter will also summarize the identified gaps in current research efforts into open problems.

### Keywords

Fairness; Federated learning

## Acknowledgements

This research/project is supported by the National Research Foundation Singapore and DSO National Laboratories under the AI Singapore Programme (AISG Award No: AISG2-RP-2020-018).

## 8.1 Introduction

Federated learning (FL) [\[15\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0075) allows multiple clients to collaborate in training a model with better performance (than before collaboration) without centralizing their local datasets [\[5](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0025),[30\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0150). However, most existing FL systems [\[5](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0025),[15](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0075),[27](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0135),[30](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0150),[31\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0155) do not explicitly consider the willingness and simply assume that all clients want to collaborate [\[15\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0075). This assumption can be problematic when the clients are self-interested and not obliged to participate. For example, clients might not participate if they are treated *unfairly* (e.g., receiving no or less reward while contributing resources) by the FL system. Therefore, it is imperative to guarantee *fairness* to encourage such collaborations in FL. This chapter discusses three fairness notions, *equitable fairness*, *collaborative fairness* and *algorithmic fairness*, by (1) motivating them in Section [8.1](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#s0010); (2) providing the formal definitions in Section [8.2](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#s0015); (3) describing the respective algorithms for achieving them in Section [8.3](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#s0035); and (4) shedding light on some open problems in Section [8.4](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#s0055).

FL systems can be viewed as a form of cost-sharing or resource-allocation collaboration. The clients share the costs of collecting data by tapping into the information from others' local datasets to train a *global model* (i.e., model trained on the server). The global model can be viewed as a “medium” of some resources to be allocated to the clients. Each client receives the same global model to make predictions on their local datasets.

However, due to the difference in their local datasets, the predictive performance (or loss/objective function) of a single global model differs across clients. In essence, the predictive performance is the resource that is allocated, through the medium that is the global model. Because the clients do not necessarily have an identical objective (i.e., are heterogeneous [\[13\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0065)), it is important the training in FL is *fair* with respect to these different objectives (i.e., training losses of their respective local datasets). Specifically, it is unfair to allocate all the resources to a single client (i.e., training the global model to exclusively optimize the performance on that client's local dataset) because it can result in poor performance on other clients' local datasets. Instead, the global model resource should be allocated fairly (among all the clients' objectives) so that the model has small performance disparities on all local datasets, formalized as *equitable fairness*.

In some other practical scenarios, the clients compete with each other (e.g., companies providing similar services/products) [\[27](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0135),[31\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0155). These clients are *self-interested*, namely they focus on maximizing their own utility (e.g., the trained model's performance on their local dataset). In contrast to the aforementioned scenario, these self-interested clients are only willing to contribute to help others if doing so (strictly) improves their own utility. Moreover, it can appear exploitative if a client *i* that contributes more than client *j* receives a reward lower than that received by client *j*, and can discourage collaboration. It thus motivates a different notion of fairness. Formally, the *contribution* of a client characterizes how much a client shares (directly or indirectly by training on its local dataset) with other clients [\[22](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0110),[25\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0125) and the *reward* of a client specifies how much a client gains from the collaboration [\[21](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0105),[29\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0145). The so-called *collaborative fairness* [\[14\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0070) stipulates that the rewards should be commensurate with the contributions, so that the clients are rewarded more if they contribute more, and vice versa.

Lastly, dealing with bias in data in machine learning (ML) is a known challenge [\[16](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0080),[33\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0165), which can be exacerbated by the multi-client setting of FL. Note that this perspective differs from the two previous settings in that it explicitly considers *how* the trained global model predicts on certain data. From the perspective of each client, the goal of removing bias is to ensure the trained model does not discriminate against certain protected groups (e.g., data whose sensitive features such as gender, race having certain values) [\[2\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0010). In practice, the clients do not necessarily have aligned goals due to different local datasets [\[1\]](#Chp008_143-160_B9780443190377000168.xhtml#br0005). Consequently, trying to eliminate/reduce discrimination among groups for one client can deteriorate that for another. Therefore, ideally, the trained model should not be biased with respect to any client's local dataset, called *algorithmic fairness*. In other words, suppose a data point is in the protected group (e.g., a record of a person), then this data point should *not* be discriminated against regardless of which local dataset it belongs to.
