## 10.3 Multi-center federated learning

Besides the advanced algorithms designed for heterogeneous FL networks, cluster-structured models are also considered for tackling the issues of non-i.i.d. data distributions over distributed networks. The underlying assumption is that there exist *K* global models and the scattered local models only belong to one of these global ones. In FeSEM [\[24\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0120), a multi-center model aggregation model is used for FL, where all the local models are partitioned into *K* clusters, denoted as {𝒞[*k*], *k* ∈ \[*K*\]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si49.png). Aside from minimizing the consensus errors and regression loss function, an assignment of each model to its nearest cluster is also included in the learning process. Specifically, the overall problem is formulated as follows:

$(\\mathbb{P}2)\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},{\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k},r\_{ik},\\forall i,k}\\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\xi \\sim \\mathcal{D}\_{i}}F\_{i}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i};\\xi) + \\frac{\\lambda}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}r\_{ik}{dist}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},{\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k}),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si50.png)(10.7) 

where *λ* controls the trade-off between the supervised loss and multi-center based model discrepancy, *d**i**s**t*(⋅, ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si51.png) denotes the distance between two model parameter spaces, ${\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si52.png) represents the *k*th center of cluster 𝒞[*k*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si53.png), and *r*[*i**k*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si54.png) is the binary assignment variable that indicate whether the *i*th model is classified to the *k*th cluster or not. The regularization term measures the distance between each local model to its nearest global model.

For the multi-center FL model, the expectation-maximization (EM) method is one of the most standard techniques for solving clustering related problems. Combining with a local supervised learning update, a stochastic block coordinate descent type of algorithm is proposed for the FL setting, called federated stochastic EM (FeSEM), in [\[24\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0120). The main idea of FeSEM is adapting the EM algorithm in searching for the multiple centers ${\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si52.png) while fixing local model parameters {**θ**[*i*], ∀*i*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si55.png), and then performing local updates of **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png) for *τ* steps to minimize the local loss function values while keeping the assignment of every model to each cluster learned from the previous step unchanged. More detailed procedures of FeSEM are shown in [Algorithm 2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0020) and explained as follows:

![Algorithm 2 FeSEM – Federated Stochastic EM \[24\].](images/B9780443190377000181/gr003.jpg)

[Algorithm 2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#cf0155) FeSEM – Federated Stochastic EM [\[24\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0120).

**E-Step**. The first step of each model is to look for the nearest clusters based on the distance between the local model parameter **θ**[*i*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si57.png) and the existing centers $\\{{\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{j}^{t},j \\in \\lbrack K\\rbrack\\}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si58.png) and obtain the assignment variable by

$r\_{ik}^{t} = \\left\\{ \\begin{array}{l} {1,\\quad\\text{if}\\ k = \\arg\\min\_{j}{dist}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{t},{\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{j}^{t}),} \\\\ {0,\\quad\\text{otherwise}.} \\\\ \\end{array} \\right.$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si59.png)(10.8) 

**M-Step**. Then, the center of each cluster is calculated by

${\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k}^{t} = \\frac{1}{\\sum\_{i = 1}^{n}r\_{ik}}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}r\_{ik}^{t}\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{t}$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si60.png)(10.9) 

while fixing model parameters and current center assignments.

**Local models**. Given the multi-centers, each local device will fine-tune the model for individual data distribution by minimizing the regression loss function and the dissimilarity between the local and assigned global model parameters, which means that each **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png) needs solving the following problem:

$\\min\\limits\_{\\theta\_{i}}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\xi \\sim \\mathcal{D}\_{i}}F\_{i}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i};\\xi) + \\lambda\\sum\\limits\_{k = 1}^{K}r\_{ik}{dist}(\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},{\\overline{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{k}).$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si61.png)(10.10) 

Here, Eq. [(10.10)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq12) is an unconstrained optimization problem. The model parameters can be updated efficiently by multiple steps of SGD, which corresponds to the local SGD update in the standard FL scenario. Finally, iterating the above three steps results in the FeSEM algorithm for solving the multi-center FL problem.

![Algorithm 3 Local\_Update.](images/B9780443190377000181/gr004.jpg)

Algorithm 3 **Local\_Update**.

## 10.4 Graph-knowledge based federated learning

Even though the multi-center FL takes the cluster structure into consideration, FeSEM still assumes that there is no overlap among the global models, which might not be true or restrict for practical heterogeneous networks. Actually, FeSEM can be considered as a special case of the two levels of the optimization problem, where one level is minimizing the regularization term in Eq. [(10.7)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq9) for searching the cluster structure and the other is minimizing the supervised loss for data feature extraction. Mathematically, the class of multi-task learning problems can be formulated as a bilevel optimization as follows [\[12\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0060):

$\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\varphi}}\\ \\ell(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) \\triangleq f\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi})\\} \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si62.png)(10.11a) 

$\\text{such\\ that}\\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) \\in \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\xi \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{i}}G\_{i}(\\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i};\\xi),\\ \\forall i \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si63.png)(10.11b) 

where ***φ*** is the UL decision variable, {**θ**[*i*], ∀*i*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si55.png) denote the LL model parameters, *f*(⋅, ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si64.png) and *G*[*i*](⋅, ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si65.png) respectively represent the UL and LL loss functions, and {**θ**[*i*]^(\*)(**φ**), ∀*i* ∈ \[*n*\]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si66.png) stand for the optimal solutions of the LL optimization variables. This model can cover a wide range of hierarchical FL learning problems, e.g., federated acoustic speech recognition [\[3\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0015), personalized meta-learning [\[4\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0020), multi-agent actor–critic schemes in reinforcement learning [\[15\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0075), etc.

Note that the structured graph knowledge is related to all the local models, so the LL optimization variables would be coupled. One example is the multi-center FL case as shown in Eq. [(10.10)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq12), where the *k*th center involved in the LL problem is calculated based on all **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png)s. Therefore, a more generalized bilevel optimization enhanced GAFL, or BiG-FL in short, is proposed in [\[25\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0125), by formulating the LL optimization problem as a competitive game as follows:

$(\\mathbb{P}3)\\quad\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\varphi}}\\ \\ell(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) = f\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi})\\} \\right)$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si67.png)(10.12a) 

$\\text{such\\ that}\\ \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}\\mathbb{E}\_{\\xi \\in \\mathcal{D}\_{i}}G\_{i}\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{- i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi});\\xi \\right),\\ \\forall i \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si68.png)(10.12b) 

where **θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si69.png) denotes {**θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**)|**θ**[*j*]^(\*)(**φ**), *j* ≠ *i*, ∀*j* ∈ 𝒩[*i*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si70.png). From this model, we can see that the UL optimization problem is targeted at minimizing the globally shareable parameter ***φ*** while the LL problem is used for integrating the UL knowledge and adapting the local data distributions. In the following, we provide one way of applying the BiG-FL to a GNN-embedded FL system.

### 10.4.1 Applications of BiG-FL

Inspired by graph embedding learning for link prediction [\[7\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0035), BiG-FL can take the connectivity of FL clients/devices (i.e., edge information in the global graph structure) as a guide in the UL optimization process and maps this topology information to weigh the similarity of neighboring clients' models.

Let **θ**^(\*)(**φ**) ∈ ℝ^(*n* × *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si71.png) denote the concatenation of all the LL optimal solutions. Constructing the embedding matrix **H** via linear message passing in GNNs yields:

**H** = **L****θ**^(\*)(**φ**)**φ**,

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si72.png)(10.13) 

where **L** ∈ ℝ^(*n* × *n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si73.png) is a Laplacian matrix (e.g., $\\mathbf{L} \\triangleq {\\widetilde{\\mathbf{D}}}^{- \\frac{1}{2}}\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{D}}}^{- \\frac{1}{2}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si74.png), where $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}} = \\mathbf{A} + \\mathbf{I}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si75.png) and ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{D}}}\_{ii} = \\sum\_{j}{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{A}}}\_{ij}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si76.png), which are commonly used in graph convolution networks (GCNs) [\[8\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0040)), **θ**^(\*)(**φ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si77.png) is learned from local models, and **φ** ∈ ℝ^(*d* × *d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si78.png) denotes the UL parameters acting as the weights in GNN with a shape of *d* × *d*![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si79.png).

**UL loss function**. With this graph-based representation, we can formulate the UL objective function using the cosine embedding loss as

$f(\\varphi,\\mathbf{\\theta}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi})) \\triangleq \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\sum\\limits\_{j \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{i}}\\left( 1 - \\cos(\\mathbf{H}\_{i},\\mathbf{H}\_{j}) \\right) + \\frac{1}{n}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{n}\\mathbb{E}\_{j \\sim P\_{i}}\\max\\left( 0,\\cos(\\mathbf{H}\_{i},\\mathbf{H}\_{j}) \\right) + \\frac{\\lambda}{2}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\varphi} - \\mathbf{I} \\right\\|^{2},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si80.png)(10.14) 

where *i* and *j* are indices of the nodes (i.e., FL clients/devices),

$\\cos(\\mathbf{H}\_{i},\\mathbf{H}\_{j}) \\triangleq \\frac{\\mathbf{H}\_{i}^{T}\\mathbf{H}\_{j}}{\\|\\mathbf{H}\_{i}\\|\\|\\mathbf{H}\_{j}\\|},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si81.png)(10.15) 

and 𝒫[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si82.png) denotes the negative sampling distribution at client *i* [\[7\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0035).

The UL objective function for BiG-Fed in Eq. [(10.14)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq18) utilizes the cosine embedding loss to calculate both the client-pair embedding similarity of all linked clients and the client-pair embedding dissimilarity of negative samples. As the embedding is derived from the local model weights, Eq. [(10.14)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq18) couples local learning tasks with the graphical link prediction task at the server side.

It is worth noting that the link prediction model learns the relative relationships among the local models. In addition, we expect that the optimized UL model can maintain the centroid of the overall weight distribution, so we initialize ***φ*** by the identity matrix **I**, and add a regularity term on ***φ*** with the identity matrix **I** at the UL loss function.

**LL loss function**. The local LL learning tasks of BiG-FL at each device are finding the Nash equilibrium of the following problem:

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) = \\arg\\min\\limits\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}g\_{i}\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{- i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) \\right),\\forall i \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si83.png)(10.16) 

where *g*[*i*](**φ**, **θ**[*i*], **θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**)) ≜ 𝔼[*ξ* ∼ 𝒟[*i*]]*G*[*i*](**φ**, **θ**[*i*], **θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**); *ξ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si84.png). In this case, the UL weight ***φ*** is introduced into the LL learning task to penalize the distance between the aggregation of neighboring weights and the local one, as we assume that the neighboring clients share a similar latent space. Hence, for each client, the loss function *g*[*i*]( ⋅ )![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si85.png) includes both the supervised learning error and distance between the local model parameter and the centroid learned from the UL graph knowledge:

$g\_{i}\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{- i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) \\right) \\triangleq \\frac{1}{2}\\mathbb{E}\_{(X\_{i},Y\_{i}) \\sim \\mathcal{D}\_{i}}{\\| Y\_{i} - h\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}(X\_{i})\\|}^{2}\\quad + \\frac{\\lambda}{2}R\_{i}\\left( \\mathbf{\\varphi},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{- i}^{\\ast}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}) \\right) + \\frac{\\kappa}{2}{\\|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}\\|}^{2},\\forall i \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si86.png)(10.17) 

where *h*[**θ**[*i*]]( ⋅ ) : *X*[*i*] → *Y*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si87.png) denotes the nonlinear mapping parametrized by a neural network with weight **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png), *X*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si88.png) and *Y*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si89.png) respectively represent the data and labels owned by the *i*th client, 𝒟[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si10.png) denotes the joint distribution of *X*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si88.png) and *Y*[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si89.png), regularization term *κ*∥**θ**[*i*]∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si90.png) is used for stabilizing the LL learning process with *κ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si91.png), and *R*[*i*](**φ**, **θ**[*i*], **θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**))![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si92.png) denotes the distance based regularization term,

*R*[*i*](**φ**, **θ**[*i*], **θ**[ − *i*]^(\*)(**φ**)) = ∥(**L**[*i*, :]−**L**[*i*, *i*])**θ**^(\*)(**φ**)**φ**+**L**[*i*, *i*]**θ**[*i*]**φ**−**θ**[*i*]∥².

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si93.png)(10.18) 

Furthermore, **L**[*i*, :]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si94.png) denotes the *i*th row of Laplacian matrix **L**. Note that term (**L**[*i*, :] − **L**[*i*, *i*])**θ**^(\*)(**φ**)**φ** + **L**[*i*, *i*]**θ**[*i*]**φ**![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si95.png) is the weight embedding, where (**L**[*i*, :] − **L**[*i*, *i*])**θ**^(\*)(**φ**)**φ**![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si96.png) does not involve current node's weight **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png) and can be approximated by the FL server in advance.

The penalization on the difference between the current weight and the weight embedding in each LL task, together with the fact that the UL variable learns the relationship of each weight embedding simultaneously via ***φ***, allows us to leverage the graph information to improve the generalization of the model by integrating the prior knowledge of similarity among the nodes. Next, we will introduce an algorithm for solving Eq. ([10.12](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq15)).

### 10.4.2 Algorithm design for BiG-FL

Solving Eq. [(10.17)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq21) exactly to get the optimal solution is not practical. Instead, following the FL algorithms, we apply SGD for several steps and obtain an approximate solution of the LL problem. To be more specific, the LL optimization variable is updated by

$\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{k + 1} = \\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{k} - \\frac{\\beta^{t}}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}}G\_{i}(\\mathbf{\\varphi}^{t},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{i}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{- i}^{k};\\xi\_{j}),\\quad\\forall i \\in \\lbrack n\\rbrack,$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si97.png)(10.19) 

where *k* denotes the index of the inner loop by initializing **θ**[*i*]⁰ = **θ**[*i*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si98.png), *β*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si99.png) is the LL step size, and ∇*G*[*i*](**φ**^(*t*), **θ**[*i*]^(*k*), **θ**[ − *i*]^(*k*); *ξ*[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si100.png) represents the gradient of the *i*th BiG-FL LL empirical loss function evaluated at the point (**φ**^(*t*), **θ**[*i*]^(*k*), **θ**[ − *i*]^(*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si101.png) with the *j*th data sample (i.e., *ξ*[*j*] ≜ (*X*[*j*], *Y*[*j*]) ∼ 𝒟[*j*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si102.png)). After consecutive *τ* steps of the inner loop update, we set **θ**[*i*]^(*t* + 1) = **θ**[*i*]^(*τ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si103.png).

Similarly, the LL variable is updated by SGD with computing the hyper-gradient [\[5\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0025) as follows:

$\\mathbf{\\varphi}^{t + 1} = \\mathbf{\\varphi}^{t} - \\frac{\\alpha^{t}}{m}\\sum\\limits\_{j = 1}^{m}\\left( \\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\varphi}}F\_{j}^{t} - \\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\varphi}\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{2}\\mathbf{G}\_{j}^{t}\\left( \\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}\\mathbf{\\theta}}^{2}\\mathbf{G}\_{j}^{t} \\right)^{- 1}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}F\_{j}^{t} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si104.png)(10.20) 

where *α*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si25.png) denotes the UL step size, ∇[*φ*]*F*[*j*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si105.png) (the abbreviation of ∇[**φ**]*F*(**φ**^(*t*), {**θ**[*i*]^(*t*)}; *ξ*[*j*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si106.png)) is the gradient of the UL empirical loss function evaluated at point (**φ**^(*t*), {**θ**[*i*]^(*t*)})![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si107.png) with the *j*th tail node of the negative sample for head node *i* (i.e., *j* ∼ 𝒫[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si108.png)), ∇[**φ****θ**]²**G**[*j*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si109.png) and (∇[**θ****θ**]²**G**[*j*]^(*t*))^( − 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si110.png) respectively stand for the stochastic approximation of the Jacobian matrix of the LL loss function with respect to both ***φ*** and {**θ**[*i*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si111.png) and the inverse of Hessian matrix of the LL loss function. Here, we assume that the LL loss functions are strongly convex (e.g., if *κ* is sufficiently large), implying that ∇[**θ****θ**]²**G**[*j*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si112.png) is invertible. The complete implementation of BiG-FL is shown in [Algorithm 4](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0030), where ***θ*** is the concatenation of {**θ**[*i*], ∀*i*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si55.png).

![Algorithm 4 Bilevel optimization enhanced GFL (BiG-FL).](images/B9780443190377000181/gr005.jpg)

Algorithm 4 Bilevel optimization enhanced GFL (BiG-FL).

The convergence guarantees of bilevel optimization algorithms have been investigated in recent works [\[5](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0025),[12\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0060). For the BiG-FL problem, it has been shown in [\[25\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0125) that when the UL and LL step sizes *α*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si25.png) and *β*^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si99.png) are chosen on the order of $1/\\sqrt{T}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si113.png), under the Lipschitz continuity of the UL loss function, as well as its Jacobian and Hessian, plus the strong convexity of the LL loss functions, [Algorithm 4](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0030) needs 𝒪(1/*ϵ*⁴)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si114.png) iterations to reach the FOSPs of Eq. ([10.12](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq15)) in the sense that both the first-order stationarity of the UL optimization variable ***φ***, i.e., 𝔼∥∇ℓ(**φ**^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si115.png), and the distance between **θ**[*i*]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si57.png) and its optimal counterpart, i.e., 𝔼∥**θ**[*i*]^(*t*) − **θ**[*i*]^(\*)(**φ**^(*t*))∥²![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si116.png), ∀*i*, are 𝒪(*ϵ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si117.png), where the expectation is taken over both the randomness of data samples and the index of the iterations.

## 10.5 Numerical evaluation of GFL models

In this section, we provide numerical experiments for testing the performance of these GFL models and algorithms with a comparison with the benchmark FedAvg [\[18\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0090) on both synthetic and real data, which were partially shown in [\[25\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0125).

### 10.5.1 Results on synthetic data

To generate a heterogeneous network with respect to local model parameters, topology-based groundtruth weights (embedding) are generated based on a predefined graph, where inputs {*X*[*i*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si118.png) are randomly generated, and the outputs {*Y*[*i*]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si119.png) are obtained by following our model in Eq. [(10.13)](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#deq17), which is further illustrated in [Fig. 10.2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0035). In order to evaluate the generalization performance of the models, we need to generate two homologous graphs so that graphs adopted in training and testing share the same distribution. To be specific, we generate two graphs that follow homologous distributions. Each of them has 50 nodes and consists of the same mixture of three standard normal distributions. The range of the centers of these distributions is \[ − 0.5, 0.5\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si120.png), and the standard deviation of all these distributions is 0.5. We use the four closest neighboring nodes to build the graph. The dimension of the generated samples is 64, which is used as the groundtruth weight (reshaped to 8 × 8![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si121.png)) of the model for each client. For data synthesis, both training and testing sets are independently generated for the 50 LL learning tasks with uniformly distributed samples (100 × 8![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si122.png)) in the range of \[ − 60, 60\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si123.png) as the input. The output is obtained by matrix multiplication of the input and the groundtruth weights. Parameters used in the synthetic data experiment are shown in [Table 10.1](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#t0010).

![Figure 10.2 Homologous graph generation and data synthesis.](images/B9780443190377000181/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 10.2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#cf0265) Homologous graph generation and data synthesis.

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/t0010.png)

The multi-layer perception followed by the sigmoid activation functions is used in the LL learning model, and the total number of layers of **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png) is 3 with shapes of 8 × 16![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si124.png), 16 × 16![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si125.png), and 16 × 8![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si126.png), respectively. The UL task is link-prediction based on negative sampling. For each head node, we randomly sample 10 tail nodes from all negative edges and use the DGL package with a GCN layer [\[22\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0110) to generate the graph embedding for learning the edge similarity. The GCN layer is used in the UL task, where ***φ*** of dimension 512 × 512![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si127.png) serves as the graph convolution kernel of the GCN layer. Each uploaded LL weight **θ**[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si56.png) acts as the node input representative, which is flattened into a shape of 1 × 512![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si128.png) and fitted into the cosine embedding loss function after message passing. As FeSEM requires prior knowledge about the number of clustering centers, we set *K* = 3![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si129.png) to reflect the setting of the three mixed Gaussian distributions.

The numerical results are shown in [Fig. 10.3](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0040). It can be observed that the consensus-based models perform the worst in comparison with the cluster or graph embedding based ones, as there are three mixture Gaussian data samples over the graph. FeSEM improves the performance of classic FedAvg and DFL as the EM algorithm is able to find the three centers and tailor the model to fit different kinds of data distributions. BiG-FL shows the best performance among all the models in this case, which justifies the power of the UL learning task for extracting embedding through the graph information and transferring this similarity to the testing phrase.

### 10.5.2 Results on real-world data for NLP

A large lookup weight table related to the number of words in the corpus plays a central role in natural language processing (NLP) tasks. Each row of the table corresponds to a word which is involved in the current task (i.e., word embedding). These word embeddings are trainable weights and are non-i.i.d. due to textual word data originating from different domains, and have different dimensions and interleaved weight spaces due to the differences in corpus words.

We adopt the datasets from [\[9\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0045) which consist of 16 different domains of review data. As shown in [Table 10.2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#t0015), the datasets differ in terms of review category, the average length of the review sentences, and the number of unique words. The goal of this task is to train a multi-domain next word prediction model. Here, we use the GloVe embedding vectors [\[19\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0095), which are commonly applied for embedding initialization to act as a global representation. We group the non-i.i.d. embeddings from multiple domains and project them into this global vector space. For the LL model, we use the classic neural probabilistic language model [\[1\]](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#br0005) for word embedding, where the embedding layer (i.e., a big lookup table) is with a dimension of 63144 × 100![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si130.png), a fully-connected hidden layer is with a dimension of 100 × 200![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si131.png) followed by a tanh function, and a decoder layer has a size of 200 × 63144![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/si132.png). The length of the sliding window for the next word prediction task is 35 and the batch size is 100. The UL model is identical to the synthetic data case. We also set the dimension of the embedding layer for each client equal to the size of the total number of tokens for the purpose of alignment. If the current client contains a word, we set the corresponding row of the lookup table matrix of the embedding layer as trainable, and the row that does not have a corresponding word as 0. The total number of trainable rows per client is shown in the last column of [Table 10.2](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#t0015).

| IMDN || 2000 || 269 || 25,195/63,144 |
| MR || 2000 || 21 || 7315/63,144 |

![Image](images/B9780443190377000181/t0015.png)

The results are shown in [Fig. 10.4](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#f0045). It can be observed that the testing losses are consistent with the synthetic dataset case. Although the testing curve of BiG-FL has some fluctuations at the early stage of the convergence, it achieves the lowest loss eventually. The reason might be due to the competition among the LL learning models, which affects the embedding search progress in the UL problem, and once the graph structure is learned, BiG-FL will showcase a stable convergence behavior. This example verifies the importance of leveraging the similarity among the word embeddings in the multi-task FL problem and superiority of BiG-FL for solving this class of problems.

![Figure 10.4 Real-data experiment results (testing loss).](images/B9780443190377000181/gr008.jpg)

[Figure 10.4](#Chp010_181-197_B9780443190377000181.xhtml#cf0310) Real-data experiment results (testing loss).

## 10.6 Summary

In this chapter, we introduced three major classes of the GFL framework, including decentralized FL, multi-center FL, and bilevel optimization enhanced FL. Each FL model is mainly applicable for different practical FL scenarios, where DFL is designed for data samples collected in a decentralized way over a graph, multi-center FL is used for the clustered data structures, and BiG-FL is superior for integrating general topology information with adaptation to local learning tasks. Given the unique features of these GFL models, we further studied efficient gradient-based algorithms for solving the corresponding optimization problems in an FL way. It is concluded that the graph structure oriented FL systems can improve the classic FedAvg FL in terms of both learning efficiency and generalization performance.
