# Chapter 11: Vertical asynchronous federated learning: algorithms and theoretic guarantees

Tianyi Chen^([a](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#aff0010)); Xiao Jin^([a](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#aff0010)); Yuejiao Sun^([b](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#aff0015)); Wotao Yin^([c](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#aff0020))    ^aRensselaer Polytechnic Institute, Troy, NY, United States  
^bUniversity of California, Los Angeles, CA, United States  
^cAlibaba Group, Bellevue, WA, United States

## Abstract

Federated learning (FL) enables model training with multi-client data where privacy concerns and coordination challenges prevent us from using conventional machine learning methods. In particular, horizontal FL handles multi-client data that share the same set of features, and vertical FL handles data of the same set of subjects but different clients hold their different features. This chapter formulates vertical FL as an optimization problem and develops a *simple, yet practical* FL method. The new method allows each client to run stochastic gradient algorithms without coordination with other clients, so it is suitable for intermittent, even uncontrollable clients. Theoretically, we present the convergence rate of our method for strongly convex, nonconvex, and even nonsmooth objectives separately. Empirically, we apply our method to federated logistic regression and deep learning on various image and healthcare datasets.

### Keywords

Vertical federated learning; Asynchronous distributed optimization; Differential privacy

## Acknowledgements

This work was supported by National Science Foundation CAREER Award 2047177, and the Rensselaer-IBM AI Research Collaboration ([http://airc.rpi.edu](http://airc.rpi.edu)), part of the IBM AI Horizons Network ([http://ibm.biz/AIHorizons](http://ibm.biz/AIHorizons)).

## 11.1 Introduction

Most of the existing federated learning (FL) methods consider the scenario where each client has data of a different set of subjects, but their data share many common features. Therefore, they can collaboratively learn a joint mapping from the feature space to the label space. This setting is also referred to data-partitioned or horizontal FL [\[20](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0100),[25\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0125). Unlike the data-partitioned setting, in many learning scenarios, multiple clients handle data about the same set of subjects, but each client has a unique set of features. This case arises in e-commerce, financial, and healthcare applications [\[15\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0075). For example, an e-commerce company may want to predict a customer's credit using her/his historical transactions from multiple financial institutions; and a healthcare company wants to evaluate the health condition of a particular patient using his/her clinical data from various hospitals [\[35\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0175). In these examples, data owners (e.g., financial institutions and hospitals) have different records of those users in their joint user base. By combining their features, they can establish a more accurate model. We refer to this setting as feature-partitioned or vertical FL [\[43\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0215).

Compared to the relatively well-studied horizontal FL setting, the vertical FL setting has its unique features and challenges. In horizontal FL, the global model update at a server is an additive aggregation of the local models, updated by each client using its data. In contrast, the global model in vertical FL is the concatenation of local models, which are coupled by the loss function, so updating a client's local model requires the information of the other clients' models. Stronger model dependence in the vertical setting leads to challenges on privacy protection and communication efficiency.

### 11.1.1 This chapter

The present chapter puts forth an optimization method for vertical FL, which has three main components:

1.  **1.**  A *general optimization formulation* for vertical FL that consists of a global model and one local embedding model for each client. The local embedding model can be linear or nonlinear, or even nonsmooth. It maps raw data to compact features and, thus, reduces the number of parameters that need to be communicated to and from the global model.
2.  **2.**  Flexible *federated learning algorithms* that allow intermittent or even strategic client participation, uncoordinated training data selections, and data protection by differential-privacy based methods (for specific loss functions, one can instead apply multiple-party secure computing protocols).
3.  **3.**  *Rigorous convergence analysis* that establishes the performance lower bound and the privacy level.

From an optimization perspective, to the best of our knowledge, our method is the first that lets multiple clients upload their local models using uncoordinated SGD samples. The method also aggregates local model updates in an asynchronous, block-coordinate gradient fashion. We have also numerically validated our vertical FL algorithms and their analyses on federated logistic regression and deep learning. Tests on image and medical datasets demonstrate the competitive performance of our algorithms relative to centralized and synchronous FL algorithms.

### 11.1.2 Related work

Since the seminal work [\[19](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0095),[25\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0125), there has been a large body of studies on FL covering diverse settings; see also a recent survey [\[21\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0105). The most common FL setting is the horizontal setting, where a large set of data are partitioned among clients that share the same feature space [\[20\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0100). To account for the personalization, multi-task FL has been studied in [\[32\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0160) that preserves the specialty of each client while also leveraging the similarity among clients. Horizontal FL with local representation learning has been empirically studied in [\[24\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0120). Communication efficiency has been an important issue in FL. Popular methods aim to: (c1) reduce the number of bits per communication round, including [\[2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0010),[3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0015),[31](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0155),[33](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0165),[34\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0170), to list a few; and (c2) save the number of communication rounds [\[8](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0040),[22](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0110),[38](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0190),[46\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0230).

More recently, feature-partitioned vertical FL has gained popularity in the financial and healthcare applications [\[15](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0075),[18](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0090),[27](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0135),[43\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0215). Unlike the aggregated gradients in the horizontal case, the local gradients in the vertical FL may involve raw data of those features owned by other clients, which raises additional concerns on privacy. Data privacy has been an important topic since decades ago [\[37](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0185),[44\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0220). But early approaches typically require expensive communication and signaling overhead when they are applied to the FL settings. Recently, the notion of differential privacy becomes popular because (i) it is a quantifiable measure of privacy [\[1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0005),[11](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0055),[13\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0065), and (ii) many existing learning algorithms can achieve differential privacy via simple modifications. In the context of learning from multiple clients, it has been studied in [\[5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0025),[14\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0070). But all these approaches are not designed for the vertical FL models and the flexible client update protocols.

As FL is distributed, communication is expensive and can cause delays, so one often applies asynchronous and parallel optimization methods. For the feature-partitioned vertical FL setting in this chapter, it is particularly related to the block coordinate descent (BCD) method [\[29](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0145),[41](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0205),[45\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0225). Asynchronous BCD and its stochastic variant have been developed under the condition of bounded delay in [\[7](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0035),[23](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0115),[28\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0140). The recent advances in this direction aim to establish convergence under weaker assumptions on delays [\[36](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0180),[39\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0195). VAFL uses some proof techniques from [\[36](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0180),[39\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0195) but is also significantly different from them in the following ways:

1.  **(C1)**  VAFL uses a distributed dataset and stochastic gradients. However, [\[36](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0180),[39\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0195) use shared memory and deterministic gradients.
2.  **(C2)**  VAFL has improves data privacy as it lets the workers keep their data but has provable differential privacy guarantees. However, [\[36](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0180),[39\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0195) use a centralized dataset and do not discuss data privacy.
3.  **(C3)**  While [\[36](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0180),[39\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0195) directly require a smooth objective, we use means to guarantee it is and also provides smoothness estimates for neural networks.

VAFL is the first distributed algorithm that provably allows different agents to be uncoordinated and use their own i.i.d. mini-batches, which is an important feature for federated learning.

## 11.2 Vertical federated learning

In this section, we introduce the formulation of vertical FL, and present our private and asynchronous algorithm.

### 11.2.1 Problem statement

Consider a set of *M* clients, ℳ :  = {1, …, *M*}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si1.png). A dataset of *N* samples, {**x**[*n*], *y*[*n*]}[*n* = 1]^(*N*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si2.png), is maintained by *M* local clients, where each client *m* maintains *x*[*n*, *m*] ∈ ℝ^(*p*[*m*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si3.png) for *n* = 1, …, *N*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si4.png). Vector *x*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si5.png) is also the *m*th block of sample vector **x**[*n*] :  = \[*x*[*n*, 1]^⊤, …, *x*[*n*, *M*]^⊤\]^⊤![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si6.png) at client *m*. Suppose the *n*th label *y*[*n*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si7.png) is stored at the server.

To preserve the privacy of data, the client data *x*[*n*, *m*] ∈ ℝ^(*p*[*m*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si3.png) are not shared with other clients as well as the server. Instead, each client *m* learns a local (linear or nonlinear, possibly nonsmooth) embedding *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) parameterized by *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png) that maps the high-dimensional vector *x*[*n*, *m*] ∈ ℝ^(*p*[*m*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si3.png) to a low-dimensional one $h\_{n,m}: = h\_{m}(\\theta\_{m};x\_{n,m}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^{\\underset{\\\_}{p\_{m}}}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si10.png) with $\\underset{\\\_}{p\_{m}} \\ll p\_{m}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si11.png). Ideally, the clients and the server want to collaboratively solve the following problem: 

$F(\\theta\_{0},\\mathbf{\\theta}): = \\frac{1}{N}\\sum\\limits\_{n = 1}^{N}\\ell\\left( \\theta\_{0},h\_{n,1},\\ldots,h\_{n,M};y\_{n} \\right) + \\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}r(\\theta\_{m}),\\text{with}\\quad h\_{n,m}: = h\_{m}(\\theta\_{m};x\_{n,m}),\\quad m = 1,\\ldots,M,$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si12.png)(11.1) 

where *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png) is the global model parameter kept at and learned by the server, and **θ** :  = \[*θ*[1]^⊤, …, *θ*[*M*]^⊤\]^⊤![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si14.png) concatenates the local models kept at and learned by local clients, *ℓ* is the loss capturing the accuracy of the global model parameters *θ*[0], *θ*[1], …, *θ*[*M*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si15.png), and *r* is the per-client regularizer that confines the complexity of or encodes the prior knowledge about the local model parameters.

For problem [(11.1)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq1), the local information of client *m* is fully captured in the embedding vector *h*[*n*, *m*], ∀*n* = 1, …, *N*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si16.png). Hence, the quantities that will be exchanged between server and clients are {*h*[*n*, *m*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si17.png) and the gradients of ℓ(*θ*[0], *h*[*n*, 1], …, *h*[*n*, *M*]; *y*[*n*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si18.png) with respect to (w.r.t.) {*h*[*n*, *m*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si17.png). See a diagram for VAFL implementation in [Fig. 11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0020). A standard optimization method to solve [(11.1)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq1) is the (synchronous) block-wise stochastic gradient method [\[42\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0210). Specifically, at iteration *k*, the server performs

$\\theta\_{0}^{k + 1} = \\theta\_{0}^{k}\\ - \\ \\frac{\\eta\_{0}^{k}}{N\_{k}}\\sum\\limits\_{n \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{k}}\\nabla\_{\\theta\_{0}}\\ell\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},h\_{n,1}^{k},\\ldots,h\_{n,M}^{k};y\_{n} \\right),$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si19.png)(11.2) 

where *h*[*n*, *m*]^(*k*) :  = *h*[*m*](*θ*[*m*]^(*k*); *x*[*n*, *m*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si20.png), 𝒩[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si21.png) is a mini-batch randomly selected at iteration *k* with the sample size *N*[*k*] = |𝒩[*k*]|![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si22.png), and *η*[0]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si23.png) is the stepsize at iteration *k*. With the *same* mini-batch of data 𝒩[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si21.png), the model update at each local client *m* is

$\\theta\_{m}^{k + 1} = \\theta\_{m}^{k}\\ - \\ \\frac{\\eta\_{m}^{k}}{N\_{k}}\\sum\\limits\_{n \\in \\mathcal{N}\_{k}}\\nabla\_{\\theta\_{m}}h\_{n,m}^{k}\\nabla\_{h\_{n,m}}\\ell\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},h\_{n,1}^{k},\\ldots,h\_{n,M}^{k};y\_{n} \\right) - \\eta\_{m}^{k}\\nabla r\\left( \\theta\_{m}^{k} \\right),$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si24.png)(11.3) 

where *η*[*m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si25.png) is the step size at iteration *k*. When *r* is nonsmooth and a proximal mapping, we can replace  − *η*[*m*]^(*k*)∇*r*(*θ*[*m*]^(*k*))![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si26.png) by an extra proximal step. Implementing updates [(11.2)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq2) and [(11.3)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq3) requires all the clients to use the same mini-batch of data to update their local model simultaneously. In FL, however, clients (e.g., devices) participate in the learning process only when they are available (plugged in, waked up, and/or connected with unmetered WiFi) and thus it is difficult to obtain the up-to-date information of all clients at any time. Moreover, the local embedding vectors and the local gradients exchanged between server and clients still have risk of privacy leakage.

![Figure 11.1 A diagram for VAFL implementation.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr003.jpg)

[Figure 11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cf0070) A diagram for VAFL implementation.

### 11.2.2 Asynchronous client updates

For FL, we consider solving [(11.1)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq1) without coordination among clients. Asynchronous optimization methods have been used to solve such problems. However, state-of-the-art methods cannot guarantee (i) the convergence when the mapping *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) is nonlinear (thus the loss is nonsmooth), and (ii) the privacy of the update which is at the epicenter of the FL paradigm. On a high level, we describe our vertical asynchronous federated learning (VAFL) algorithm as follows. During the learning process, from the server side, it waits until receiving a message from an active client *m*, which is either (i) **a query** of the loss function's gradient w.r.t. to the embedding vector *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png); or (ii) **a new embedding vector** *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) calculated using the updated local model parameter *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png).

To response to the query (i), the server calculates the gradient for client *m* using its current {*h*[*n*, *m*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si17.png), and sends it to the client; and, upon receiving (ii), the server computes the new gradient w.r.t. *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png) using the embedding vectors it currently has from other clients and updates its model *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png). For each interaction with server, each *active* client *m* randomly selects a datum *x*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si5.png), queries the corresponding gradient w.r.t. *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) from server, and then it securely uploads the updated embedding vector *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png), and then updates the local model *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png). The mechanism that ensures secure uploading will be described in Section [11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#s0060). Without introducing cumbersome iteration, client, and sample indexes, we summarize the asynchronous client updates in [Algorithm 1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0010).

![Algorithm 1 Vertical asynchronous federated learning.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr001.jpg)

Algorithm 1 Vertical asynchronous federated learning.

Specifically, since clients update the model without external coordination, we thereafter use *k* to denote the global counter (or iteration), which increases by one whenever i) the server receives the new embedding vector *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) from a client, calculates the gradient, and updates the server model *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png); and ii) the corresponding client *m* obtains the gradient w.r.t. *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png), and updates the local model *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png). Accordingly, we let *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si28.png) denote the client index that uploads at iteration *k*, and *n*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si29.png) denote the sample index used at iteration *k*.

For notation brevity, we use a single datum *n*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si29.png) for each uncoordinated update in the subsequent algorithms, but the algorithm and its analysis can be easily generalized to a mini-batch of data 𝒩[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si21.png). Let *ĝ*[0]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si30.png) denote the stochastic gradients of the loss at *n*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si29.png)th sample w.r.t. server model *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png) as

*ĝ*[0]^(*k*) = ∇[*θ*[0]]ℓ(*θ*[0]^(*k*),*h*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k*)),…,*h*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k*));*y*[*n*[*k*]])

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si31.png)(11.4a) 

and the gradients w.r.t. the local model *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png) as

*ĝ*[*m*]^(*k*) = ∇[*θ*[*m*]]ℓ(*θ*[0]^(*k*),*h*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k*)),…,*h*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k*));*y*[*n*[*k*]]) = ∇[*θ*[*m*]]*h*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)∇[*h*[*n*[*k*], *m*]]ℓ(*θ*[0]^(*k*),*h*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k*)),…,*h*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k*));*y*[*n*[*k*]]).

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si32.png)(11.4b) 

The delay for client *m* and sample *n* will increase via

$\\tau\_{n,m}^{k + 1} = \\begin{cases} {1,} & {m = m\_{k},\\ n = n\_{k},} \\\\ {\\tau\_{n,m}^{k} + 1,} & {\\text{otherwise}.} \\\\ \\end{cases}$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si33.png)(11.5) 

With the above short-hand notation, at iteration *k*, the **server-side** update is

*θ*[0]^(*k* + 1) = *θ*[0]^(*k*) − *η*[0]^(*k*)*ĝ*[0]^(*k*).

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si34.png)(11.6) 

For the **active local client** *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si28.png) at iteration *k*, its update is

*θ*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k* + 1) = *θ*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k*) − *η*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k*)*ĝ*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k*) − *η*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k*)∇*r*(*θ*[*m*[*k*]]^(*k*)),

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si35.png)(11.7a) 

and for the **other clients** *m* ≠ *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si36.png), the update is

*θ*[*m*]^(*k* + 1) = *θ*[*m*]^(*k*),

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si37.png)(11.7b) 

where *η*[*m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si25.png) is the step size and *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si28.png) is the index of the client for the *k*th update.

### 11.2.3 Types of flexible update rules

As shown in ([11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq4)), the stochastic gradients are evaluated using delayed local embedding information *h*[*m*]^(*k* − *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*))![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si38.png) from each client *m*, where *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si39.png) is caused by both asynchronous communication and stochastic sampling. Unexpected delays can cause the divergence of the algorithm. To ensure convergence, we consider several flexible update protocols:

1.  **1.**  *Uniformly bounded delay*. During the training process, whenever the delay of *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si39.png) exceeds *D* ( > 0)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si40.png), the server must query fresh *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) from client *m* before continuing the server update process.
2.  **2.**  *Stochastic unbounded delay.* In this case, the activation of each client is a stochastic process. The delays is determined by the hitting times of the stochastic processes. For example, if the activation of all the clients follows independent Poisson processes, the delays will be geometrically distributed.
3.  **3.**  *t-synchronous update,* *t* > 0![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si41.png)*.* While fully asynchronous update is most flexible, *t*\-synchronous update is also commonly adopted. In this case, the server computes the gradient w.r.t. *θ*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si13.png) until receiving {*h*[*n*, *m*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si17.png) from *t* different clients, and then updates the server's model using the newly computed gradient. The *t*\-synchronous updates have more stable performance empirically, which is listed in [Algorithm 2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0015).

![Algorithm 2 Vertical t-synchronous federated learning.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr002.jpg)

Algorithm 2 Vertical *t*\-synchronous federated learning.

1.  

In this chapter, we do not consider dishonest and malicious clients and server, but it is possible to incorporate robust learning techniques into our vertical FL algorithms based on recent works [\[4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0020),[10\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0050).

## 11.3 Convergence analysis

We present the convergence results of our vertical asynchronous federated learning (VAFL) method for the nonconvex and strongly convex cases, and under different update rules. Due to space limitation, this section mainly presents the convergence rates for fully asynchronous version of VAFL ([Algorithm 1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0010)). The proofs and the convergence results for *t*\-synchronous one ([Algorithm 2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0015)) can be also found in the online version [\[9\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0045).

To analyze the performance of [Algorithm 1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0010), we first make the following assumptions on sampling and smoothness. 

Assumption 11.1

*Sample indexes* {*n*[*k*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si42.png) *are i.i.d. from* {1, …, *N*}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si43.png) *and* ℙ(*n*[*k*] = *n*) = 1/*N*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si44.png)*. And the variance of gradient follows*

𝔼\[∥*g*[*m*]^(*k*)−∇[*θ*[*m*]]*F*(*θ*[0]^(*k*),**θ**^(*k*))∥²\] ≤ *σ*[*m*]², *m* = 0, …, *M*,

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si45.png)(11.8) 

*where* *g*[*m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si46.png) *is the stochastic gradient* *ĝ*[*m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si47.png) *without delay, e.g.,*

*g*[*m*]^(*k*) = ∇[*θ*[*m*]]ℓ(*θ*[0]^(*k*),*h*[*n*[*k*], 1]^(*k*),…,*h*[*n*[*k*], *M*]^(*k*);*y*[*n*[*k*]]).

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si48.png)

Assumption 11.2

*The optimal loss is lower bounded,* *F*^(\*) >  − ∞![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si49.png)*. The gradient* ∇*F is L-Lipschitz continuous, and* ∇[*θ*[*m*]]*F*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si50.png) *is* *L*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si51.png)*\-Lipschitz continuous.*

[Assumption 11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0010) is common in analyzing SGD [\[6\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0030). Generally, [Assumption 11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0015) cannot be satisfied under our general vertical FL formulation with *nonsmooth* local embedding functions such as neural networks. However, techniques will be introduced to enforce smoothness in Section [11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#s0060). To handle asynchrony, we need the following standard assumption in the analysis of asynchronous BCD.

Assumption 11.3

*The uploading client index* *m*[*k*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si28.png) *is random, independent of* *m*[0], …, *m*[*k* − 1]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si53.png)*, and satisfies*

ℙ(*m*[*k*] = *m*) = *q*[*m*] > 0.

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si54.png)(11.9) 

A simple scenario satisfying this assumptions is that the activation of all clients follows independent Poisson processes. That is, if the time difference between two consecutive activations of client *m* follows an exponential distribution with parameter *λ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si55.png), then the activation of client *m* is a Poisson process with $q\_{m} = \\lambda\_{m}^{- 1}/\\sum\_{j = 1}^{M}\\lambda\_{j}^{- 1}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si56.png). We first present the convergence results for bounded *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si39.png).

### 11.3.1 Convergence under bounded delay

We make the following assumption *only* for this subsection.

Assumption 11.4

Uniformly bounded delay

*For each client m and each sample n, the delay* *τ*[*n*, *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si57.png) *at iteration k is bounded by a constant D, i.e.,* *τ*[*n*, *m*]^(*k*) ≤ *D*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si58.png)*.*

To handle the delayed information, we leverage the following Lyapunov function for analyzing VAFL:

$V^{k} = F\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{k} \\right)\\ + \\ \\sum\\limits\_{d = 1}^{D}\\gamma\_{d}\\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{k - d + 1}\\ - \\ \\mathbf{\\theta}^{k - d} \\right\\|^{2},$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si59.png)(11.10) 

where {*γ*[*d*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si60.png) are a set of constants to be determined later. 

Lemma 11.1

*Under* Assumptions [11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0010)–[11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0025)*, for* $\\eta\_{0}^{k} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{4L}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si61.png)*,* $\\eta\_{m}^{k} \\leqslant \\frac{1}{4(L + 2\\gamma\_{1})}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si62.png)*, it follows that (with* *γ*[*D* + 1] = 0![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si63.png)*)*

$\\mathbb{E}V^{k + 1} - \\mathbb{E}V^{k}\\quad \\leqslant - \\left( \\frac{\\eta\_{0}^{k}}{2} - L{(\\eta\_{0}^{k})}^{2} \\right)\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\left\\| \\nabla\_{\\theta\_{0}}F\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{k} \\right) \\right\\|^{2} \\right\\rbrack\\qquad - \\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}q\_{m}\\left( \\frac{\\eta\_{m}^{k}}{2} - L{(\\eta\_{m}^{k})}^{2} - 2\\gamma\_{1}{(\\eta\_{m}^{k})}^{2} \\right)\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\left\\| \\nabla\_{\\theta\_{m}}F\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{k} \\right) \\right\\|^{2} \\right\\rbrack\\qquad + \\sum\\limits\_{d = 1}^{D}\\left( Dc^{k} + D\\gamma\_{1}\\max\\limits\_{m}2\\left( \\eta\_{m}^{k} \\right)^{2}L\_{m}^{2} + \\gamma\_{d + 1} - \\gamma\_{d} \\right)\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\left\\| \\mathbf{\\theta}^{k + 1 - d} - \\mathbf{\\theta}^{k - d} \\right\\|^{2} \\right\\rbrack\\qquad + L\\left( \\eta\_{0}^{k} \\right)^{2}\\sigma\_{0}^{2}\\ + \\ \\sum\\limits\_{m = 1}^{M}q\_{m}\\left( L + 2\\gamma\_{1} \\right)\\left( \\eta\_{m}^{k} \\right)^{2}\\sigma\_{m}^{2}.$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si64.png)(11.11) 

If {*γ*[*d*]}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si60.png) are chosen properly as specified in the supplementary materials, the first three terms on the right-hand side of [(11.11)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq15) are negative. By carefully choosing {*η*[0]^(*k*), *η*[*m*]^(*k*)}![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si65.png), we can ensure the convergence of [Algorithm 1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0010). We first present the convergence for the nonconvex case.

Theorem 11.1

*Under the assumptions of* [Lemma 11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0030)*, if* $\\eta\_{0}^{k} = \\eta\_{m}^{k} = \\min\\{\\frac{1}{4(1 + D)L},\\frac{c\_{\\eta}}{\\sqrt{K}}\\}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si66.png) *with* *c*[*η*] > 0![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si67.png)*, we have*

$\\frac{1}{K}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack {\\|\\nabla F\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{k} \\right)\\|}^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathcal{O}\\left( 1/\\sqrt{K} \\right).$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si68.png)(11.12) 

Under the additional strong convexity, the convergence rate is improved.

Theorem 11.2

*Assume F is μ-strongly convex. Under the same assumptions of* [Lemma 11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0030)*, if* $\\eta^{k} = \\frac{4}{\\mu\\min\\limits\_{m}\\sqrt{q\_{m}}(k + K\_{0})}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si69.png) *with* $K\_{0} = \\frac{4(4(D + 1)L + \\mu\\min\\limits\_{m}\\sqrt{q\_{m}}D)}{\\mu\\min\\limits\_{m}\\sqrt{q\_{m}}}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si70.png)*, then*

𝔼*F*(*θ*[0]^(*K*),**θ**^(*K*)) − *F*^(\*) = 𝒪(1/*K*).

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si71.png)(11.13) 

It is worth mentioning that, under the assumption of bounded delay, without even coordinating clients' gradient samples and local model updates, our algorithm achieves the same order of convergence as that of block-wise SGD in both nonconvex and strongly convex cases [\[42\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0210). In addition, the convergence rate in Theorems [11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0035) and [11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0040) depends on the number of workers *M* through the maximum delay *D*, which is typically *D* = 𝒪(*M*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si72.png). Specifically, the condition on step sizes in Theorem [11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0035) depends on *D*, and the condition on step sizes in Theorem [11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0040) depends on *D* through *K*[0]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si73.png). Therefore, step sizes need to decrease as *D* increases, otherwise the error will increase as *D* increases.

### 11.3.2 Convergence under stochastic unbounded delay

We next present the convergence results for the case where *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si39.png) is unbounded but stochastic. We make the following assumption *only* for this subsection.

Assumption 11.5

Stochastic unbounded delay

*For each client m, delay* *τ*[*n*[*k*], *m*]^(*k*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si39.png) *is a random variable with unbounded support. There exists* ${\\overline{p}}\_{m},\\rho > 0$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si75.png) *such that*

$\\mathbb{P}\\left( \\tau\_{n\_{k},m}^{k} = d \\right) \\leqslant {\\overline{p}}\_{m}\\rho^{d}.$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si76.png)(11.14) 

Under [Assumption 11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0045), we obtain the convergence rates of the same order as those the under bounded delay.

Theorem 11.3

*Under* Assumptions [11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0010)–[11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0020) and [11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0045)*, if* $\\eta\_{0}^{k} = \\eta\_{m}^{k} = \\min\\left\\{ \\frac{1}{4(1 + \\min\_{m}\\sqrt{c\_{m}})L},\\frac{c\_{\\eta}}{\\sqrt{K}} \\right\\}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si77.png)*, we have*

$\\frac{1}{K}\\sum\\limits\_{k = 0}^{K - 1}\\mathbb{E}\\left\\lbrack \\left\\| \\nabla F\\left( \\theta\_{0}^{k},\\mathbf{\\theta}^{k} \\right) \\right\\|^{2} \\right\\rbrack = \\mathcal{O}\\left( 1/\\sqrt{K} \\right).$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si78.png)(11.15) 

Additionally, assuming strong convexity, the convergence rate is improved.

Theorem 11.4

*Assume that F is μ-strongly convex in* (*θ*[0], **θ**)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si79.png)*. Then under* Assumptions [11.1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0010)–[11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0020) and [11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0045)*, if* $\\eta\_{0}^{k} = \\eta\_{m}^{k} = \\frac{2}{\\nu(k + K\_{0})}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si80.png) *where* $K\_{0} = \\frac{4(1 + \\max\_{m}\\sqrt{c\_{m}})L}{\\nu}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si81.png) *and ν is a positive constant depending on μ, L,* ${\\overline{p}}\_{m}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si82.png)*, ρ, then it follows that*

𝔼*F*(*θ*[0]^(*K*),**θ**^(*K*)) − *F*^(\*) = 𝒪(1/*K*).

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si83.png)(11.16) 

## 11.4 Perturbed local embedding for smoothness

In this section, we introduce a local perturbation technique that is applied by each client to smooth the otherwise non-smooth mapping of local embedding so the convergence analysis in Section [11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#s0045) can be applied.

### 11.4.1 Local perturbation

Recall that *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) denotes a local embedding function of client *m* with the parameter *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png) which embeds the information of local data *x*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si5.png) into its outputs *h*[*n*, *m*] :  = *h*[*m*](*θ*[*m*]; *x*[*n*, *m*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si84.png). When *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) is linear embedding, it is as simple as *h*[*m*](*θ*[*m*]; *x*[*n*, *m*]) = *x*[*n*, *m*]^⊤*θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si85.png). To further account for nonlinear embedding such as neural networks, we represent *h*[*n*, *m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si27.png) in the following form:

*u*[0] = *x*[*n*, *m*],

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si86.png)(11.17a) 

*u*[*l*] = *σ*[*l*](*w*[*l*]*u*[*l* − 1] + *b*[*l*]),   *l* = 1, …, *L*,

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si87.png)(11.17b) 

*h*[*n*, *m*] = *u*[*L*],

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si88.png)(11.17c) 

 where *σ*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si89.png) is a linear or nonlinear function, and *w*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si120.png), *b*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si119.png) corresponds to the parameter *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png) of *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png), e.g., *θ*[*m*] :  = \[*w*[1], …, *w*[*L*], *b*[1], …, *b*[*L*]\]^⊤![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si92.png). Here we assume that *σ*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si89.png) is *L*[*σ*[*l*]]⁰![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si93.png)\-Lipschitz continuous. Specially, when *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) is linear, the composite embedding ([11.17](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq21)) corresponds to *L* = 1![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si94.png), *σ*[1](*z*) = *z*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si95.png).

We perturb the local embedding function *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) by adding a random neuron with output *Z*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si96.png) at each layer *l* (cf. [(11.17b)](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq22))

*u*[*l*] = *σ*[*l*](*w*[*l*]*u*[*l* − 1] + *b*[*l*] + *Z*[*l*]),   *l* = 1, …, *L*,

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si97.png)(11.18) 

where *Z*[1], …, *Z*[*L*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si98.png) are independent random variables. With properly chosen distributions of *Z*[*l*], *l* = 1, …, *L*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si99.png), we show below *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png) is smooth and enables differential privacy. While it does not exclude other options, our choice of the perturbation distributions is

*Z*[*L*] ∼ 𝒩(0,*c*²),

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si100.png)(11.19a) 

$Z\_{l} \\sim \\mathcal{U}\\lbrack - \\sqrt{3}c\_{l},\\sqrt{3}c\_{l}\\rbrack,\\ \\ \\ l = 1,\\ldots,L - 1,$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si101.png)(11.19b) 

where 𝒩(0,*c*²)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si102.png) denotes the Gaussian distribution with zero mean and variance *c*²![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si103.png), and $\\mathcal{U}\\lbrack - \\sqrt{3}c\_{l},\\sqrt{3}c\_{l}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si104.png) denotes the uniform distribution over $\\lbrack - \\sqrt{3}c\_{l},\\sqrt{3}c\_{l}\\rbrack$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si105.png).

### 11.4.2 Enforcing smoothness

We now connect the perturbed local embedding technique with the convergence theories in Section [11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#s0045).

The convergence results in Section [11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#s0045) hold under [Assumption 11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0015) which requires the smoothness of the overall loss function. Inspired by the randomized smoothing technique [\[12](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0060),[26\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0130), we are able to smooth the objective function by taking expectation with respect to the random neurons. Intuitively this follows the fact that the smoothness of a function can be increased by convolving with proper distributions. By adding random neuron *Z*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si96.png), the landscape of *σ*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si89.png) will be smoothed in expectation with respect to *Z*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si96.png). And by induction, we can show the smoothness of local embedding vector *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png). Then so long as the loss function *ℓ* is smooth w.r.t. the local embedding vector *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png), the global objective *F* is smooth by taking expectation with respect to all the random neurons.

We formally establish this result in the following theorem.

Theorem 11.5

*For each embedding function* *h*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si106.png)*, if the activation functions follow* *σ*[*l*] = *σ*, ∀*l*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si107.png)*, and the variances of the random neurons follow* ([11.19](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#deq25))*, and we assume* ∥*w*[*l*]∥![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si108.png) *is bounded, then with* **Z** = \[*Z*[1]^⊤, …, *Z*[*L*]^⊤\]^⊤![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si109.png)*, the perturbed loss satisfies* [Assumption 11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0015)*, given by*

*F*[*c*](*θ*[0],**θ**) = 𝔼[**Z**]\[*F*(*θ*[0],**θ**;**Z**)\].

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si110.png)(11.20) 

*Starting from* *L*[*b*[*L*]]^(*h*) = *L*[*σ*]⁰*d*/*c*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si111.png)*, the smoothness constants of the local model* *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png) *denoted as* *L*[*θ*[*m*]]^(*F*[*c*])![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si113.png) *satisfy the following recursion* (*l* = 1, …, *L* − 1)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si114.png)*:*

$\\left. L\_{b\_{l}}^{h} = L\_{b\_{l + 1}}^{h} \\right\\|\\left. w\_{l + 1} \\right\\|\\left. \\left( L\_{\\sigma}^{0} \\right)^{2}\\ + \\ L\_{\\sigma}^{0} \\right\\|\\left. w\_{L} \\right\\|\\left. \\cdots L\_{\\sigma}^{0} \\right\\|\\left. w\_{l + 1} \\right\\| L\_{\\overline{\\sigma}}(c\_{l}),L\_{w\_{l}}^{h} = \\mathbb{E}{{\\lbrack\\|}\\left. u\_{l - 1} \\right\\|\\rbrack}L\_{b\_{l}}^{h},L\_{\\theta\_{m}}^{F\_{c}} = L\_{h\_{m}}^{\\ell}\\left( L\_{h\_{m}}^{0} \\right)^{2}\\ + \\ L\_{\\ell}^{0}\\sum\\limits\_{l = 1}^{L}\\left( L\_{w\_{l}}^{h} + L\_{b\_{l}}^{h} \\right)\\ + \\ L\_{\\theta\_{m}}^{r},$

![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si115.png)(11.21) 

*where* *L*[*θ*[*m*]]^(*r*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si116.png) *is the smoothness constant of the regularizer w.r.t.* *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png)*;* *L*[*b*[*l*]]^(*h*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si117.png) *and* *L*[*w*[*l*]]^(*h*)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si118.png) *are the smoothness constants of the perturbed local embedding h w.r.t. the bias* *b*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si119.png) *and weight* *w*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si120.png)*; and* $L\_{\\overline{\\sigma}}(c\_{l}) = 2\\sqrt{d}L\_{\\sigma}^{0}/c\_{l}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si121.png) *is the smoothness constant of the neuron at the lth layer under the uniform perturbation.*

[Theorem 11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#enun0060) implies that the perturbed loss is smooth w.r.t. the local model *θ*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si112.png), and a large perturbation (large *c*[*l*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si122.png) or *c*) leads to a smaller smoothness constant.

## 11.5 Numerical tests

To evaluate the performance of our proposed VAFL method, numerical tests have been conducted on both federated logistic regression and neural network models on multiple datasets. We benchmark the fully asynchronous version of VAFL (**async**) in [Algorithm 1](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0010), and *t*\-synchronous version of VAFL (**t-sync**) in [Algorithm 2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0015) with the synchronous block-wise SGD (**sync**), which requires synchronization and sample index coordination among clients in each iteration. To simulate the client asynchrony, we use multiple threads as local clients and add random delay to each client.

### 11.5.1 VAFL for federated logistic regression

**Data allocation.** The datasets we choose are CIFAR-10, Parkinson Disease, MNIST, and Fashion MNIST. The batch size is selected to be approximate 0.01 fraction of the entire training dataset. The data are uniformly distributed among *M* = 8![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si123.png) clients for CIFAR-10, *M* = 3![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si124.png) for Parkinson Disease, and *M* = 7![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si125.png) for both MNIST and Fashion MNIST.

The step size is *η* = 1 × 10^( − 2)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si126.png) for Parkinson Disease, *η* = 2 × 10^( − 4)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si127.png) for CIFAR-10, and *η* = 1 × 10^( − 4)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si128.png) for both MNIST and Fashion MNIST.

**Parameters.** The random delay follows a Poisson distribution with client-specific parameters to reflect heterogeneity. The delay on each worker *m* follows the Poisson distribution with parameter 2*m* and scaled by 1/2*M*![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si129.png), where *M* is the number of workers and *m* is the worker index. The expectation of maximum worker delay is one second.

The noise added to the output of each local client follows the Gaussian distribution of each task is 𝒩(0, 0.01)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si130.png) for CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion MNIST, and 𝒩(0, 1)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si131.png) for Parkinson Disease. For each task, we run the algorithms sufficiently many epochs and record the training loss. Testing accuracy and clock time are recorded at the end of epoch.

We first conduct logistic regression on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and Parkinson disease [\[30\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0150) datasets. The *l*[2]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si132.png)\-regularizer coefficient is set as 0.001. We select *M* = 7![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si125.png) for MNIST and MNIST, *M* = 8![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si123.png) for CIFAR10, and *M* = 3![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si124.png) for PD dataset. The training loss and testing accuracy versus wall-clock time are reported in Figs. [11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0025) and [11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0030). The dashed horizontal lines represent the results trained on the centralized (non-federated) model, and the dashed curves represent private variants of considered algorithms with variance *c* = 0.1![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si133.png). In all cases, the VAFL algorithms learn a federated model with accuracies comparable to that of the centralized model that requires collecting all raw data. And async and *t*\-sync VAFL algorithms have a 2× speed-up in most cases.

![Figure 11.2 Training loss and testing accuracy versus clock time (s) in MNIST (left two) and Fashion-MNIST (right two) datasets.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr004.jpg)

[Figure 11.2](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cs0125_1) Training loss and testing accuracy versus clock time (s) in MNIST (left two) and Fashion-MNIST (right two) datasets.

![Figure 11.3 Training loss and testing accuracy versus clock time (s) in CIFAR10 (left two) and Parkinson disease (right two) datasets.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 11.3](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cs0125_2) Training loss and testing accuracy versus clock time (s) in CIFAR10 (left two) and Parkinson disease (right two) datasets.

### 11.5.2 VAFL for federated deep learning

#### 11.5.2.1 Training on ModelNet40 dataset

We train a convolutional neural network-based model consisting of two parts: the local embedding models and the server model. Each local model is a 7-layer convolutional neural network. The server part is a centralized 3-layer fully connect neural network. The data we chose is ModelNet40, and we vertically distributed images of the objects in the dataset from 12 angles and assigned to each local client. Each client deals with the data assigned by its local convolutional network and generates a vector whose dimension is 512 as local output.

**Parameters.** The random delay follows an exponential distribution with client-specific parameters to reflect heterogeneity. For each worker *m*, the delay follows the exponential distribution with parameter *m*. We use ReLU as the local embedding activation function. We add a random noise on the output of each local embedding convolutional layer. The noises follow the following distributions: 𝒰( − 0.1, 0.1)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si134.png) (the first two layers), 𝒰( − 0.01, 0.01)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si135.png) (the other convolutional layers except for the last layer), and 𝒩(0, 1)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si131.png) (the last convolutional layer). The server then combines the 12 vectors and passes them into the three-layer fully connected neural network and classify into 40 classes. The number of nodes of each layer is 256, 100, and 40. The step size of the local update *η*[*m*]![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si136.png) is 10^( − 3)![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si137.png) and the server step size $\\eta\_{0} = \\frac{\\eta\_{m}}{M}$![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si138.png) where *M* is the number of workers.

We first train a neural network modified from MVCNN with 12-view data [\[40\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0200). We use *M* = 4![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si139.png) clients, and each client has 3 views of each object and uses a 7-layer CNN as local embedding functions, and the server uses a fully connected network to aggregate the local embedding vectors. Results are plotted in Figs. [11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0035) and [11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0040). The centralized model in this multi-view learning case coincides with sync, and is omitted. Again async and *t*\-sync have sizable speed-up relative to sync, and private async (with *c* = 1![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si140.png)) does not sacrifice much in accuracy.

![Figure 11.4 Training loss of VAFL with nonlinear local embedding on ModelNet40 dataset.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr006.jpg)

[Figure 11.4](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cs0130_1) Training loss of VAFL with nonlinear local embedding on *ModelNet40* dataset.

![Figure 11.5 Testing accuracy of VAFL with local embedding on ModelNet40 dataset.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr007.jpg)

[Figure 11.5](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cs0130_2) Testing accuracy of VAFL with local embedding on *ModelNet40* dataset.

#### 11.5.2.2 Training on MIMIC-III dataset

We further test our VAFL algorithm on MIMIC-III—an open dataset comprising de-identified health data [\[17\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0085). The data are allocated to 4 workers having different feature dimensions. The local embedding part is a two-layer LSTM model and the server part is a fully connected layer. The first layer is a bidirectional LSTM, and the number of units is 16. The second layer is a normal LSTM layer, and the number of units is also 16. The random delay follows an exponential distribution with client-specific parameters to reflect heterogeneity. A random noise following Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0, 10^( − 4))![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si141.png) is also added to the output of each local embedding layer. We perform the in-hospital mortality prediction as in [\[16\]](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#br0080) among *M* = 4![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si139.png) clients. Each client uses LSTM as the embedding function. In Figs. [11.6](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0045) and [11.7](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0050), we can still observe that async and *t*\-sync VAFL learn a federated model with accuracy comparable to that of the centralized model, and require less time relative to the synchronous FL algorithm. We conduct an ablation study to demonstrate how the convergence rate is affected by different number of clients. Since in the vertical FL scenarios, clients are financial institutions and healthcare companies, the number of which is usually not large, in Figs. [11.8](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0055) and [11.9](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#f0060), we report the training loss and the test AUC of VAFL for the number of clients *M* = 6, 8, 10![Image](images/B978044319037700020X/si142.png). From these two figures, we can observe that when the number of clients increases, the actual runtime needed to achieve given training loss and test AUC does not decrease. This is because adding more clients in vertical FL does not increase the batch size or reduce the effective variance, and, in contrast, it introduces additional asynchrony that may even impede the learning process. This is different from the *linear speedup* in the horizontal FL setting.

![Figure 11.6 Training loss of VAFL with local LSTM embedding on MIMIC-III dataset.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr008.jpg)

![Figure 11.7 AUC curve of VAFL with local LSTM embedding on MIMIC-III dataset.](images/B978044319037700020X/gr009.jpg)

[Figure 11.7](#Chp011_199-217_B978044319037700020X.xhtml#cs0135_2) AUC curve of VAFL with local LSTM embedding on *MIMIC-III* dataset.
