## 14.1 Introduction

Classic federated learning (FL) is designed for supervised learning, i.e., multiple agents/clients collaborate to train a supervised learning model such as a neural network (NN) [\[54\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0270) or a decision tree-based model [\[44](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0220),[45\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0225). However, in addition to supervised learning, many other machine learning methods which are *sequential decision-making* problems in nature, such as the celebrated methods of *Bayesian optimization* (BO) [\[28\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0140) and *reinforcement learning* (RL) [\[71\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0355), also find important applications in the federated setting. For example, BO has been the most popular method for tuning the hyperparameters of ML models, and hence hyperparameter tuning of ML models in the federated setting naturally calls for algorithms for *federated BO* (FBO); RL has been widely adopted for clinical decision support, and therefore collaborative clinical treatment recommendation among multiple hospitals is a natural and important application for *federated RL* (FRL). Therefore, extending these classic sequential decision-making algorithms (such as BO and RL) into the federated setting holds considerable promise for more widespread applications of FL.

However, the extension of these classic algorithms into the federated setting is non-trivial and faced with significant challenges. First of all, these classic sequential decision-making algorithms need to be modified to satisfy the core principles of FL. As a prime example, an important principle in FL is that the raw data of an agent can never be transmitted [\[35\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0175). Similarly, during federated sequential decision-making, the raw data of an agent, such as the history of observations in BO and the raw trajectories in RL, must also be retained by the agent and hence never shared with others. This requirement, as well as other requirements stemming from the core principles of FL, may necessitate non-trivial problem-dependent algorithmic designs. Moreover, when modifying these sequential decision-making algorithms for the federated setting, it is challenging to preserve their rigorous theoretical guarantees (e.g., the sub-linear regret upper bound of classic BO algorithms and the sample complexity of classic policy gradient algorithms for RL) and at the same time consistently improve their empirical performances by exploiting the federation of multiple agents. In recent years, a number of works have tackled these challenges and hence introduced federated versions of classic sequential decision-making algorithms, such as FBO [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) and FRL [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) algorithms.

The works of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) and [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) have proposed FBO algorithms. The work of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has introduced the first FBO algorithm, named *federated Thompson sampling* (FTS), which addressed several important challenges in FBO. Specifically, the FTS algorithm is free from the requirement to transmit the observations of BO, requires a small number of parameters to be exchanged, and is theoretically guaranteed to be no-regret despite agent heterogeneity [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075). The more recent work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has extended the FTS algorithm of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) to incorporate a rigorous privacy guarantee and to further improve its practical performance via the method of distributed exploration. Regarding FRL, the recent work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has introduced the first FRL framework with a theoretically guaranteed convergence. Specifically, building on the classic policy gradient algorithm, [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) only requires the agents to exchange their policy gradients instead of their raw trajectories and has achieved low sample complexity by leveraging variance-reduced optimization techniques. Moreover, [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has also achieved theoretically guaranteed robustness against Byzantine agents (i.e., caused by random failures or adversarial attacks), which is another important consideration in FL. These recent works on FBO [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) and FRL [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) have been shown to be both theoretically grounded and practically effective, and we will discuss them in more detail in Sections [14.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0015) and [14.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0045), respectively. In addition to FBO and FRL, another line of recent works has extended *multi-armed bandits* [\[40\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0200), which is another classic sequential decision-making problem, to the federated setting and hence introduced federated bandits [\[16](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0080),[22](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0110),[66\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0330). These recent works on federated bandits mostly focus on the theoretical perspective, and we will discuss them in Section [14.4.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0090).

In the remainder of this chapter, we will separately discuss FBO (Section [14.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0015)) and FRL (Section [14.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0045)), including their background, representative existing works, algorithms/frameworks, as well as theoretical and empirical results. Subsequently, in Section [14.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0075), we will briefly review other recent related works on FBO (Section [14.4.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0080)), FRL (Section [14.4.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0085)) and federated bandits (Section [14.4.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0090)). Lastly, we will discuss open problems and potential future directions in the area of federated sequential decision-making (Section [14.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0095)).

## 14.2 Federated Bayesian optimization

In this section, we firstly present some technical background on BO (Section [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020)) and FBO (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)). Next, we give an overview of the representative existing works on FBO [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) (Section [14.2.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0030)), and then discuss their algorithms (Section [14.2.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0035)) as well as their theoretical and empirical results (Section [14.2.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0040)).

### 14.2.1 Background on Bayesian optimization

*Bayesian optimization* (BO) aims to use sequential queries to maximize an objective function *f* : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si1.png), i.e., to find **x**^(\*) ∈ arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]*f*(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si2.png), in which 𝒳 ⊂ ℝ^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si3.png) is a discrete subset of the *d*\-dimensional domain.^([^(23)](#fn23))

A GP 𝒢𝒫(*μ*( ⋅ ), *k*(⋅, ⋅ ))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si13.png) is characterized by its mean function *μ* and kernel function *k*. We assume without loss of generality that *μ*(**x**) = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si14.png) and *k*(**x**, **x**^′) ≤ 1, ∀**x**![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si15.png), **x**^′ ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si16.png), and we mainly focus on the widely used *squared exponential* (SE) kernel here [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075). In iteration *t* + 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si17.png) of BO, given the first *t* observed input–output pairs, the GP posterior is given by 𝒢𝒫(*μ*[*t*]( ⋅ ), *σ*[*t*]²(⋅, ⋅ ))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si18.png) where

*μ*[*t*](**x**) :  = **k**[*t*](**x**)^⊤(**K**[*t*] + *λ***I**)^( − 1)**y**[*t*], *σ*[*t*]²(**x**, **x**^′) :  = *k*(**x**, **x**^′) − **k**[*t*](**x**)^⊤(**K**[*t*] + *λ***I**)^( − 1)**k**[*t*](**x**^′),

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si19.png)(14.1) 

where **k**[*t*](**x**) :  = (*k*(**x**, **x**[*τ*]))[*τ* = 1, …, *t*]^⊤![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si20.png) is a *t*\-dimensional column vector, **y**[*t*] :  = (*y*[*τ*])[*τ* = 1, …, *t*]^⊤![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si21.png) is also a *t*\-dimensional column vector, **K**[*t*] :  = (*k*(**x**[*τ*], **x**[*τ*^′]))[*τ*, *τ*^′ = 1, …, *t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si22.png) is a *t* × *t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si23.png)\-dimensional matrix and *λ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si24.png) is a regularization parameter [\[10\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0050). In iteration *t* + 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si17.png), the GP posterior [(14.1)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq1) is used to calculate an *acquisition function*, which is then maximized to select the next query **x**[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si25.png). For example, the classic *Thompson sampling* (TS) [\[10\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0050) algorithm first samples a function *f*[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si26.png) using the GP posterior [(14.1)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq1) and then uses it as the acquisition function to chooses **x**[*t* + 1] = arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]*f*[*t* + 1](**x**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si27.png). BO algorithms are usually analyzed in terms of *regrets* [\[70\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0350). A hallmark for well-performing BO algorithms is to be asymptotically *no-regret*, which requires the *cumulative regret* $R\_{T}: = \\sum\_{t = 1}^{T}(f(\\mathbf{x}^{\\ast}) - f(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si28.png) to grow sub-linearly so that the simple regret *S*[*T*] :  = min[*t* = 1, …, *T*](*f*(**x**^(\*)) − *f*(**x**[*t*])) ≤ *R*[*T*]/*T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si29.png) goes to 0 asymptotically.

To reduce the computational cost of GP posterior inference [(14.1)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq1), *random Fourier features* (RFFs) [\[59\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0295) is commonly adopted to approximate the kernel function *k* using *M*\-dimensional random features ***ϕ***: *k*(**x**, **x**^′) ≈ **ϕ**(**x**)^⊤**ϕ**(**x**^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si30.png). RFFs offers a high-probability guarantee on the approximation quality, i.e., we have that sup[**x**, **x**^′ ∈ 𝒳]|*k*(**x**, **x**^′) − **ϕ**(**x**)^⊤**ϕ**(**x**^′)| ≤ *ε*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si31.png), in which *ε* = 𝒪(*M*^( − 1/2))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si32.png) [\[59\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0295). Of note, RFFs makes it particularly convenient to approximately sample a function from the GP posterior [(14.1)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq1). Specifically, define **Φ**[*t*] :  = (**ϕ**(**x**[*τ*]))[*τ* ∈ \[*t*\]]^⊤![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si33.png) (i.e., a *t* × *M*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si34.png)\-dimensional matrix), **Σ**[*t*] :  = **Φ**[*t*]^⊤**Φ**[*t*] + *λ***I**![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si35.png), and **ν**[*t*] :  = **Σ**[*t*]^( − 1)**Φ**[*t*]^⊤**y**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si36.png). To sample a function *f̃*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si37.png) from the GP posterior with the approximate kernel *k̃*(**x**, **x**^′) ≈ **ϕ**(**x**)^⊤**ϕ**(**x**^′)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si38.png), we only need to sample an *M*\-dimensional vector

**ω** ∼ 𝒩(**ν**[*t*], *λ***Σ**[*t*]^( − 1))

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si39.png)(14.2) 

and then set *f̃*(**x**) = **ϕ**(**x**)^⊤**ω**![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si40.png), ∀**x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si41.png). Refer to [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) for more details on RFF approximations of GP.

### 14.2.2 Background on federated Bayesian optimization

Here we present the problem setting of *federated BO* (FBO), which follows the works of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) and [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075). FBO involves a central server and *N* agents/clients 𝒜[1], …, 𝒜[*N*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si42.png). Every agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) attempts to maximize its own objective function *f*^(*n*) : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si44.png), i.e., to find **x**[\*]^(*n*) ∈ arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]*f*^(*n*)(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si45.png), by querying **x**[*t*]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si46.png) and observing *y*[*t*]^(*n*), ∀*t* = 1, …, *T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si47.png). As a representative motivating example, *N* mobile phone users (agents) who use DNNs for next-word prediction in a smart keyboard application may wish to collaboratively tune the hyperparameters of their DNNs. In this application, agent (mobile phone user) 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) sequentially queries the hyperparameter configurations **x**[*t*]^(*n*) ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si48.png), ∀*t* = 1, …, *T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si49.png) in order to maximize its validation accuracy denoted by the function *f*^(*n*) : 𝒳 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si44.png). As another example, a hospital can use BO to select the patients to perform a medical test to assess the possibility of readmission [\[81\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0405), and multiple hospitals may wish to collaborate to achieve better patient selection strategies. In this case, the input query **x**[*t*]^(*n*) ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si48.png) selected by hospital 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) in iteration *t* corresponds to the features representing the selected patient, and the corresponding value of the objective function *f*^(*n*)(**x**[*t*]^(*n*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si50.png) represents the test score for the selected patient **x**[*t*]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si46.png).

As a common ground for the collaboration among different agents, we assume that all participating agents share the same set of random features **ϕ**(**x**), ∀**x** ∈ 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si51.png). Similar to BO discussed above, in FBO, every agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) aims to minimize its own cumulative regret, $R\_{T}^{n} \\triangleq \\sum\_{t = 1}^{T}(f^{n}(\\mathbf{x}\_{\\ast}^{n}) - f^{n}(\\mathbf{x}\_{t}^{n}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si52.png). Without loss of generality, when presenting the theoretical results in Section [14.2.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0040), we focus on the perspective of agent 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png). That is, we derive an upper bound on the cumulative regret of agent 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png) denoted as *R*[*T*]¹![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si54.png). We characterize the similarity between agents 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png) and 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) by *d*[*n*] :  = max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]|*f*¹(**x**) − *f*^(*n*)(**x**)|![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si55.png) such that *d*[1] = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si56.png) and a smaller *d*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si57.png) indicates a larger degree of similarity (or equivalently, a smaller degree of heterogeneity) between 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png) and 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png). In the theoretical analysis, we assume that the objective functions of all agents have a bounded norm induced by the *reproducing kernel Hilbert space* (RKHS) associated with the kernel *k*, i.e., ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx001.jpg), ∀*n* ∈ \[*N*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si58.png). This essentially assumes that the objective functions are smooth and is a common assumption in the analysis of BO algorithms [\[10\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0050).

**Core principles and challenges of FBO.** Since FBO needs to follow the core principles of FL, it also inherits a number of important challenges of the federated setting. Firstly, the raw data (e.g., the history of queried hyperparameter configurations and observed validation accuracies during BO) of every agent can never be shared with others. Secondly, the heterogeneity among different agents is another crucial challenge of FBO. For example, since different mobile phone users may have distinct typing habits, the optimal hyperparameters of their DNNs for next-word prediction may vary significantly. In addition, same as FL, there are also other important challenges in FBO, such as communication efficiency (i.e., the total number of exchanged parameters), rigorous privacy guarantees for the agents, decentralized communication, fairness among different agents, etc. As we will discuss in detail in Section [14.2.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0030), the works of [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) have tackled a number of these challenges (e.g., retaining the raw data, agent heterogeneity, communication efficiency and rigorous privacy guarantees), whereas the others are still important open problems for FBO.

### 14.2.3 Overview of representative existing works on FBO

The work of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has introduced the *federated Thompson sampling* (FTS) algorithm, which is the first algorithm for FBO. The FTS algorithm [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has mainly tackled three of the major challenges faced by FBO (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)).

The first challenge results from the requirement to retain (hence not transmit) the raw data, which is a unique challenge faced by FBO yet not FL. Specifically, the information about a BO task is contained in its GP surrogate model (Section [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020)). However, unlike DNNs in standard FL for supervised learning, GPs are *nonparametric* [\[60\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0300). Therefore, a BO task has no parameters (except for the raw data of BO) that can represent the GP surrogate and thus be exchanged among agents, while the raw data of BO should never be transmitted [\[39\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0195). To overcome this challenge, the work of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has exploited RFFs (Section [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020)) to approximate a GP, which naturally yields parameters that contain the information about the approximate GP surrogate and can thus be communicated among the agents without exchanging the raw data. The second challenge concerns the communication efficiency, for which [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has adopted TS as the acquisition function (Section [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020)), which reduces the number of exchanged parameters while maintaining competitive performances. The third challenge is caused by the potential heterogeneity among different agents, which is an important practical consideration in FL since different agents can have highly distinct properties [\[48\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0240). In FBO, heterogeneity arises because different agents may have disparate objective functions. To address this challenge, [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) has derived a theoretical convergence guarantee to ensure that their FTS algorithm is asymptotically no-regret even when all agents have highly different objective functions.

More recently, the work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has extended the FTS algorithm [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) by additionally addressing the challenge of rigorous privacy guarantees (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)) through the classic method of *differential privacy* (DP) [\[24\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0120). Specifically, [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has incorporated the general DP framework adopted by the DP-SGD [\[1\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0005) and DP-FedAvg [\[55\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0275) algorithms into (a modified version of) the FTS algorithm [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075), to protect the *user-level privacy* of the agents in FBO. By achieving a guarantee on the user-level privacy, [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) guarantees that an adversary, even with arbitrary side information, cannot infer whether an agent has participated in FBO, hence assuring every agent that its participation will not reveal its sensitive information. In addition, to compensate for the performance loss due to privacy preservation, [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has proposed the technique of *distributed exploration* (DE) to further improve the practical performance (i.e., utility) of their algorithm. Intuitively, the DE technique is based on the idea of local modeling in GP [\[25\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0125) and is incorporated into the general DP framework in a seamless way thanks to the flexibility of the framework to model multiple parameter vectors [\[53\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0265).

Since the method introduced by [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070), named DP-FTS-DE, is the state-of-the-art algorithm for FBO, we will introduce the details of the DP-FTS-DE algorithm in the next section (Section [14.2.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0035)), and then discuss its theoretical guarantees and empirical performances in Section [14.2.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0040).

### 14.2.4 Algorithms for FBO

For ease of understanding, in this section, we will firstly introduce the DP-FTS algorithm without the DE technique, and then describe how DP-FTS can be modified to incorporate DE to derive the DP-FTS-DE algorithm.

**The DP-FTS algorithm.** [Fig. 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0010)(a) illustrates the DP-FTS algorithm. Every iteration *t* of DP-FTS consists of the following steps:

![Figure 14.1 (a) DP-FTS algorithm without distributed exploration; (b)–(c) replacing steps (3) and (5) in (a) with that in (b) and (c) to derive the DP-FTS-DE algorithm (P = 2 sub-regions).](images/B9780443190377000235/gr001.jpg)

Figure 14.1 (a) DP-FTS algorithm without distributed exploration; (b)–(c) replacing steps (3) and (5) in (a) with that in (b) and (c) to derive the DP-FTS-DE algorithm (*P* = 2 sub-regions).

**Steps** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx002.jpg)**and** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx003.jpg)**by the agents.** Every agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) samples a vector **ω**[*n*, *t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si59.png) following equation [(14.2)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq2) using its own current history of *t* input–output pairs (step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx004.jpg)), and then sends **ω**[*n*, *t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si59.png) to the central server – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx005.jpg).

**Steps** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx006.jpg)**and** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx007.jpg)**by the central server.** Next, the central server processes the *N* received vectors {**ω**[*n*, *t*]}[*n* = 1, …, *N*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si60.png) using a sub-sampled Gaussian mechanism – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx008.jpg)– which consists of four steps: 

1.  **A.**  Selecting a random subset of agents 𝒮[*t*] ⊂ {1, …, *N*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si61.png) by choosing each agent with probability *q*,
2.  **B.**  Clipping the vector **ω**[*n*, *t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si59.png) of every selected agent such that its *L*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si62.png) norm is upper-bounded by *S*, ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx009.jpg),
3.  **C.**  Calculating a weighted average of the clipped vectors with {*φ*[*n*]}[*n* = 1, …, *N*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si63.png), $\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{t} = {(q)}^{- 1}\\sum\_{n \\in \\mathcal{S}\_{t}}\\varphi\_{n}{\\widehat{\\mathbf{\\omega}}}\_{n,t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si64.png), and
4.  **D.**  Adding noise *ϵ* ∼ 𝒩(0, (*z**S**φ*[max]/*q*)²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si65.png) to **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png) where *φ*[max] = max[*n* = 1, …, *N*]*φ*[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si67.png) and *z* is a parameter controlling the privacy-utility trade-off. The final vector **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png) is then broadcast to all agents – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx010.jpg).

**Step** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx011.jpg)**by the agents.** After an agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) receives the vector **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png) from the central server, it can choose its next query **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) (step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx012.jpg)). Choose *δ* ∈ (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si69.png) and define $\\beta\_{t}: = B + \\sigma\\sqrt{2(\\gamma\_{t - 1} + 1 + \\log(4/\\delta)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si70.png), in which *B* is an upper bound on the RKHS norm of the objective functions *f*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si71.png)'s (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)), *σ* is the noise standard deviation (Section [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020)), and *γ*[*t* − 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si72.png) is the maximum information gain about *f*^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si71.png) from any set of *t* − 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si73.png) queries [\[70\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0350).

Then, with probability of *p*[*t* + 1] ∈ (0, 1\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si74.png), 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) chooses **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) using standard TS by sampling a function *f*[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si75.png) from its posterior of 𝒢𝒫(*μ*[*t*]^(*n*)( ⋅ ), *β*[*t* + 1]²*σ*[*t*]^(*n*)(⋅, ⋅ )²)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si76.png) [(14.1)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq1) and then choosing **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*) = arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]*f*[*t* + 1]^(*n*)(**x**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si77.png). Otherwise, with probability of 1 − *p*[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si78.png), 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) chooses **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) using **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png) received from the server, **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*) = arg max[**x** ∈ 𝒳]**ϕ**(**x**)^⊤**ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si79.png). The sequence (*p*[*t*])[*t* ∈ ℤ^+]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si80.png) is chosen as a monotonically increasing sequence such that *p*[*t*] ∈ (0, 1\], ∀*t*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si81.png) and *p*[*t*] → 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si82.png) as *t* → ∞![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si83.png). This ensures that, when 1 − *p*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si84.png) is large, an agent can leverage the information from the other agents (via **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png)) to improve its convergence by accelerating its exploration.

After choosing **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) and observing *y*[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si85.png), the agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) adds (**x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*), *y*[*t* + 1]^(*n*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si86.png) to its history of observations and then samples a new vector **ω**[*n*, *t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si87.png) – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx004.jpg). Next, 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) sends **ω**[*n*, *t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si87.png) to the central server – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx005.jpg)– and the algorithm is repeated.

**The DP-FTS-DE algorithm.** The DP-FTS-DE algorithm is obtained by incorporating the technique of DE into DP-FTS described above.

Specifically, DE divides the entire domain 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si4.png) into *P* ≥ 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si88.png) disjoint sub-regions 𝒳[1], …, 𝒳[*P*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si89.png), and the incorporation of DE requires three major modifications to DP-FTS. Firstly, during the initialization stage, every agent only explores a local sub-region 𝒳[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si90.png) instead of the entire domain 𝒳![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si4.png).

Next, instead of a single vector **ω**[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si66.png), the central server produces and broadcasts *P* vectors {**ω**[*t*]^((*i*))}[*i* = 1, …, *P*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si91.png), each corresponding to a different sub-region 𝒳[*i*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si90.png) and using a different set of weights {*φ*[*n*]^((*i*))}[*n* = 1, …, *N*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si92.png). Interestingly, the different privacy-preserving transformations performed by the central server to produce *P* vectors can be interpreted as a single sub-sampled Gaussian mechanism producing a single joint vector **ω**[*t*]^(joint) ≜ (**ω**[*t*]^((*i*)))[*i* ∈ \[*P*\]]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si93.png) ([Fig. 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0010)(b)).

Then, if agent 𝒜[*n*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si43.png) uses the vector **ω**[*t*]^(joint) = (**ω**[*t*]^((*i*)))[*i* ∈ \[*P*\]]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si94.png) received from the central server to choose the next query **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) (with probability 1 − *p*[*t* + 1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si78.png)), it chooses **x**[*t* + 1]^(*n*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si68.png) by maximizing the reconstructed functions for all sub-regions, as illustrated in [Fig. 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0010)(c). Refer to the work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) for a more complete description of the DP-FTS-DE algorithm.

### 14.2.5 Theoretical and empirical results for FBO

The work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has provided theoretical guarantees on both the privacy and utility of DP-FTS-DE. The privacy guarantee is given by the proposition below:

Proposition 14.1

*There exist constants* *c*[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si95.png) *and* *c*[2]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si96.png) *such that for fixed q and T and any* *ϵ* < *c*[1]*q*²*T*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si97.png)*,* *δ* > 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si98.png)*, DP-FTS-DE is* (*ϵ*, *δ*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si99.png)*\-DP if* $z \\geqslant c\_{2}q\\sqrt{T\\log(1/\\delta)}/\\epsilon$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si100.png)*.*

The following theorem gives a guarantee on the utility/performance of DP-FTS-DE in terms an upper bound on *R*[*T*]¹![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si54.png) (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)), in which all notations have been defined in Sections [14.2.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0020), [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025) and [14.2.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0035):

Theorem 14.1

Informal

*With high probability,*

$R\_{T}^{1} = \\widetilde{\\mathcal{O}}\\left( \\left( B + 1/p\_{1} \\right)\\gamma\_{T}\\sqrt{T}\\ + \\ \\sum\_{t = 1}^{T}\\psi\_{t}\\ + \\ B\\sum\_{t = 1}^{T}\\vartheta\_{t} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si101.png)

*where* $\\psi\_{t}: = \\widetilde{\\mathcal{O}}((1 - p\_{t})P\\varphi\_{\\max}q^{- 1}(\\Delta\_{t} + zS\\sqrt{M}))$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si102.png)*, and* $\\Delta\_{t}: = \\sum\_{n = 1}^{N}\\widetilde{\\mathcal{O}}(\\varepsilon Bt^{2} + B + \\sqrt{M} + d\_{n} + \\sqrt{\\gamma\_{t}})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si103.png)*.* $\\vartheta\_{t}: = (1 - p\_{t})\\sum\_{i = 1}^{P}\\sum\_{n \\in \\mathcal{C}\_{t}}\\varphi\_{n}^{(i)}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si104.png)*,* $\\left. \\mathcal{C}\_{t}: = \\{ n \\in \\lbrack N\\rbrack \\middle| ||\\mathbf{\\omega}\_{n,t}||\_{2} > S/\\sqrt{P}\\} \\right.$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si105.png)*.*

The first interesting insight from [Theorem 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0015) is that agent 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png) is asymptotically *no-regret* even if all other agents are heterogeneous, i.e., all other agents have significantly different objective functions from 𝒜[1]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si53.png). This ensures that DP-FTS-DE is robust against the heterogeneity of agents, which is a significant challenge in FBO (Section [14.2.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0025)).

Moreover, [Theorem 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0015), when interpreted together with [Proposition 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0010), also reveals some interesting theoretical insights regarding the **privacy–utility trade-off**. Firstly, a larger *z* (i.e., larger variance for the added Gaussian noise, Section [14.2.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0035)) improves the privacy guarantee ([Proposition 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0010)), yet results in a worse utility since it leads to a worse regret upper bound (through *ψ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si106.png)). Secondly, a larger *q* (i.e., more selected agents in each iteration, Section [14.2.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0035)) improves the utility since it tightens the regret upper bound (by reducing the value of *ψ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si106.png)) at the expense of a worse privacy guarantee ([Proposition 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0010)). The value of the clipping threshold *S* affects the regret upper bound (hence the utility) through two conflicting effects: a smaller *S* (1) reduces the value of *ψ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si106.png) (hence, the regret bound) but is also likely to enlarge the cardinality of the set 𝒞[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si107.png) which increases the value of *ϑ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si108.png) and hence, the regret bound ([Theorem 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#enun0015)). Refer to Section 4 of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) for a more detailed discussion on the theoretical guarantees of DP-FTS-DE, as well as the associated insights.

**Empirical results.** The work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) has also demonstrated the practical effectiveness of DP-FTS-DE using three real-world experiments on landmine detection, human activity recognition, and EMNIST image classification. Some of the experimental results are displayed in [Fig. 14.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0015), which show that FTS (from the work of [\[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075)) consistently outperforms standard (non-federated) TS whereas FTS-DE (with the DE technique) further improves the performance of FTS. Moreover, [Fig. 14.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0015) shows that with small privacy losses (in the single digit range [\[1\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0005)), DP-FTS-DE achieves a competitive performance (utility) and significantly outperforms standard TS in all settings. Furthermore, the figure also reveals a clear privacy–utility trade-off, i.e., a smaller privacy loss (more to the left) generally results in a worse utility (larger vertical value). Refer to Section 5 of the work of [\[14\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070) for more details on the experimental settings, as well as more experimental results and discussions.

![Figure 14.2 Scatter plots showing the trade-off between privacy loss and performance after 60 iterations for (a) the landmine detection, (b) human activity recognition, and (c) EMNIST experiments. In the above plots, plotted points leaning more towards the left (bottom) correspond to trade-off that favors privacy (utility), respectively.](images/B9780443190377000235/gr002.jpg)

Figure 14.2 Scatter plots showing the trade-off between privacy loss and performance after 60 iterations for (a) the landmine detection, (b) human activity recognition, and (c) EMNIST experiments. In the above plots, plotted points leaning more towards the *left* (*bottom*) correspond to trade-off that favors privacy (utility), respectively.

## 14.3 Federated reinforcement learning

In this section, we will first present some technical background on RL (Section [14.3.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0050)) and FRL (Section [14.3.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0055)). Next, we will briefly overview the representative existing works on FRL (Section [14.3.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0060)) and discuss its framework (Section [14.3.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0065)), as well as its corresponding theoretical and empirical results (Section [14.3.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0070)).

### 14.3.1 Background on reinforcement learning

*Reinforcement learning* (RL) considers a discrete-time Markov decision process (MDP) [\[71\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0355), *M* ≜ {𝒮, 𝒰, 𝒫, ℛ, *γ*, *ρ*}![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si109.png), in which 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si110.png) and 𝒰![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si111.png) represent the state space and action space, respectively, 𝒫(*s*^′|*s*, *a*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si112.png) defines the transition probability from state *s* to *s*^′![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si113.png) after taking action *a*, ℛ(*s*, *a*) : 𝒮 × 𝒰 → ℝ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si114.png) is the reward function for each state–action pair (*s*, *a*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si115.png), *γ* ∈ (0, 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si116.png) is the discount factor, and *ρ* is the initial state distribution. The behavior of an agent is controlled by a policy *π*, where *π*(*a*|*s*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si117.png) defines the probability that the agent chooses action *a* at state *s*. We consider episodic MDPs with trajectory horizon *H*. A trajectory *τ* ≜ {*s*[0], *a*[0], *s*[1], *a*[1], …, *s*[*H* − 1], *a*[*H* − 1]}![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si118.png) is a sequence of state–action pairs traversed by an agent following any stationary policy, where *s*[0] ∼ *ρ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si119.png); $\\mathcal{R}(\\tau) \\triangleq \\sum\_{t = 0}^{H - 1}\\gamma^{t}\\mathcal{R}\\left( s\_{t},a\_{t} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si120.png) gives the discounted cumulative reward along *τ*.

Policy gradient (PG) methods have achieved impressive successes in model-free RL \[[63](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0315),[64](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0320), etc.\]. Compared with deterministic value function-based methods such as Q-learning [\[56\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0280), PG methods are generally more effective in high-dimensional problems and enjoy the flexibility of stochasticity. In PG, we use *π*[**θ**]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si121.png) to denote the policy parameterized by **θ** ∈ ℝ^(*d*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si122.png) (e.g., a neural network), and *p*(*τ*|*π*[**θ**])![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si123.png) to represent the trajectory distribution induced by the policy *π*[**θ**]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si121.png). For brevity, we use ***θ*** to denote the corresponding policy *π*[**θ**]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si121.png). The performance of a policy ***θ*** can be measured by *J*(**θ**) ≜ 𝔼[*τ* ∼ *p*( ⋅ |**θ**)]\[ℛ(*τ*)|*M*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si124.png). Taking the gradient of *J*(**θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si125.png) with respect to ***θ*** gives

∇[**θ**]*J*(**θ**) = ∫[*τ*]ℛ(*τ*)∇[**θ**]*p*(*τ*|**θ**)*d**τ* = 𝔼[*τ* ∼ *p*( ⋅ |**θ**)]\[∇[**θ**]log*p*(*τ*|**θ**)ℛ(*τ*)|*M*\].

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si126.png)(14.3) 

Then, the policy ***θ*** can be optimized using gradient ascent. Since computing [(14.3)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq4) is usually prohibitive, stochastic gradient ascent is typically used. In each iteration, we sample a batch of trajectories {*τ*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si127.png) using the current policy ***θ***, and update the policy by $\\mathbf{\\theta}\\leftarrow\\mathbf{\\theta} + \\eta{\\widehat{\\nabla}}\_{B}J\\left( \\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si128.png), where *η* is the step size and ${\\widehat{\\nabla}}\_{B}J(\\mathbf{\\theta})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si129.png) is an estimate of [(14.3)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq4) using the sampled trajectories {*τ*[*i*]}[*i* = 1]^(*B*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si127.png), ${\\widehat{\\nabla}}\_{B}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{B}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{B}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}\\log p\\left( \\tau\_{i}|\\mathbf{\\theta} \\right)\\mathcal{R}\\left( \\tau\_{i} \\right)$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si130.png). The commonly used policy gradient estimator, namely GPOMDP [\[6\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0030), can be expressed as

${\\widehat{\\nabla}}\_{B}J(\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\frac{1}{B}\\sum\\limits\_{i = 1}^{B}g(\\tau\_{i}|\\mathbf{\\theta}),g(\\tau\_{i}|\\mathbf{\\theta}) = \\sum\\limits\_{h = 0}^{H - 1}\\left\\lbrack \\sum\\limits\_{t = 0}^{h}\\nabla\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}\\log\\pi\_{\\mathbf{\\theta}}\\left( a\_{t}|s\_{t} \\right) \\right\\rbrack\\left( \\gamma^{h}r(s\_{h},a\_{h}) - C\_{b\_{h}} \\right),$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si131.png)(14.4) 

in which *τ*[*i*] = {*s*[0]^(*i*), *a*[0]^(*i*), *s*[1]^(*i*), *a*[1]^(*i*), …, *s*[*H* − 1]^(*i*), *a*[*H* − 1]^(*i*)}![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si132.png) and *g*(*τ*[*i*]|**θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si133.png) is an *unbiased* estimation of ∇[**θ**]log *p*(*τ*[*i*]|**θ**)ℛ(*τ*[*i*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si134.png) [\[58](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0290),[77\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0385).

To improve the sample efficiency of the estimation of [(14.4)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq5), *stochastic variance-reduced gradient* (SVRG) [\[4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0020),[34](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0170),[61](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0305),[75\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0375) has recently been adopted to reduce the variance of policy gradient estimators. The work of [\[58\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0290) has adapted the theoretical analysis of SVRG to PG to introduce the *stochastic variance-reduced policy gradient* (SVRPG) algorithm. More recently, [\[77\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0385) has refined the analysis of SVRPG [\[58\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0290) and shown that SVRPG enjoys a sample complexity of *O*(1/*ϵ*^(5/3))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si135.png).

### 14.3.2 Background on federated reinforcement learning

It is well established that RL systems suffer from poor sample efficiency in real-world applications [\[23](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0115),[42\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0210), which has motivated the development of *federated RL* (FRL) [\[86\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0430). Here, we present the problem statement of FRL following the work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130). In FRL, *K* distributed agents/computing nodes 𝒜^((1)), …, 𝒜^((*K*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si136.png) are operating in separate copies of the same underlying MDP with random initial state distributions *ρ*^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si137.png)'s. Each agent independently runs an RL algorithm by interacting with its environment. Like FBO, FRL involves a central server which is assumed to be trustworthy and governs the federation process. The objective/incentive for agents to participate in the federation is to obtain a well-performing policy **θ**^(\*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si138.png) with *fewer* agent-environment interactions compared to independent learning on their own. As a representative motivating example, *K* hospitals, each of which only possesses a limited number of admission records, who apply RL algorithms to provide clinical decision support may wish to collaboratively discover better treatment protocols for the same disease. To improve the sample efficiency of this application, in every iteration, each agent (hospital) 𝒜^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si139.png) interacts with its environment following a parameterized policy (clinical trial protocols) **θ**^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si140.png) and then shares some information with the trustworthy server (e.g., government), who aggregates all received information and then broadcasts it back to all agents to improve their subsequent decision making.

FRL assumes that all participating RL agents share the same sets of states 𝒮![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si110.png) and actions 𝒰![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si111.png) as a common ground for collaboration. In addition, an FRL system is concerned with only a single task (e.g., treatment for a single disease), and hence the underlying MDP *M* (i.e., the transition probability 𝒫![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si142.png) and reward function ℛ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si143.png)) is assumed to be the same for all agents. Similar to RL discussed above, every agent 𝒜^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si139.png) in FRL aims to maximize the objective function *J*^((*k*)) ≜ 𝔼[*τ* ∼ *p*( ⋅ |**θ**^((*k*)))]\[ℛ(*τ*)|*M*\]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si144.png) with *fewer* interactions with the environment compared with independent learning. That is, to reach a certain performance threshold, the required total number of trajectories |*τ*^((*k*))|![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si145.png) of agent-environment interactions of agent 𝒜^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si139.png) should be smaller than that of independent learning on its own. In other words, the agent aims to improve its sample efficiency by joining the federation. To ensure that FRL leads to a speedup in sample efficiency with a larger number of agents, [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has presented a convergence guarantee for their proposed federated policy gradient framework and derived an upper bound on the average number of trajectories required by each agent for the policy to reach an *ϵ*\-stationary performance point (Section [14.3.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0070)). In their theoretical analysis, the objective function *J*(**θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si125.png) is assumed to be *L*\-smooth, which is a commonly adopted assumption in non-convex optimization [\[4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0020),[61\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0305) and recent convergence results of policy gradient [\[58](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0290),[77\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0385). Furthermore, the initial states of the agents are assumed to be uniformly distributed, i.e., the *ρ*^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si137.png)'s are uniform distributions.

**Core principles and challenges of FRL.** In addition to the fundamental challenge of retaining the raw data (i.e., the trajectories of agent–environment interactions *τ*^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si146.png) shall never be shared), FRL is faced with a few other critical challenges. Firstly, with *N* agents independently interacting with their own copy of the environment, does FRL theoretically guarantee the convergence and proportionally improved sampled efficiency thanks to the federation? Unlike FL where the training data can be collected offline, FRL requires every agent to sample trajectories online by interacting with the environment, which can be slow and expensive. Therefore, theoretical guarantees on the convergence and sample efficiency speedup provide assurance and incentives for practical applications. Secondly, FRL systems need to account for fault tolerance, which is a critical challenge in practical decision-making applications since distributed systems are likely to fail periodically. Being fault-tolerant allows the FRL system to continue operating properly without interruption when one or more of its agents fail. Furthermore, the heterogeneity among different agents (e.g., the difference in their initial state distributions, computational budgets, etc.) is another crucial challenge for FRL. For example, since different hospitals may administer patients from distinct geographic locations, their initial state distributions may vary significantly. Similarly, hospitals may possess different computational budgets and hence can adopt disparate policy parameterization schemes and optimization methods. Moreover, FRL is also faced with other challenges which plague FL in general, such as rigorous privacy guarantees, decentralized communication, fairness, etc. The representative work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130), which we will discuss in Section [14.3.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0060), has tackled a number of these challenges (e.g., retaining the raw data, guaranteed convergence and proportional sample efficiency speedup, and fault tolerance), whereas the others remain important open problems for FRL.

### 14.3.3 Overview of representative existing works on FRL

Firstly introduced by [\[86\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0430), FRL has been applied to a number of practical applications \[[50](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0250),[51](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0255),[57](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0285), etc.\]. The first general-purpose framework for FRL is the *federated policy gradient with Byzantine resilience* (FedPG-BR) framework introduced by [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130). The FedPG-BR framework [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has mainly addressed three of the aforementioned challenges faced by FRL (Section [14.3.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0055)). For brevity, we defer the details of the FedPG-BR algorithm to Section [14.3.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0065), followed by discussions on its theoretical guarantees and empirical performances in Section [14.3.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0070).

The first challenge addressed by [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) is regarding the theoretical guarantees on the convergence and sample efficiency improvements. To this end, [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has adopted the *stochastically controlled stochastic gradient* (SCSG) algorithm [\[41\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0205), which is a variant of SVRG (Section [14.3.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0050)), in the federated policy gradient framework, which provides a refined control over the variance of the gradient estimation. Their theoretical analysis has shown that their proposed framework is guaranteed to converge and enjoys a proportional sample efficiency speedup with respect to the number of agents. The second challenge results from the fact that distributed systems are vulnerable to random failures or adversarial attacks coming from the distributed agents, which may slow down or completely disrupt the convergence of the FRL systems. These random failures and adversarial attacks are modeled as *Byzantine faults*, which is the most stringent fault formalism in distributed computing [\[7](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0035),[52\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0260). Byzantine faults consider a distributed computing system with up to half of the computing nodes being random failures or adversarial attackers. They are hard to detect when the raw data of the agents is not accessible to the server, which makes them a considerable practical challenge in FL [\[79\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0395). To address this challenge, [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has designed a gradient-based Byzantine filter on top of their proposed federated policy gradient framework, in order to remove those gradients that are likely sent by Byzantine agents with high probability. This has enabled the algorithm of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) to be tolerant to Byzantine faults when less than half of the agents are Byzantine agents.

### 14.3.4 Frameworks and algorithms for FRL

In this section, we will describe the details of the FedPG-BR framework [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130), which consists of the *federated policy gradient* (FedPG) algorithm and the *Byzantine resilience* (BR) filter.

**The FedPG algorithm**. [Fig. 14.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0020)(a) illustrates the FedPG algorithm. Every iteration *t* of FedPG includes the following steps:

![Figure 14.3 Workflows of (a) the federated policy gradient algorithm (without fault tolerance) and (b) the federated policy gradient algorithm with Byzantine resilience filter (i.e., the FedPG-BR framework); and (c) visualizing diagram of the concentration bound constructed by the BR filter.](images/B9780443190377000235/gr003.jpg)

Figure 14.3 Workflows of (a) the federated policy gradient algorithm (without fault tolerance) and (b) the federated policy gradient algorithm with Byzantine resilience filter (i.e., the FedPG-BR framework); and (c) visualizing diagram of the concentration bound constructed by the BR filter.

**Step** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx002.jpg)**by the central server.** FedPG starts with a randomly initialized parameter ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{0}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si147.png) at the server. At the beginning of the *t*th iteration, the server keeps a snapshot of its parameter from the previous iteration (i.e., $\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{0}^{t}\\leftarrow{\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{t - 1}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si148.png)) and broadcasts this parameter to all agents.

**Step** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx003.jpg)and ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx013.jpg)Every agent 𝒜^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si139.png) samples *B*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si149.png) trajectories {*τ*[*t*, *i*]^((*k*))}[*i* = 1]^(*B*[*t*])![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si150.png) using the policy **θ**[0]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si151.png), computes a gradient estimate $\\mu\_{t}^{(k)} \\triangleq 1/B\_{t}\\sum\_{i = 1}^{B\_{t}}g(\\tau\_{t,i}^{(k)}|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{0}^{t})$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si152.png) following equation [(14.4)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq5) – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx005.jpg)– and sends *μ*[*t*]^((*k*))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si153.png) back to the server – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx008.jpg).

**Steps** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx007.jpg)**and** ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx014.jpg)The server computes the batch gradient *μ*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si154.png) by averaging the received gradient estimates – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx010.jpg)– and updates the policy parameters **θ**[0]^(*t*)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si151.png) via the following semi-stochastic gradient – step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx012.jpg)– according to SCSG optimization [\[41\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0205), $v\_{n}^{t} \\triangleq \\frac{1}{b\_{t}}\\sum\_{j = 1}^{b\_{t}}\\left\\lbrack g(\\tau\_{n,j}^{t}|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{n}^{t}) - g(\\tau\_{n,j}^{t}|\\mathbf{\\theta}\_{0}^{t}) \\right\\rbrack + \\mu\_{t}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si155.png), in which *b*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si156.png) trajectories are sampled *independently* by the server on a separate copy of the MDP *M* and the number *N*[*t*]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si157.png) of optimization steps is sampled from a geometric distribution with the parameter $\\frac{B\_{t}}{B\_{t} + b\_{t}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si158.png). The server then stores a new snapshot of the updated parameter, and the algorithm is repeated.

**The BR filter**. [Fig. 14.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0020)(b) demonstrates the complete FedPG-BR framework, which is obtained by incorporating the Byzantine resilience filter ([Fig. 14.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0020)(c)) into the FedPG algorithm described above. After receiving all the gradients, the server applies the BR filter (step ![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/fx010.jpg)), which is designed based on the following assumptions: firstly, at any given iteration *t*, there are less than *K*/2![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si159.png) Byzantine agents; secondly, the gradient estimates sent by the good (non-Byzantine) agents should concentrate in a region containing the true analytical gradient defined in [(14.3)](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#deq4). In particular, the work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has assumed that there exists a constant *σ* such that ∥*g*(*τ*|**θ**) − ∇*J*(**θ**)∥ ≤ *σ*![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si160.png) for any *τ* ∼ *p*( ⋅ |**θ**)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si161.png) and any policy *π*[**θ**]![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si121.png), which implies that the discrepancy between any two gradient estimates is at most 2*σ* in the Euclidean space. Therefore, the BR filter computes the pair-wise Euclidean distances of all gradients^([^(24)](#fn24))

### 14.3.5 Theoretical and empirical results for FRL

The work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has provided theoretical guarantees on the convergence of FedPG-BR:

Theorem 14.2

Informal

*The output of FedPG-BR,* $\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si167.png)*, satisfies*

$\\mathbb{E}\\lbrack{\\|\\nabla J({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{a})\\|}^{2}\\rbrack\\ \\leqslant \\ \\frac{2\\Psi\\left\\lbrack J({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}^{\\ast}) - J({\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}\_{0}) \\right\\rbrack}{TB^{1/3}}\\ + \\ \\frac{8\\sigma^{2}}{{(1 - \\alpha)}^{2}KB}\\ + \\ \\frac{96\\alpha^{2}\\sigma^{2}V}{{(1 - \\alpha)}^{2}B},$

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si168.png)

*where α denotes the ratio of Byzantine agents such that* 0 ≤ *α* < 0.5![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si169.png) *and* ${\\widetilde{\\mathbf{\\theta}}}^{\\ast}$![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si170.png) *is a global maximizer of J;* Ψ *is a smoothness constant and V is another constant used to refine the concentration bound of the BR filter. For brevity, readers are referred to* [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) *for the detailed definitions of* Ψ *and V.*

This theorem leads to many interesting insights, such as the sample complexity (of each agent in FedPG-BR) to reach an *ϵ*\-stationary point which is summarized in [Table 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#t0010). The table reveals that the sample complexity of FedPG-BR in the single-agent setting matches that of SVRPG derived by [\[77\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0385). In addition, when *K* > 1![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si171.png), *α* = 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si172.png), [Table 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#t0010) shows that the total number of trajectories required by each agent is upper-bounded by *O*(1/(*ϵ*^(5/3)*K*^(2/3)))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si173.png). This result gives us the theoretical grounds to encourage more agents to participate in the federation since the number of trajectories each agent needs to sample decays at a rate of *O*(1/*K*^(2/3))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si174.png). Furthermore, for a more realistic system where an *α*\-fraction (*α* > 0)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si175.png) of the agents are Byzantine agents, the results in [Table 14.1](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#t0010) assure us that the total number of trajectories required by each agent will be increased by *only an additive term of* *O*(*α*^(4/3)/*ϵ*^(5/3))![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si176.png), the impact of which vanishes when *α* → 0![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si177.png).

Table 14.1

![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/t0010.png)

**Empirial results.** The work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has also demonstrated the practical effectiveness of FedPG-BR using standard RL benchmarks including CartPole balancing [\[5\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0025), LunarLander, and the 3D continuous locomotion control task of HalfCheetah [\[21\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0105). The experimental results shown in [Fig. 14.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0025) suggest that the performance of FedPG-BR is comparable to SVRPG in the single-agent training setting (*K* = 1)![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si182.png), and is improved significantly with the federation of *K* = 3![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si183.png) and *K* = 10![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si184.png) agents. This corroborates our theoretical insights implying that the sample efficiency of FedPG-BR is guaranteed to improve proportionally with the number of agents *K*. Furthermore, [Fig. 14.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0030) shows another experiment on the HalfCheetah task with *K* = 10![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si184.png) agents, among which 3 are Byzantine agents.

![Figure 14.4 Performance of FedPG-BR in ideal systems with α = 0 for the three tasks.](images/B9780443190377000235/gr004.jpg)

Figure 14.4 Performance of FedPG-BR in ideal systems with *α* = 0 for the three tasks.

![Figure 14.5 Performance of FedPG-BR in practical systems with α > 0 for HalfCheetah. Each subplot corresponds to a different type of Byzantine failure exercised by the 3 Byzantine agents.](images/B9780443190377000235/gr005.jpg)

[Figure 14.5](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#cf0865) Performance of FedPG-BR in practical systems with *α* > 0 for HalfCheetah. Each subplot corresponds to a different type of Byzantine failure exercised by the 3 Byzantine agents.

The Byzantine agents are simulated using the following three schemes: *random noise (RN)*: each Byzantine agent sends a random vector to the server; (b) *random action (RA)*: every Byzantine agent ignores the policy from the server and takes actions randomly, which is used to simulate random system failures (e.g., hardware failures); and (c) *sign flipping (SF)*: each Byzantine agent computes the correct gradient but sends the scaled negative gradient, which is used to simulate adversarial attacks aiming to manipulate the direction of policy updates at the server. The three subplots show that the existence of only 3 Byzantine agents causes the performance of federated policy gradient systems (GPOMDP and SVRPG) to be worse than that in the single-agent setting. In contrast, our FedPG-BR is robust against all three types of Byzantine failures. That is, FedPG-BR (*K* = 10![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si184.png), *B* = 3![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si185.png)) with 3 Byzantine agents still significantly outperforms the single-agent setting, and more importantly, *performs comparably to FedPG-BR (**K* = 10![Image](images/B9780443190377000235/si184.png)*) with 10 good agents* (shown in the rightmost subplot in [Fig. 14.4](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#f0025)). These results demonstrate that even in practical systems with random failures or adversarial attacks, FedPG-BR is still able to deliver superior performances, providing an assurance on the reliability of the framework to promote its practical deployment and significantly improving the practicality of FRL. 

## 14.4 Related work

### 14.4.1 Federated Bayesian optimization

To the best of our knowledge, the works of [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) (Section [14.2.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0030)) are the only works on FBO to date. However, a number of previous works on BO have considered similar settings to the FBO setting, which we review here.

The work of [\[68\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0340) has also considered collaborative BO involving multiple agents. However, since their method is not designed for the FBO setting, they did not address the important challenges faced by FBO (e.g., they have assumed that all agents share the same objective function and hence did not consider the issue of heterogeneity), but have instead focused on the issue of fairness among the agents [\[68\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0340). Furthermore, a number of works such as [\[13](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0065),[65\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0325) have studied BO in the multi-agent setting from the perspective of *game theory*. FBO also shares similarities with *batch/parallel BO*, which has seen a large body of works in recent years [\[12](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0060),[18](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0090),[20](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0100),[27](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0135),[30](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0150),[37](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0185),[72\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0360). However, batch BO has many important differences with FBO. For example, batch BO aims to maximize a single objective function whereas FBO allows different agents to have different objective functions, and the sharing of the raw observations in batch BO is not prohibited. Another popular line of works on BO which is also related to FBO is *multi-fidelity BO* [\[17](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0085),[36](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0180),[83](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0415),[84\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0420). This is because, from the point of view of an agent in FBO, the information from the other agents (received via the central server) can be considered as low-fidelity information.

### 14.4.2 Federated reinforcement learning

FRL was initially introduced by [\[86\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0430) which studied how to collaboratively learn two Q-networks when one of the two agents does not receive rewards from the MDP. Thereafter, FRL has been applied to a number of practical applications, such as autonomous driving [\[50](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0250),[62\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0310), fast personalization [\[57\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0285), robots navigation [\[51\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0255), traffic sign control [\[80\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0400), and resource management in networking [\[82\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0410). Despite their promising applications, these works were not equipped with theoretical guarantees and hence did not provide theoretical understandings to the important challenges faced by FRL we have discussed in Section [14.3.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0055).

The work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has presented the first federated policy gradient framework in the FRL setting which guarantees a proportional sample efficiency improvement with respect to the number of agents and achieves robustness against faulty (Byzantine) agents, hence tackling the challenges of theoretical guarantees and fault tolerance (Section [14.3.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0055)). Regarding the challenge of the heterogeneity among different agents, the work of [\[76\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0380) has defined the heterogeneity in FRL as the data heterogeneity resulting from the difference in the initial state distributions and environment dynamics among different agents. As a result, [\[76\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0380) has proposed an FRL framework to tackle such heterogeneity in FRL by penalizing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (i.e., encouraging the similarity) between the local policies and the global policy.

FRL also bears close similarity to another line of works on distributed and parallel RL [\[2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0010),8,[31](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0155),3[8\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0040), because some of the challenges faced by FRL (Section [14.3.2](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0055)), such as theoretical guarantees and fault tolerance, are also important considerations for these works. However, there are also substantial differences between these settings and FRL, since FRL also poses some unique challenges such as the requirement to retain the raw data. One representative work in distributed and parallel RL is [\[9\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0045), which has proposed the Byzantine-robust mean estimation technique for both online and offline distributed RL.

### 14.4.3 Federated bandits

*Multi-armed bandits* is another popular sequential decision-making problem [\[40\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0200) with important applications such as recommender systems. A growing number of recent works have introduced federated versions of classic bandit algorithms.

Some works have focused on federated *K*\-armed bandits where the number *K* of arms is finite and the arms are not associated with feature vectors. The works of [\[46\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0230) and [\[47\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0235) have focused on federated *K*\-armed bandits with rigorous privacy guarantees, and have considered both centralized and decentralized communication. The work of [\[66\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0330) has proposed a setting for federated *K*\-armed bandits in which the goal is to minimize the regrets of a global bandit model, which has the same set of arms as the agents. The reward of every arm for the global bandit model is the average of the rewards of the corresponding arm from all agents. The more recent work of [\[67\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0335) has extended [\[66\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0330) to incorporate personalization such that every agent attempts to maximize a weighted combination between the global and its local rewards. After that, subsequent works have focused on other aspects of federated *K*\-armed bandits, such as decentralized communication via the gossiping algorithm [\[85\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0425), the security of federated *K*\-armed bandits through cryptographic techniques [\[11\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0055), uncoordinated exploration [\[78\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0390), and robustness against Byzantine attacks [\[19\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0095).

In addition, a number of works have considered the problem of federated linear contextual bandits. The work of [\[73\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0365) has proposed a distributed linear contextual bandit algorithm that allows every agent to use the observations from the other agents without requiring them to share their raw data. Subsequently, the work of [\[22\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0110) has extended the method from [\[73\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0365) to incorporate differential privacy and decentralized communication. The work of [\[32\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0160) has considered a setting of federated linear contextual bandits where every agent is associated with a unique context vector. The works of [\[29](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0145),[43\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0215) have both focused on extending the method from [\[73\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0365) in order to allow asynchronous communication. The work of [\[33\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0165) has focused on the robustness of federated linear contextual bandits against Byzantine attacks. A few recent works have relaxed the assumption of a linear reward function adopted by linear contextual bandits to consider non-linear reward functions. The work of [\[16\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0080) has introduced the first *federated neural bandit* algorithm which is able to exploit neural networks to learn the reward function. Moreover, the works of [\[49\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0245) and [\[69\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0345) have, respectively, extended *χ*\-armed bandits and combinatorial bandits to the federated setting.

## 14.5 Open problems and future directions

As we have discussed in this chapter, extending classic sequential decision-making algorithms (e.g., BO and RL) into the federated setting holds enormous potential, yet is also faced with immense challenges. Some of these challenges have been addressed by recent works, such as the works of [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) for FBO (Section [14.2.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0030)) and the work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) for FRL (Section [14.3.3](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#s0060)). However, some other challenges remain to be tackled and are hence still important open problems.

For FBO, note that the theoretical analyses from the works of [\[14](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0070),[15\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0075) have focused on the robustness against agent heterogeneity. Therefore, it remains an open problem to theoretically show the benefit of the federation when the agents are in fact homogeneous (or when the degree of heterogeneity is low), i.e., to show that a larger number of agents lead to better regret upper bounds. Furthermore, extending FBO algorithms to cater to other important considerations of the federated setting also represents important future directions in order to make FBO algorithms more practical. For example, allowing decentralized and asynchronous communication in FBO is an important challenge and a meaningful extension, since it allows FBO to work under more flexible communication protocols. Ensuring fairness among different agents in FBO is another significant open problem, since societal issues such as fairness have been receiving growing concerns and are hence crucial considerations for the real-world deployment of FBO algorithms. To this end, the method from [\[68\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0340), which has studied fairness in collaborative BO among multiple agents, may provide interesting inspirations.

For FRL, although the work of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has managed to avoid the transmission of the raw data (i.e., RL trajectories) of the agents, they have not provided a rigorous privacy guarantee. Therefore, it is an intriguing future direction to equip FRL systems with rigorous privacy guarantees (e.g., via differential privacy) in order to protect the privacy of the participating agents in a principled way. In addition, the theoretical analysis of [\[26\]](#Chp014_257-279_B9780443190377000235.xhtml#br0130) has focused on improving the sample efficiency for homogeneous agents. Therefore, a natural future extension is to derive theoretical guarantees when the agents are in fact heterogeneous and to study situations under which the benefits of the federation can be guaranteed in the presence of heterogeneity. Furthermore, designing decentralized FRL systems and achieving fairness among different FRL agents also represent promising future directions for FRL.
